In the instant case, since the impugned notice under section 148 is issued on 28-7-2022, it is barred by limitation and therefore bad in law, liable to be quashed resulting into making the impugned re-assessment proceedings and reassessment order also bad in law, liable to be quashed. [Para 5.5]

■ On this submission made by the assessee, the revenue observed that case of the assessee does not fall within the judgments of Ashish Agarwal (supra) and Rajeev Bansal (supra) since the time line prescribed in these judgments of two weeks for filing of reply by the assessee to the show cause notices issued under section 148A(b) has not been complied with. According to the revenue, assessee filed a letter of adjournment dated 9-6-2022 which was accepted by the Assessing Officer by granting extension of time limit up to 24-6-2022. Assessee filed its reply on 28-6-2022 which is beyond the period of two weeks as prescribed by the Apex Court and therefore according to the revenue, assessee cannot claim relief provided in the judgment of Rajeev Bansal (supra). [Para 6]

■

According to revenue, reply by the assessee is not within the permissible period of two weeks as provided by the aforesaid judgments and therefore provisions of section 148A(d) which provides for a period of 30 days is to be taken into account for passing the order under section 148A(d) and issuing notice under section 148. Thus, applying the provisions of section 148A(d), the Assessing Officer had time till 30-7-2022 and therefore impugned notice dated 28-7-2022 is well within the time allowed as per the provisions of section 148A read with section 149. [Para 6.1]

■

In the light of these arguments, first specific observations made by the Apex Court in its judgment of Rajeev Bansal (supra) was to be noted wherein it explained the purpose of creating the legal fiction, supplementing the existing legal framework of procedure of reassessment and exercising its discretionary jurisdiction under article 142 of the Constitution of India. It states that purpose is to strike a balance between the rights of the assessees and the revenue, to avoid any further appeals by the revenue on the same issue and to give effect to the legislative scheme of reassessment under the new regime by modifying the procedure of reassessment with a remedy, grounded in equitable standards. [Para 7]

■

The Apex Court while propounding its judgment in Rajeev Bansal (supra) elaborately analysed and discussed about the legal fiction it created, its consequences, incidental or inevitable corollaries, inhibition faced by the Assessing Officers from performing their responsibility under section 148A. The Court also noted that ''…The effect of creating the legal fiction is that this Court has to imagine as real all the consequences and incidents that will inevitably flow from the fiction.'' Thus, to give logical effect to the legal fiction and modified procedure, it brought out the concept of ''exclusion period'' and ''surviving time limit''. [Para 7.1]

■

At this juncture, it is important to note that legal framework of procedure for reassessment under Act created by the Supreme Court through its judgments in Ashish Agarwal and Rajeev Bansal (supra), is a fiction by deeming the notice issued under section 148 of the old regime as a show cause notice under section 148A(b) of the new regime on which modified procedure is to be applied to give it a logical effect. Hence, the modified procedure is to be applied strictly for the purpose to be achieved, as already stated and extracted above. It is a well-established principle of interpretation that the courts must give full effect to a legal fiction by having due regard to the purpose for which the legal fiction is created. A legal fiction is created for a definite purpose and it should be limited to the purpose for which it is enacted or applied. [Para 7.2]

■

On the contention of revenue that since assessee did not furnish its response within the stipulated time of two weeks to the show cause notice issued by the Assessing Officer on 26-5-2022, it is out of the purview of the judgments of Rajeev Bansal (supra), one cannot ascribe to the same since Apex Court very categorically laid down the law on pan India applicability from its judgment in Ashish Agarwal and Rajeev Bansal (supra) to include ninety thousand reassessment notices issued under the old regime during the period from 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021. Instant case of the assessee unhesitatingly falls well within the purview of both the judgments. [Para 8]

■

, the surviving time left was only two days for issuing a notice under the new regime under section 148 after completion of the procedure laid down under section 148A(b) to 148(d).

■

Ergo, the Assessing Officer was required to issue notice under section 148 of the new regime within the time surviving under the Income-tax Act read with TOLA and any notices issued beyond the surviving period was declared to be time barred by the Supreme Court. [Para 10] ■

Here in this case no reply was filed by the assessee in response to show-cause notice under section 148A(b) which was fixed by the Assessing Officer to be furnished on or before 7-6-2022. Once the time limit for reply to the show-cause notice had expired then the Supreme Court have categorically held that the Assessing Officer had to complete the procedure laid down under section 148A(c), passed under section 148(d) and issued notice under section 148 within the surviving time limit which was originally available to the Assessing Officer. Here in this case the surviving time was only two days which is to be calculated from 28-6-2021 to 30-6-2021 and therefore, only two days shall be available to the Assessing Officer from the time granted to the assessee to give reply to the notice. Here in this case also the clock started ticking for the Assessing Officer on the expiry of permissible limit i.e. that is between 7-6-2022 to 9-6-2022. Thus, only 2 days were the surviving time available to the Assessing Officer and he was required to pass order under section 148A(d) and issue notice under section 148 on or before 9-6-2022. Accordingly, the impugned notice under section 148 dated 28-7-2022 does not fit in the 'surviving time limit' as laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Rajeev Bansal. Accordingly, it is held that notice under section 148 dated 28-7-2022 is barred by limitation, therefore, the entire notice is quashed. Consequently, the entire reassessment proceedings as well as reassessment order is non-est. Thus, on this ground, entire reassessment order is quashed and consequently, the revenue's appeal is dismissed. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: Section  149,  read with sections  147,  148  and  271, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and section 3 of Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 -  Income escaping assessment  -  Time-limit for issuance of notice  (Scope of provision) - Assessment year  2014-15  - Whether reassessment notice dated 29-7-2022 for assessment year 2014-15 was barred by limitation under section 149 read with TOLA, since time-limit, even if reckoned as six years, expired on 31-3-2021 and, after applying TOLA, stood extended only up to 30-6-2021 - Held, yes - Whether consequently, resultant assessment under section 147 and penalty proceedings under section 271 were also liable to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 13 to 16] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of steel products, filed its return of income for relevant assessment year 2014-15 on 31-7-2014.

■

The Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 148 on 29-7-2022, followed by assessment order dated 30-5-2023 along with consequential demand and penalty proceedings.

■

In instant writ petition, the assessee contended that re-opening of assessment was barred by limitation under section 149 as amended by Finance Act, 2021 and, even after applying relaxations under TOLA.

HELD: ■

The Finance Act, 2021 substituted the entire scheme of reassessment under sections 147 to 151 with effect from 1-4-2021. [Para 7]

■

Prior to the coming into force of Finance Act, 2021 initiation of reassessment proceedings was governed by the provisions of sections 147 to 151. [Para 8]

■

Despite the substituted sections 147 to 151, by the Finance Act, 2021 which came into force on 1-4-2021 many reassessment notices under section 148 were issued to the assessees after coming into force of Finance Act, 2021 i.e. after 1-4-2021, which were assailed before different High Courts on different grounds. Different High Courts quashed the reassessment notices under section 148. Union of India challenged the judgments passed by different High Courts setting aside reassessment notices under section 148, which were issued after 1-4-2021 i.e. after coming into force of Finance Act, 2021 before the Supreme Court in Union of India and Others v. Ashish Aggarwal [2022] 140 taxmann.com 1 (SC). The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeals filed by the Union of India. [Para 9]

■

Therefore, in above referred to judgment of the Supreme Court in case of Union of India and Others v. Ashish Aggarwal (supra), the Supreme Court held that the impugned notices under section 148 issued to the respective assessees which were issued under unamended section 148 and were subject matter of writ petitions before the various respective High Courts shall be deemed to have been issued under section 148A as substituted by the Finance Act, 2021 and be construed or treated to be show cause notices in terms of section 148A(b). It was further held that the Assessing Officer shall, within 30 days from the date of passing of the judgment i.e. 4-5-2022, provide to the respective assessees information and material relied upon by the revenue, so that the assessees can reply to the show cause notices within 2 weeks thereafter. It was further held by the Supreme Court that the requirement of conducting any enquiry, if required, with the prior approval of specified authority under section 148A(a) is dispensed with as one time measure viz-a-viz those notices which were issued under section 148 of the unamended act from 1-4-2021 (Finance Act, 2021) till date i.e. 4-5-2022 (Decision in Ashish Aggarwal). Further that the Assessing Officer shall thereafter pass orders in terms of section 148A(d) in respect of each of the concerned assessees and thereafter, after following the procedure as required under section 148A may issue notice(s) under section 148 (as substituted). [Para 10]

■

of the President on 28-9-1996. The Act omitted the words ‘not being less than 30 days’ from section 148 with effect from 1-4-1989. When notice dated 1-10-1993 and the fresh notice dated 28-3-1996 were issued, the Finance Act (No. 2) was not in force. The assessing authority had, therefore, rightly applied the then existing law. [Para. 5] Section 148 provides for initiation of assessment proceedings which starts with the issue of notice. Initiation of proceedings by the assessing authority on 1-10-1993 was not valid and consequently it was dropped. Fresh notice was, therefore, issued under section 148 in conformity with the time prescribed under section 148. When the Finance Act was passed a legally valid proceeding was in existence. Notice prescribed under section 148 for the purpose of initiating reassessment proceedings is a condition precedent to the validity of an assessment made. The assessing authority was only curing the defect of not following the time-limit when it was pointed out by the assessee and, therefore, notice was issued strictly on the basis of the then existing statutory provision. The mere fact that the time-limit prescribed under section 148(1) was taken away would not make an invalid notice valid so as to render the assessment order dated 26-3-1997 invalid in terms of section 153(2). The assessee could not be allowed to raise such a plea after having persuaded the assessing authority to withdraw notice dated 1-10-1993 pointing out that it was not in conformity with the statutory provision. The assessee could not be allowed to take advantage of the plea of limitation in terms of section 153(2) contending that the notice dated 1-10-1993 was valid due to the omission of time-limit vide the Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 with effect from 1-4-1989. [Para 6]

On the strength of notice dated 28-3-1996, the return of income was filed and such return could not be ignored. [Para 7]

The mere fact that the time-limit has been taken away with effect from 1-4-1989 would not vitiate the proceedings validly initiated applying the then existing law. The object and purpose of the amendment is only to take away the time-limit for giving time for the assessee to file a return which the Legislature thought unnecessary. If the Legislature wanted to undo all that was done by the assessing authority applying the then existing law, it should have been specifically provided in the statute. In the absence of specific provision in the Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 invalidating those proceedings initiated by the ITO, it could not be said that the action taken by the ITO applying the then existing law was invalid. Once the notice issued under section 148 on 28-3-1996 was upheld the plea of limitation raised by the assessee under section 153(2) had to be rejected. The Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 as amended would not validate an invalid notice which was issued under section 148(1). [Para 9]

HEADNOTE: Section  149,  read with section  148,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and section 3 of the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation of Certain Provisions) Ordinance, 2020 -  Income escaping assessment  -  Time limit for issuance of notice  (TOLA Scheme) - Assessment year  2013-14  - Assessing Officer issued notice under section 148 (old regime) on 28-6-2021 during extended time period as per TOLA - Pursuant to directions of Supreme Court, Assessing Officer provided information on 28-5-2022 and assessee filed reply on 11-6-2022 - Thereafter, order under section 148A(d) as well as notice under amended section 148 was issued on 27-7-2022 - Whether considering date of earlier notice under section 148 read with TOLA up to 30-06-2021, last permissible date for issuance of reassessment notice under section 148 would be 18-06-2022 - Held, yes - Whether thus, impugned notice dated 27-07-2022 issued under section 148 having been issued beyond surviving time would be invalid notice - Held, yes [Paras 7 and 10] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The Assessing Officer issued notice dated 28-6-2021 under section 148 (old regime) for the assessment year 2013-14 during the extended time period as per Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation of Certain Provisions) Ordinance, 2020 (TOLA).

■

In view of the decision of Supreme Court in case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC), the aforesaid notice was to be treated as notice under section 148A(b) which has come into statute with effect from 1-4-2021.

■

The Assessing Officer had provided information pursuant to the directions issued by the Supreme Court in case of Ashish Agarwal (supra) on 28-5-2022 and allowed assessee 15 days time i.e. 11-6-2022 to file reply. The assessee filed reply on 11-6-2022.

■

Thereafter, the order under section 148A(d) as well as notice under section 148 was issued on 27-7-2022.

■

On writ petition, the assessee challenged the validity of the notice on ground that same was invalid and time barred :

HELD: ■

In the facts of the case, the Assessing Officer has provided information pursuant to the directions issued by the Apex Court in case of Union of India and others v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC)on 28-5-2022 and therefore, considering 15 days’ time to file reply by the assessee, the due date would be 11-6-2022. The petitioner filed reply on 11-6-2022. The order under section 148A(d) as well as notice under section 148 was issued on 27-7-2022. However, considering the period of limitation from the date of issuance of notice under section 148 read with TOLA upto 30-6-2021, the limitation for issuance of notice under section 148 applying the decision of the Apex Court in case of Ashish Agarwal (supra) as well as Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC), would be 18-6-2022. [Para 7]

■

In view of above, the impugned notice dated 27-7-2022 issued under section 148 would be invalid notice as the said notice is issued after 18-6-2022 as per the decision of the Apex Court in case of Ashish Agarwal (supra). Therefore, the impugned notice having been issued beyond the ‘surviving time’ would be invalid notice as held by the Apex Court in case of Rajeev Bansal (supra). [Para 9]

■

In view of foregoing reasons, impugned notice dated 27-7-2022 is hereby quashed and set aside and all consequential proceedings are also quashed and set aside. [Para 10]

Laws (Relaxation and Amendment Of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020, (TOLA, 2020) various notifications were issued from time-to-time extending the time line prescribed under section 149 for issuance of reassessment notice under section 148. The latest amongst the notification was the Notification No. 38 of 2021 dated 27-4-2021 whereby the time limit was extended till 30-6-2021. [Para 5.3] Notwithstanding that the amended sections 147 to 151 came into force with effect from 1-4-2021 under the Finance Act, 2021, the Income-tax Department issued innumerable notices during the period from 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021 for reopening the assessment under the provisions of the old regime. The Department for issuing such notices, relied on explanation to the aforesaid notification whereby the time limit was extended as stated above. These notices became subject matter of challenge before different High Courts. The Notifications issued for extension of time were prayed to be declared ultra vires. [Para 5.3.1]

The Supreme Court had an occasion to consider such cases arrived before it from different High Courts, wherein the notices issued during the period from 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021 in relation to the earlier assessment years were challenged. The provisions post-Finance Act, 2021, under the new regime had come into force. This controversy before the Apex Court culminated into decision in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 83/444 ITR 1 (SC). [Para 5.4]

The Supreme Court striking balance between the notices issued by the Department under the old regime and the provisions brought into force under the new regime held that all notices issued under section 148 between 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021 shall be deemed to have been issued under section 148A to be treated as show-cause notices under section 148A(b). The Supreme Court observed that new provisions substituted by the Finance Act, 2021 were remedial and benevolent in nature, came to be inserted with an object to protect the right and interests of the assessee as well to sub-serve the public interest. [Para 5.4.1]

While allowing various appeals in part, the Supreme Court in Ashish Agarwal (supra), modified the judgment and orders passed by the different High Courts from where the matters had travelled by issuing directions. [Para 5.4.2]

Thus, one of the direction and clarification in Ashish Agarwal (supra), is that all the defences that were available to the assessee under section 149 under the Finance Act, 2021 and in law whatever rights are available to the Assessing Officer under the Finance Act, 2021 are kept open to be continued to be available. [Para 5.4.4]

In simple words, the notice which could not have been issued in the old regime period due to becoming time barred as per then operating provision, would also not be permissible to be issued post-1-4-2021. [Para 5.4.6]

As already noticed, section 149 as it stood immediately before commencement of Finance Act, 2021, that is before 1-4-2021 in the old regime inter alia provided for time limit for notice. It stated inter alia that no notice under section 148 shall be issued for the relevant assessment year, as per clause (b), if four years, but not more than six years, have elapsed from the end of the relevant assessment year unless the income chargeable to tax, which has escaped assessment, amounts to or is likely to amount to one lakh rupees or more for that year. [Para 5.4.7]

In other words, limitation of six years from the end of relevant assessment year operated as timeline in the old regime for issuance of notice under section 148 beyond which period, it was not competent for the Assessing Officer to issue notice for reassessment. This embargo is made to continue in the new regime also. [Para 5.4.8]

Now the reopening notices which related to the period prior to 1-4-2021, but issued between 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021 came to be challenged before the Division Bench of this Court in Keenara Industries (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2023] 147 taxmann.com 585/453 ITR 51, by placing reliance on directions in Ashish Agarwal (supra), and thus by contending that since they were issued after six years from the end of the relevant assessment year, they were barred and were without jurisdiction.[Para 5.5]

In Keenara Industries (P.) Ltd. (supra), the Division Bench noticed the crux of the contents on that count raised by the petitioners. [Para 5.6]

HEADNOTE: Section 148, read with section 149, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Reassessment - Issue of notice - Assessment year 1966-67 - Whether, where reassessment notice under section 148 was issued within period of limitation prescribed under section 149 but was served on assessee after expiry of period of limitation, initiation of reassessment proceedings by ITO was barred by limitation and, therefore, invalid - Held, no

FACT: For the assessment year 1966-67, assessment was reopened under section 148 by the ITO in the case of assessee, an individual. In the reassessment, the ITO included certain amount as unexplained investment in the income assessed earlier in the original assessment. The notice under section 148 was issued on 29-3-1975 but it was served on the assessee on 7-4-1975. On appeal before the AAC, the assessee contended that the notice having been served after the expiry of period of limitation, the reassessment proceedings were barred by limitation. The AAC rejected the assessee's contention. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the notice under section 148 was not only to be issued but served within the period of limitation as laid down in section 149, and since the notice was served on the assessee after the expiry of 8 years, the order of reassessment was set aside.

On reference:

HELD: In R.K. Upadhyaya v. Shanabhai P. Patel [1987] 166 ITR 163, the Supreme Court categorically held that a clear distinction has been made out under the Income-tax Act, 1961 between 'issue of notice' and 'service of notice'. Section 149 prescribes the period of limitation. It prohibits issue of notice under section 148 after the expiry of the prescribed period of limitation. Section 148(1) provides for service of notice as condition precedent to making of the order of assessment. Once a notice is issued within the period of limitation, jurisdiction becomes vested with the ITO to proceed to reassess. The requirement of issue of notice is satisfied when a notice is actually issued Section 148(1) deals with making of the reassessment and mandates that reassessment shall not be made until there has been service. Under the Act, service is not a condition precedent to conferment of jurisdiction on the ITO to deal with the matter but it is a condition precedent to the making of the order of assessment.

In the Instant case, notice under section 148 was issued by the ITO within the period of limitation prescribed under section 149. There was also no controversy about the fact that the order of reassessment was made only after service of notice on the assessee. The ratio of the decision in R.K. Upadhyaya's case (supra ) of the Supreme Court squarely applied to the present case. The ITO having issued the notice under section 148 within limitation, the order of reassessment was valid. Therefore, the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the initiation of reassessment proceedings by the ITO was barred by limitation and in setting aside the orders of the AAC and the ITO.

Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020, (TOLA, 2020) various notifications were issued from time-to-time extending the time line prescribed under section 149 for issuance of reassessment notice under section 148. The latest amongst the notification was the Notification No. 38 of 2021 dated 27-4-2021 whereby the time limit was extended till 30-6-2021.[Para 5.3] Notwithstanding that the amended sections 147 to 151 came into force with effect from 1-4-2021 under the Finance Act, 2021, the Income-tax Department issued innumerable notices during the period from 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021 for reopening the assessment under the provisions of the old regime. The Department for issuing such notices, relied on explanation to the aforesaid notification whereby the time limit was extended as stated above. These notices became subject matter of challenge before different High Courts. The Notifications issued for extension of time were prayed to be declared ultra vires.[Para 5.3.1]

The Supreme Court had an occasion to consider such cases arrived before it from different High Courts, wherein the notices issued during the period from 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021 in relation to the earlier assessment years were challenged. The provisions post-Finance Act, 2021, under the new regime had come into force. This controversy before the Apex Court culminated into decision in Union Of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 [Para 5.4]

The Supreme Court striking balance between the notices issued by the Department under the old regime and the provisions brought into force under the new regime held that all notices issued under section 148 between 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021 shall be deemed to have been issued under section 148A to be treated as show-cause notices under section 148A(b). The Supreme Court observed that new provisions substituted by the Finance Act, 2021 were remedial and benevolent in nature, came to be inserted with an object to protect the right and interests of the assessee as well to sub-serve the public interest.[Para 5.4.1]

While allowing various appeals in part, the Supreme Court in Ashish Agarwal (supra), modified the judgment and orders passed by the different High Courts from where the matters had travelled by issuing directions.[Para 5.4.2]

Thus, one of the direction and clarification in Ashish Agarwal (supra), is that all the defences that were available to the asessee under section 149 under the Finance Act, 2021 and in law whatever rights are available to the Assessing Officer under the Finance Act, 2021 are kept open to be continued to be available.[Para 5.4.4]

In simple words, the notice which could not have been issued in the old regime period due to becoming time barred as per then operating provision, would also not be permissible to be issued post-1-4-2021.[Para 5.4.6]

As already noticed, section 149 as it stood immediately before commencement of Finance Act, 2021, that is before 1-4-2021 in the old regime inter alia provided for time limit for notice. It stated inter alia that no notice under section 148 shall be issued for the relevant assessment year, as per clause (b), if four years, but not more than six years, have elapsed from the end of the relevant assessment year unless the income chargeable to tax, which has escaped assessment, amounts to or is likely to amount to one lakh rupees or more for that year.[Para 5.4.7]

In other words, limitation of six years from the end of relevant assessment year operated as timeline in the old regime for issuance of notice under section 148 beyond which period, it was not competent for the Assessing Officer to issue notice for reassessment. This embargo is made to continue in the new regime also.[Para 5.4.8]

Now the reopening notices which related to the period prior to 1-4-2021, but issued between 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021 came to be challenged before the Division Bench of this Court in Keenara Industries (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2023] 147 taxmann.com 585/453 ITR 51 by placing reliance on directions in Ashish Agarwal (supra), and thus by contending that since they were issued after six years from the end of the relevant assessment year, they were barred and were without jurisdiction.[Para 5.5]

In Keenara Industries (P.) Ltd. (supra), the Division Bench noticed the crux of the contents on that count raised by the petitioners.[Para 5.6]

The new scheme of reassessment as contained in Finance Act, 2021 when is noticed the time limit for issuance of notice for reassessment appear to have been changed. HEADNOTE: Section  149,  read with sections  68  and  148, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Income escaping assessment  -  Time limit for issuance of notice  (Illustration) - Assessment year  2015-16  - Assessing Officer issued notice under section 148 after 31-3-2021 on pretext that due to operation of TOLA, time limit for issuance of notice would be extended upto 30-6-2021 - Thereafter, considering decision of Supreme Court in case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183, notice issued under section 148 between 1-4-2021 and 30-6-2021 for assessment year 2015-16 was deemed to be a notice under section 148A(b) which had came into operation with effect from 01.04.2021 - Thereafter, as per direction issued by Supreme Court in case of Ashish Agarwal (supra), department issued notices under section 148 between July, 2022 and August, 2022 after following procedure of inviting reply and passing order under section 148A(d) - Assessee challenged such notices issued by Assessing Officer for assessment year 2015-16 - Whether impugned notice issued under section 148 for assessment year 2015-16 was to be quashed and set aside as same was issued during extended period from 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021 under TOLA - Held, yes [Para 17] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The Assessing Officer issued notice under section 148 for assessment year 2015-16 on 4-6-2021. Thereafter, considering the decision of Supreme Court in case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183, notice issued under section 148 between 1-4-2021 and 30-6-2021 for assessment year 2015-16 was deemed to be notice under section 148A(b) which had come into operation with effect from 1-4-2021.

■

Thereafter as per the direction issued by the Supreme Court in case of Ashish Agarwal (supra), department had issued the notices under section 148 between the month of July, 2022 and August, 2022 after following the procedure of inviting reply and passing order under section 148A(d).

■

The petitioners challenged such notices issued by the Assessing Officer for assessment year 2015-16 pursuant to the order of Supreme Court in case of Ashish Agarwal (supra).

HELD: ■

The Supreme Court in case of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46decided the issues raised with regard to delay as per the provisions of section 149 which has come into operation after 1-4-2021 as well as validity of sanction granted under section 155. [Para 8]

■

During the course of hearing before the Supreme Court, revenue conceded to the effect that so far as assessment year 2015-16 is concerned, revenue could not have issued the notices under section 3(1) of TOLA as considering the time period as prescribed under section 149 with effect from 1-4-2021, three years would be over on 31-3-2019 which is prior to coming into force of TOLA and six years would be completed on 31-3-2022 which is after operation of TOLA. In such circumstances, notices for assessment year 2015-16 are held to be invalid by Supreme Court in case of Rajeev Bansal (supra). [Para 9]

■

The Supreme Court in case of Deepak Steel and Power Ltd. v. CBDT reported in [2025] 174 taxmann.com 144 (SC) after recording the concession of the revenue and in view of the concession given before the Supreme Court by revenue as recorded in case of Rajeev Bansal (supra), has quashed and set aside the notice issued after 31-3-2021 under TOLA for assessment year 2015-16. [Para 10]

■

In view of above, the impugned notice issued under section 148 for assessment year 2015-16 is held to be invalid as same was issued during the extended period from 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021 under TOLA. [Para 17]

It thus included the factor of prescription of time limit-the limitation.[Para 5.2.4] It may be mentioned that in wake of spread of pandemic of Covid-19 around March 2020 and onwards, leading to the lockdown resulting into societal affairs coming to a standstill, Ordinance No. 2/20 dated 31-3-2020 was promulgated by the Central Government, titled as the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Ordinance, 2020, which became the Act subsequently, to be applied retrospectively from 31-3-2020, being the date of ordinance. It stated inter alia that no notice under section 148 shall be issued for the relevant assessment year, as per clause (b), if four years, but not more than six years, have elapsed from the end of the relevant assessment year unless the income chargeable to tax, which has escaped assessment, amounts to or is likely to amount to one lakh rupees or more for that year.[Para 5.4.7]

In other words, limitation of six years from the end of relevant assessment year operated as timeline in the old regime for issuance of notice under section 148 beyond which period, it was not competent for the Assessing Officer to issue notice for reassessment. This embargo is made to continue in the new regime also.[Para 5.4.8]

Now the reopening notices which related to the period prior to 1-4-2021, but issued between 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021 came to be challenged by contending that since they were issued after six years from the end of the relevant assessment year, they were barred and were without jurisdiction. [Para 5.5]

In other words, it was the contention that as per the provisions of section 149 in the old regime, a notice under section 148 could have been issued to the assessee, if four years had elapsed from the end of the assessment year, but not six years. HEADNOTE: Section  149,  read with sections  148  and  148A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  282,  read with sections  280  and  281  of the Income-tax Act, 2025, and section  3(1)  of the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 – Income escaping assessment – Time limit for issuance of notice (TOLA) - Assessment year  2015-2016  - Whether in view of decision of Supreme Court in case of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC), notice issued under Section 148, for Assessment year  2015-2016, is invalid as same was issued during extended period from 01-04-2021 to 30-06-2021 under TOLA - Held, yes [Paras 7, 8 and 15] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee–petitioner challenged reassessment proceedings for A.Y. 2015-16, asserting that a notice under Section 148 was issued on 30.06.2021 during the TOLA-extended period after 01.04.2021, under the erstwhile regime and without complying with Section 148A(b).

■

Following the Supreme Court’s decision in Ashish Agarwal, the department treated notices issued between 01.04.2021 and 30.06.2021 as deemed notices under Section 148A(b), invited replies, passed orders under Section 148A(d), and in the petitioner’s case issued a fresh notice under Section 148 dated 26.05.2022.

■

On writ petition before the High Court.

HELD: ■

The matter was carried to the Apex Court wherein the Apex Court in case of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC) decided the issues raised with regard to delay as per the provisions of Section 149 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, which has come into operation after 01.04.2021 as well as validity of sanction granted under Section 155. During the course of hearing before the Apex Court, Revenue conceded to the effect that so far as Assessment Year 2015-2016 is concerned, Revenue could not have issued the notices under Section 3(1) of the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 as considering the time period as prescribed under Section 149, with effect from 01.04.2021, three years would be over on 31.03.2019 which is prior to coming into force of TOLA and six years would be completed on 31.03.2022 which is after operation of TOLA. In such circumstances, notices for Assessment Year 2015-2016 are held to be invalid by the Apex Court in case of Rajeev Bansal ([2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC)). [Para 7]

■

The Apex Court followed the decision of Rajeev Bansal (supra) in case of Deepak Steel and Power Ltd. v. CBDT [2025] 174 taxmann.com 144/305 Taxman 169/476 ITR 369 (SC) and after recording the concession of the learned advocate for the department and in view of the concession given before the Apex Court by learned advocate appearing for the Revenue as recorded in para 19(f) of the judgment in case of Rajeev Bansal (supra), has quashed and set aside the notice issued after 31.03.2021 under TOLA for A.Y. 2015-16. [Para 8]

■

In view of above, for the foregoing reasons, the writ petition is allowed. The impugned notice issued under Section 148, for Assessment Year 2015-2016, is held to be invalid as same was issued during the extended period from 01.04.2021 to 30.06.2021 under TOLA. [Para 15]

■

Accordingly, the present petition is disposed of. Rule is made absolute to the above extent. No order as to costs. [Para 16]
