In reassessment on 23-10-1975, the ITO determined the total assessable income at Rs.1,93,822 after adding Rs. 1,24,610 on account of unexplained cash credits and Rs. 32,621 as interest, on the basis of material available in duplicate account books. On appeal, the ACC quashed the assessment holding that the notice under section 148 was invalid as it was issued without prior permission of the Commissioner as required under section 151(2). After obtaining approval of the CBDT under section 151(1), the ITO issued on 13-03-1978 a fresh notice under section 148. In writ petition, the assessee challenged the legality of the notice and assessment by contending: (i) that, since the escaped income was estimated at Rs. 45,000 in the assessment order dated 19-03-1974, the present case was governed by section 149(1)(a )(i) so that the notice issued on 3-03-1978 was beyond time; (ii) that the income assessed on 23-10-1975 had been deliberately inflated so as to confer jurisdiction on the ITO even beyond the period of eight years; (iii) that once the ITO had estimated the concealed income at Rs. 45,000, he could not have arrived at a different figure exceeding Rs. 50,000 as per order dated 23-10-1975, and as such, the ITO had no jurisdiction to reassess only on the ground of taking a different view of the matter; (iv) that the ITO's belief that an income of Rs. 1,57,083 had escaped assessment on account of assessee's default was illusory or dishonest; and (v) that the notice under section 148 was issued (a) without concluding that the duplicate books belonged to the assessee, and (b) without prior approval of CBDT under section 151(1). The ITO was, therefore, not competent to issue the notice since it was the IAC alone who could issue the same, because of section 125A(1).

■

The assessees, engaged in the business of construction, development of township, housing projects and other realty projects, had shown work-in-progress and customer advances received/taken over from group entities/partners.

■

The Assessing Officer initiated reassessment proceedings under sections 147/148 pursuant to directions issued by Commissioner (Appeals) under section 150(2) while deciding appeals for subsequent assessment year and made additions under sections 68 and 69C towards unexplained expenditure, work-in-progress and customer advances.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that directions issued under section 150(2), forming basis for issuance of notice under section 148, had already been expunged by Tribunal in assessee-group cases and, further, notice issued under section 148 was barred by limitation prescribed under section 149. Accordingly, reassessment proceedings and consequential assessment orders were quashed as void ab initio.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

For the assessment years 1963-64, 1964-65 and 1965-66, the ITO completed the original assessments prior to 1-04-1968. The ITO thereafter reopened these assessments under section 148. On 20-04-1968, the assessee filed the returns for the said years disclosing the income as per original assessment. The ITO, however, completed the reassessments by making the aggregate addition of Rs. 19,400 in three assessment years and initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c). Both the AAC and the Tribunal upheld the ITO's order. The IAC imposed the total penalty of Rs. 20,200 for these years under section 271(1)( c), as amended by the Finance Act, 1968 with effect from 1-04-1968. On appeal,

the Tribunal reduced the quantum of penalty holding that (i ) the returns at the original stage were filed prior to 1-04-1968 and the default was attributable only to these returns; and (ii ) the said amended law would not, therefore, apply since the amendment will not have any restrospective operation.

On reference, however, the assessee contended that the concealment of income in the returns filed by the assessee in response to notices under section 148 would relate back to the assessment year for which the return was filed.

The notice under section 148 for all the relevant assessment years was served upon the assessee on 7-12-1964. After having repeatedly sought time for filing the returns of income for those three years in compliance with the said notice, the assessee filed the returns on 15-3-1965. However, period to that, the assessee had filed the writ petition challenging the validity of the said notice and the High Court had stayed all further proceedings for all the assessment years on 12-3-1965. The said stay order was vacated on 25-7-1975, when the writ petition was dismissed. Thereafter, the assessee was allowed eight weeks time in two instalments to enable it to file an appeal from the said order of the High Court dismissing the writ petition. The assessment proceedings were thus stayed during the period from 12-3-1965 to 18-9-1975. The High Court again stayed the proceedings on 29-9-1975, in the appeal filed against the order dismissing the writ petition and disposed of the appeal with the direction that the respondents would, however, be at liberty to proceed with the reassessment but the final orders, if any, and notice of demand would not be served on the petitioner pending disposal of this application. The said order of the High Court stood vacated on 12-7-1979, when the appeal was dismissed and, thereafter, the assessee filed a special leave petition before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held that all further proceedings in respect of the three purported draft orders of assessment should go on but final orders should not be passed. That order of the Supreme Court stood vacated on 4-8-1980, when the special leave petition was dismissed. During the assessment proceedings, the draft assessment order was forwarded by the ITO to the IAC on 17-9-1979, the copy of which was received by the assessee on 19-9-1979, and the directions of the IAC after hearing the objections of the assessee were communicated to the ITO on 14-10-1980. The ITO completed the assessments for all the three years on 15-10-1980. The assessee contended that all the assessment orders were bad since they were barred by limitation. However, this contention was rejected.

On reference:

The assessee claimed the benefit under section 80HHC for the assessment year 1995-96. However, in the subsequent assessment year, the assessee claimed the bad debt on the ground that, in the earlier year, the export was not materialized and therefore, the proceedings under section 154 were initiated by the revenue.

During the pendency of the said proceedings, the revenue also initiated the proceedings under section 147/148 and reopened the assessment for assessment year 1996-97. The Assessing Officer passed the Assessment Order.

The assessment proceedings reopened under section 148 were quashed and set aside by Tribunal by holding that as the proceedings under section 154 initiated against the assessee were pending, no re-opening proceedings under section 147/148 could have been issued/initiated.

On appeal, the High Court, by the impugned judgment and order, allowed the said appeal preferred by the revenue and remanded the matter to the Tribunal by observing that as the proceedings under section 154 were beyond the period of limitation prescribed under section 154(7), the said notice was invalid and therefore, the reopening proceedings under section 147/148 would be maintainable.

The review application preferred by the assessee had been dismissed.

On appeal before the Supreme Court:

The original assessment for the relevant assessment year was made in 1952. In 1966, the ITO issued notice under section 148 to reopen the assessment for the relevant assessment year that was originally completed in 1952. The assessee filed a return and revised return under protest claiming that no income had escaped assessment and that the notice under section 148 was illegal and barred by time. On writ, the Single Judge held that according to the affidavit filed by the department, the escaped income in the case was more than Rs. 1 lakh and since in respect of the escaped income of over a lakh of rupees the Act of 1922 did not prescribe any period of limitation, the reopening was not barred under the old Act. The Single Judge, however, held that since the department had not disclosed material on the basis of which the ITO could form the belief that there had been omission or failure on part of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts, it could not be said that the belief was held by the ITO in good faith.

On revenue’s appeal:

The assessee filed a return of income and an assessment was made under section 143(1). Thereafter, the Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 148. In compliance with the said notice, the assessee filed a return of income claiming the status of a registered firm. The assessment was completed in the status of an AOP. Thereafter, the Assessing Officer passed an order under section 154 stating that there had been a mistake in mentioning the status of the assessee in the assessment order and that in place of (AOP), unregistered firm be read throughout the assessment order. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the appeal on the ground that an assessment on an AOP could not be made without issuing a notice to the AOPs and, therefore, set aside the assessment directing that the assessment be made again, in accordance with law. On cross appeal, the Tribunal dismissed the revenue’s appeal and allowed the appeal by the assessee quashing the assessment on the ground that in the circumstances of the case, no assessment could be made on the AOPs. During the time taken in the said proceedings, the assessment proceedings that had commenced on the basis of the notice under section 148 became barred by time. Consequently, the Assessing Officer issued a fresh notice under section 148.

On writ, the assessee challenged the said subsequent notice under section 148 on the grounds that (1) the original notice under section 148 having not been quashed and a return in pursuance of that notice having been filed, the department had no jurisdiction to issue subsequent notice, on the same facts for the same assessment year, during the pendency of the earlier proceedings and that (2) the notice having been issued with a view to circumvent the period of limitation, was, therefore, illegal, arbitrary and without jurisdiction. The Department filed a counter affidavit stating that a search was conducted at the business premises of the assessee as well as the residential premises of the partners and some incriminating material was found and seized, and the Commissioner directed that the assessment for the year under consideration might be reopened under section 147 and in compliance of those directions, the case was reopened with the approval of the Commissioner and the impugned notice under section 148 was issued to assess the income which was surrendered by the assessee itself during the course of search and seizure operation. In the rejoinder affidavit, the assessee stated that from the counter affidavit itself it was apparent that the assessment was reopened under the dictates of the Commissioner while section 147 provided that an assessment could be reopened only if the Assessing Officer had reason to believe that the income had escaped assessment.

■

The Assessing Officer issued notice under section 148 for assessment year 2015-16 after 31-3-2021 on the pretext that due to operation of TLA, time limit for issuance of notice would be extended upto 30-6-2021.

■

Thereafter, considering the decision of Supreme Court in case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64 (SC)/[2022] 286 Taxman 183 (SC)/[2022] 444 ITR 1 (SC) notice issued under section 148 between 1-4-2021 and 30-6-2021 for assessment year 2015-16 was deemed to be notice under section 148A(b) which had come into operation with effect from 1-4-2021.

■

Thereafter as per the direction issued by the Supreme Court in case of Ashish Agarwal (supra) department had issued the notices under section 148 between the month of July, 2022 and August, 2022 after following the procedure of inviting reply and passing order under section 148A(d).

■

The petitioners challenged such notices issued by the Assessing Officer for assessment year 2015-16 pursuant to the order of Supreme Court in case of Ashish Agarwal (supra).

For relevant year, the assessee-company filed its return declaring certain taxable income. The Assessing Officer completed assessment under section 143(3).

Subsequently, Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 148 seeking to reopen the assessment. The reason assigned by Assessing Officer was that assessee had claimed 100 per cent deduction on temporary site accommodation whereas assessee was entitled only to 7.5 per cent depreciation on temporary accommodation and 15 per cent depreciation on shuttering and mining equipments. Thus, assessee had claimed excessive depreciation and debited the same to its profit and loss account.

The Tribunal took a view that firstly reassessment notice was issued after four years from the relevant assessment year, therefore, it was barred by limitation and, secondly, that there was no failure on the part of assessee and entire things were disclosed by it while claiming 100 per cent depreciation and nothing was detected subsequently by Assessing Officer, hence, section 148 was not at all attracted in the case in hand. The Tribunal thus set aside reassessment proceedings.

On appeal:

A search and seizure operation under section 132(1) was carried out at premises of assessee.

During assessment proceedings, the assessee explained each and every seized document and after considering same the Assessing Officer passed assessment order making certain addition in the income of the assessee.

Thereafter assessment for the assessment year 1992-93 was made on 31-3-1995. While disposing of the appeal filed for the assessment year 1992-93, the appellate authority made observation that for the assessment year 1991-92 the Assessing Officer should have worked out the exact quantum of credit balance and the bogus purchases which had been introduced in the books of account of the assessee by means of blank bill books found during search.

Pursuant to the said observations, the Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 148 for assessment year 1991-92 on 10-4-2001 and a reassessment order was passed making certain additions on account of bogus purchase.

On appeal, the appellate authority held that the Assessing Officer was justified in reopening the assessment.

However, on second appeal, the Tribunal held that as there was no failure on the part of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for making an assessment, notice issued under section 148 beyond a period of four years from the end of the assessment year in question was invalid.

On appeal to the High Court the revenue contended that the Tribunal erred in observing that the issue of notice under section 148 was beyond the period of four years from the end of relevant assessment year without appreciating that the notice under section 148 was issued by the Assessing Officer in consequence to the directions given by the Commissioner (Appeals) and as per the provisions of section 150(1).

The petitioner held 50 per cent equity share capital in company, S and 25 per cent in company P&A. During relevant assessment year, P&A received advance on behalf of company, S from a partnership firm in which company S and petitioner held 100 per cent interest.

The Assessing Officer held that the amount advanced by partnership firm constituted dividend in hands of company P&A under section 2(22)(e).

On appeal, the Commissioner and the Tribunal held that the addition under section 2(22)(e ) could be made only in the hands of the shareholder and since P&A was not the shareholder of company, S said additions were to be deleted.

On revenue's appeal, the Delhi High Court also held that advances could not be treated as deemed dividend in the hands of the company P&A which was not a shareholder of company S.

Thereafter, relying on the observations of the Delhi High Court, the Assessing Officer at Delhi issued a notice dated 22-3-2013 under section 148 to petitioner. Later, on petitioner's contention that he was assessed to tax at Mumbai, case of assessee was transferred to Mumbai.

The Assessing Officer at Mumbai issued notice dated 10-1-2014 under section 148 stating that he had reasons to believe that income chargeable to tax for assessment year 2006-07 had escaped assessment within the meaning of section 147 read with section 150 and said notice was issued as per section 150 in view of the decision of the Delhi High Court.

In instant writ, petitioner had challenged the impugned notice on ground that same was barred by limitation since it was issued beyond a period of six years from the end of the relevant assessment year, which is the time limit within which the impugned notice was required to be issued as per section 149(1)(b).

The assessee was a proprietory concern engaged in the fabrication and the sale of tins. The assessee also derived the share income from certain firms. The assessee in response to notice under section 148 dated 1-10-1993 and notice under section 142(1) dated 13-3-1995 filed the return of income for the assessment year 1992-93 on 27-3-1995 declaring a total income of Rs. 1,36,970 and agricultural income of Rs. 1,50,000. During the course of assessment proceedings, the assessee pointed out that the notice under section 148 had not given more than 30 days’ time for filing the return of income and, therefore, the assessment would be treated as null and void. Thereafter, the Assessing Officer cancelled the said notice. The assessing authority had reason to believe that the income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment and, consequently, the assessment proceedings were again initiated by issuing a fresh notice under section 148 dated 28-3-1996. Consequently, the reassessment order was passed on 26-3-1997.

The assessee’s case was that the notice dated 1-10-1993 issued under section 148 was legal and valid in the light of the amendment in section 148 by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1996 and it was also contended by the assessee that the assessment order dated 26-3-1997 was barred by limitation in terms of section 153(2).

On appeal :

■

The Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 148 dated 22.06.2021 for the assessment year 2014-15, during the extended time period available under the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation of Certain Provisions) Ordinance, 2020 (TOLA).

■

Pursuant to the decision of the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC), such notice was to be treated as one issued under section 148A(b).

■

In terms of the directions in Ashish Agarwal (supra), the Assessing Officer provided the requisite information to the assessee on 24.05.2022, granting 15 days’ time to file a reply, i.e., up to 07.06.2022.

■

The assessee did not file any reply.

■

Subsequently, the Assessing Officer passed an order under section 148A(d) and issued a fresh notice under section 148 on 28.07.2022.

■

In the instant writ petition the assessee contended that as per the ratio laid down by the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC), such reassessment notices were to be treated as valid only if issued within the “surviving time” available under the Act read with TOLA, which, for AY 2014-15, expired on 16.06.2022. Since the impugned notice dated 28.07.2022 was issued beyond the said surviving period, the same was contended to be invalid and time-barred.

The Assessing Officer reopened assessment for relevant assessment year by issue of notice under section 148 on 24-2-1993 on ground that assessee had created provision towards unexpired warranty out of sale proceeds; thereby had suppressed sale to that extent; and, thus, income had escaped assessment. However, no action was taken by him. Again he issued notice under section 148 on 13-10-1995 for the same reason and on the basis of said notice, completed assessment under section 143(3)/147 on 31-3-1997. On appeal, the assessee contended that reassessment made was barred by limitation, as the Assessing Officer did not make any assessment with reference to notice issued on 24-2-1993. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that section 153(2) did not bar an assessment on the basis of second notice, as the second initiation was an independent action and, therefore, the Assessing Officer was justified in reopening of assessment by issue of notice dated 13-10-1995.

On second appeal, the assessee submitted that the Assessing Officer had not taken any action on notice issued on 24-2-1993. Therefore, he was satisfied that there was no escapement of income, and issue of second notice was a change of opinion. The assessee further submitted that when notice under section 148 dated 13-10-1995 was issued, no fresh information came into possession of the Assessing Officer and, therefore, the assessment framed was bad in law.

For the assessment year 1950-51, the ITO made the assessment of the assessee-HUF on 28-2-1955 at a loss of Rs. 5,174. Subsequently, the ITO, having found certain cash credits entered in a duplicate set of account books, reopened the aforesaid assessment under section 147(a) and issued a notice to the assessee under section 148 thereof on 26-11-1965. Pursuant to that notice, the assessee filed a return disclosing income as per the original assessment. Subsequently, purportedly in order to buy peace with the department, the assessee surrendered credits amounting to Rs. 76,201 on 26-3-1970 and the ITO made the reassessment at a total income of Rs. 71,030. On 30-11-1970, the assessee filed an application under section 154 seeking cancellation of the reassessment order on the ground that the issue of notice under section 148 was bad in law in view of the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of J.P. Jain, ITO v. Jnduprasad Devshanker Bhatt [1969] 72 ITR 595 . The ITO rejected the application and the AAC confirmed the ITO's order. On second appeal, the revenue contended (i) that under clause (ii ) of the first proviso to section 34(1) of the 1922 Act, the ITO could assume jurisdiction if he had bona fide belief that income had escaped assessment for a number of years and the aggregated concealed income was Rs. 1 lakh or more; (ii ) that for the relevant assessment year the ITO had found that the concealment was in excess of Rs. 76,201 and that if the additions made in the original assessments for the assessment years 1954-55, 1955-56 and 1956-57 were also taken into account, the income concealed would exceed Rs. 1 lakh; and (iii ) that in confidential file of the ITO there was material which indicated that the concealment which he had in mind was in excess of Rs. 1 lakh. The revenue also prayed for producing that confidential record before the Tribunal. The Accountant Member of the Tribunal held that the additions made by the ITO in the assessments for the assessment years 1954-55,1955-56 and 1956-57 could not have been considered for assuming jurisdiction for the assessment year 1950-51 because for those three years notices had been issued before eight years had elapsed. He also observed that there was no suggestion of any income escaping assessment for the period prior to the assessment year 1950-51 and no indication that the income for the earlier years were considered along with the year 1950-51 before the ITO assumed jurisdiction. In this view of the matter, he accepted the assessee's appeal and rejected the revenue's request for production of fresh material. Although the Judicial Member observed that the confidential record of the department could have been taken on record and that a disputed question of fact was involved in the case, yet he did not disagree with the ultimate conclusion of the Accountant Member. Accordingly, the Tribunal held that the reassessment made on 28-3-1970 constituted a mistake apparent from record which could be rectified under section 154 and, consequently, cancelled the order under section 154 passed by the ITO.

On reference, the revenue contended that as the Judicial Member had recorded a clear finding that the confidential record could have been taken on record and that a debatable question was involved in the case, it would be in the interest of justice that the matter be remanded for fresh hearing by the Tribunal.

The notifications dated 31-3-2021 and 27-4-2021 issued by the Central Government under section 3(1) of TOLA contained an explanation declaring that the provisions under the old regime shall apply to the reassessment proceedings initiated under them. Thus, the notifications directed the assessing officers to apply the provisions of the old regime for reassessment notices issued after 1-4- 2021. The assessing officers accordingly issued reassessment notices between 1-4-2021 and 30-6-2021 by relying on the provisions under section 148 of the old regime. These reassessment notices were challenged by the assessees before various High Courts.

The High Courts allowed the writ petitions and quashed all the reassessment notices issued between 1-4-2021 and 30-6-2021 under the old regime on the ground that: (i) Sections 147 to 151 stood substituted by Finance Act, 2021 from 1 April 2021; (ii) In the absence of any saving clause, the Revenue could initiate reassessment proceedings after 1-4-2021 only in accordance with the provisions of the new regime since they were remedial, beneficial, and meant to protect the rights and interests of the assessees; and (iii) the Central Government could not exercise its delegated authority to ‘re-activate the pre-existing law.’

In Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 this Court held that it was ‘in complete agreement with the view taken by various High Courts in holding’ that ‘the benefit of the new provisions shall be made available even in respect of the proceedings relating to past assessment years, provided Section 148 notice has been issued on or after 1-4-2021.’ However, the Court observed that the Revenue issued the reassessment notices under a ‘bona fide belief that the amendments may not yet have been enforced.’ This Court exercised its discretionary jurisdiction under article 142 in order to balance the interests of the Revenue and the assessees and directed that the reassessment notices issued under the old regime shall be deemed to have been issued under Section 148A(b) of the new regime.

On 11-5-2022, the Central Board of Direct Taxes issued an Instruction for the implementation of the decision Ashish Agarwal (supra). The Instruction “clarified” that Ashish Agarwal (supra) will apply “to all cases where extended reassessment notices have been issued [...] irrespective of the fact whether such notices have been challenged or not.” Paragraph 6.1 of the Instruction stated that the reassessment notices will “travel back in time to their original date when such notices were to be issued and then new section 149 of the Act is to be applied at that point.” Thus, the Instruction is based on the presumption that the notices issued under Section 148 of the new regime will travel back in time to their original dates, that is, the date when the Section 148 notice under the old regime was issued.

Paragraph 6.2 of the Instruction elaborated on the mechanism for issuing notices under section 148 of the new regime.

The assessing officers accordingly considered the replies furnished by the assessees and passed orders under section 148A(d). Subsequently, notices under section 148 of the new regime were issued to the assessees by the assessing officers between July and September 2022 for the assessment years 2013-2014, 2014-2015, 2015-2016, 2016-2017, and 2017-2018. These notices were challenged before several High Courts. The High Courts declared the notices to be invalid on the ground that they were: (i) time-barred; and (ii) issued without the appropriate sanction of the specified authority.

On the revenue's appeal to the Supreme Court :

The regular return filed by the assessee for the assessment year 1996-97 was completed under section 143(1)(a). Thereafter, a search was carried out in the premises of the assessee under section 132(1), during which certain gold/silver ornaments, cash, bill books, etc., were found and seized. Subsequently, in response to a notice under section 158BC, the assessee filed a return declaring certain undisclosed income. Thereafter, the Assessing Officer passed an order under section 158BC, which was held to be barred by limitation under section 158BE by the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal.

Thereafter, the Assessing Officer found that some income of the assessee had escaped assessment and, therefore, he initiated an action under section 147 by issue of notice under section 148. The assessee, thereafter, demanded a copy of the reasons recorded for issuing notice under section 148, but no reasons were supplied to the assessee. After some time the Assessing Officer supplied reasons for reopening the assessment. The assessee further alleged that notice under section 148 was issued on the direction of the Joint Commissioner, which was not permitted under law. But ignoring all the arguments of the assessee on this legal ground, as well as on merits, the Assessing Officer proceeded further and passed an order under sections 143(3)/147, in which various additions were made. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) quashed the notice under section 148 and set aside the reassessment order.

On revenue’s appeal :

The assessee was assessed by the ITO, for the assessment year 1947-48 by an assessment order dated 31-1-1952. The ITO thereafter received information that a certain profit made by the assessee in the name of a benamidar of the assessee had escaped assessment by reason of the assessee not having disclosed it at the time of the original assessment. The ITO, therefore, after obtaining the approval of the Commissioner issued a notice dated 27-3-1956, under section 34(1)(a). The notice could not be served personally, and, therefore, was served by affixing on a conspicuous part of the assessee's house. The assessee objected to the service of the notice and did not file a return stating that there had been no valid service. When the ITO threatened to proceed ex-parte, a return was filed under protest on 16-1-1957. Despite the objection of the assessee that there was no proper service of notice under section 34(1)(a), the ITO proceeded to assess the income of the assessee for the assessment year 1947-48 and made an order dated 29-3-1957, determining the total income at Rs. 89,000 by including the profit alleged to have been earned by the benamidar. The assessee preferred an appeal to the AAC who allowed the appeal and set aside the order of assessment on the ground that there was no valid service of the notice. The decision of the AAC was given on 5-1-1963, by which time the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, had been repealed and the Income-tax Act, 1961 had come into force with effect from 1-4-1962. The time for taking action for assessment or reassessment in case of escaped income exceeding Rs. 50,000 but less than Rs. 1,00,000 was enlarged from 8 years to 16 years under the new Act. On 4-1-1963, the ITO issued a notice calling upon the assessee to show cause why proceedings should not be taken under section 147(a) of the new Act for bringing to tax the escaped profit of the assessee. The assessee protested against the new notice on the ground that action under the old Act had became time barred and the new Act had no application to his case. Subsequently, a notice under section 148 of the new Act was issued on 13-11-1963, and this notice was followed by another notice dated 9-1-1964, issued under section 142(1).

The assessee, therefore, preferred Special Civil Application in the High Court praying for a writ of certiorari to quash the notices dated 13-11-1963, and 9-1-1964, by the first appellant. The High Court took the view that on a true construction of section 227(2)(d)( ii) of the new Act, the ITO could not issue a notice under section 148 in order to reopen the assessment in a case where the right to reopen the assessment was barred under the old Act at the date when the new Act came into force. The High Court observed that the right of the ITO to reopen the assessment of the assessee in the instant case was admittedly barred under section 34(1)(a) of the old Act at the commencement of the new Act and it was, therefore, not competent to the ITO to issue a notice under section 148 of the new Act in order to reopen the assessment of the assessee and to reassess the income of the assessee relying on the provisions enacted under section 297(2)(d)( ii) of the new Act. The High Court accordingly allowed the Special Civil Application and set aside the notices dated 13-11-1963, and 9-1-1964.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

• The assessee was carrying on the business of running flour mills. Its principal place of business was at Agra and it was having its registered head office at New Delhi.

• It was filing its return with the Assessing Officer, ward 3(1), New Delhi which had jurisdiction in the matter of the assessee.

• Following a search and seizure operation carried out in 'G' group of cases, it was found that loan given to the assessee was bogus and was nothing but its own undisclosed income routed through 'G' group of persons.

• Based on the above report, a notice under section 148 was issued by the Income tax Officer, Agra at assessee's Agra address.

• The above notice was returned bye the assessee on the ground that it was not addressed to its principal place of business at Delhi.

• Thereafter, the notice was sent to the assessee at its Delhi address.

• The assessee filed objections to the notice challenging the jurisdiction. It was also stated that notice was barred by limitation as it had been issued 6 years after the end of the relevant assessment year.

• Correspondence ensued between the Assessing Officer, Agra and the Assessing Officer, ward 3(1) Delhi who returned the papers to ITO, Agra, following which the Assessing Officer, Agra, sought directions from the Commissioner (Agra) on the question of jurisdiction.

• The ITO, Agra on instructions of Assistant Commissioner, Agra issued a notice to the assessee with reference to notice under section 148 to furnish information about cash creditors/loans, list of all bank accounts and all account book etc.

Assessee's submission

• The ITO, Agra, had exercised jurisdiction to make reassessment under section 147, which was not vested in him under section 124.

• The notice could only be issued by the Assessing Officer, Delhi.

• The notice was issued without any valid transfer by Joint Commissioner/Assistant Commissioner under section 151(2).

held.text:
factual aspects are not deal with in any of the petitions and all these petitions are allowed on the issue of limitation. [Para 57]

Resultantly, these petitions are allowed. Notices under section 148 and impugned orders under section 148A(d) are quashed and set aside on the ground of limitation. [Para 58]

All these petitions are accordingly disposed of. [Para 59]

As per Mauna M. Bhatt, J. [Supplementing View] It was contended that the decision in the case of UOI v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC) shall apply only to those notices, which were challenged before different High Courts:

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in this case has adjudicated on the validity of reassessment notices issued by the Assessing Officers during the period 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021 i.e.; the time extended by TOLA and various notifications issued thereunder. As new law came in to force w.e.f 1-4-2021, it has held that these notices issued under section 148 (between 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021) shall be deemed to be the show cause notices issued under section 148A(b) of the new provision and further directed the Assessing Officer to follow the procedure with respect to such notices. Thus, it has created a fiction by directing to treat the notices issued under section 148 (unamended law), as notices issued under section 148A(b) (substituted provision) with a clear intention to save about 90,000/- proceedings, being conscious of the fact that there were approximately 90,000 such notices, which have been issued on a bonafide belief that old provisions would be applicable. Therefore, to strike a balance between rights of the revenue as well as respective assessees, keeping in mind that the revenue may not suffer as ultimately it is a public exchequer, the Supreme Court in exercise of its power under Article 142 of the Constitution of India, has made the order, which shall be applicable PAN India. Therefore, submissions of petitioners that the decision in the case of Ashish Agarwal (supra) would be applicable to the cases, where such notices have been challenged before different High Courts cannot be agreed upon. [Para 21.1]

It was contended that there cannot be any Notification when the provision itself was repealed. Further, by issuing notification, the executive cannot expand legislative power because it would amount to re-writing the law. By Notification, the subordinate legislation cannot override any statute enacted by Parliament.

On the aforesaid issue it is submitted by all counsel that by virtue of notification Nos. 20 of 2021 and 38 of 2021 dated 31-3-2021 and 27-4-2021 respectively, the time limit for issuing notice under section 148 has been extended up to 30-6-2021. By Notification No. 20 of 2021 dated 31-3-2021, the time limit to issue notice was extended up to 31-4-2021. When the Notification No 20 of 2021, was issued on 31-3-2021, the old law was in existence, and it ceases to exist w.e.f 1-4-2021. When the law itself ceases to exist w.e.f. 1-4-2021, the Notification will die a natural death and therefore there cannot be any Notification in respect of the repealed Act. Moreover, as the Notification No. 38 of 2021, dated 27-4-2021, was in continuation of the earlier Notification dated 31-3-2021 and once earlier notification ceases to apply, the consequential second Notification also ceases to apply. Various High Courts for the precise reason have held the said Notifications to be bad in Law and these findings have been upheld by the Supreme Court. It was further submitted that the two Notifications issued by the CBDT, dated 31-3-2021 and 27-4-2021, respectively amounts to extension of legislation or rewriting of legislation, not permitted under Law.

The only issue which arises for consideration (and that too concerning assessment year 2016-17 and 2017-18) is whether the impugned order passed under section 148A(d) and the consequent notice issued under section 148 of the amended 1961 Act [as obtaining with the enactment of FA 2021], falls foul of the limitation prescribed in clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 149? [Para 25]

Section 149(1) of the amended 1961 Act mandates that no notice under section 148 would be issued for the relevant assessment year if three (03) years have elapsed from the end of the said assessment year. The Assessing Officer can take recourse to the extended limitation period if the conditions precedent prescribed in clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 149 are fulfilled. In other words, in a case where three (03) years from the end of the relevant assessment year have elapsed, the Assessing Officer can issue a notice under section 148 provided the conditions prescribed in clause (b) of section 149(1) of the amended 1961 Act are fulfilled. [Para 26]

A careful perusal of clause (b) of section 149 would show that one of the conditions for triggering the extended period, which goes up to ten (10) years in cases where three (03) years have elapsed, is that income chargeable to tax which has escaped assessment amounts to, or is likely to amount to Rs. 50 lakhs or more for the assessment year in issue. [Para 27]

Therefore, after the coming into force of FA 2021, in cases where, for the relevant assessment year, the alleged escaped income was less than Rs. 50 lakhs, notice under section 148 could only be issued for commencement of reassessment proceedings within the limitation period provided in clause (a) of section 149(1) of the amended 1961 Act. [Para 28]

Thus, in the ordinary course, the limitation for assessment year 2016-17 would expire on 31-3-2020; likewise, for assessment year 2017-18, the end date for the culmination of the limitation period would be 31-3-2021. [Para 29]

The revenue seeks to take recourse to the provisions of section 3(1) of TOLA and the Notifications issued thereunder, from time-to-time, which, in effect, extended the end date for completion of proceedings and compliances up until 30-6-2021. [Para 30]

In this regard, the last two notifications. Via Notification dated 31-3-2021, the end date was extended till 30-4-2021 may be refund. The Notification immediately following the said Notification, i.e., Notification dated 27-4-2021, extended the end date to 30-6-2021. Thus, the span concerning the extension of end dates was spread between 20-3-2020 and 30-6-2021. [Para 30.1]

It is, therefore, the revenue's case that the impugned actions, which involved passing of orders under section 148A(d) and issuance of notices under section 148 taken between 1-4-2021 (when FA 2021 kicked in) and 30-6-2021 were valid in the eyes of the law. [Para 31]

Briefly, the Supreme Court was called upon to grapple with a piquant situation, which was the creation of the revenue, concerning the viability of notices issued on or after 1-4-2021, when FA 2021 had already kicked in. [Para 32.1]

The Supreme Court noticed that with the enactment and enforcement of FA 2021, sections 147 to 149 and section 151, as they stood on 31-3-2021, had been substituted, bringing about radical and reformative changes in the matters concerning reassessment proceedings. Taking cognizance of this state of affairs, the Supreme Court held that, since the new provisions substituted by FA 2021 were both remedial and benevolent, they would apply to past Assessment years provided section 148 notices had been issued on or after 1-4-2021. This was also the view taken by various High Courts; a view which was sustained by the Supreme Court. [Para 32.2]

The Supreme Court, however, having regard to the fact that the procedure prescribed under the new regime (which was encapsulated in FA 2021) had not been followed, modified the judgments of the High Courts by issuing specific directions to balance the interests of the assessees and the revenue. [Para 32.3]

■

From the perusal of the findings of the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC), it is evident that the Supreme Court directed that while computing the time limit for issuance of notice under section 148, the time during which the show cause notice was stayed till the supply of relevant information or material by the Assessing Officer and further period of two weeks allowed to the assessee to respond to the show cause notice should be excluded. [Para 9]

■

Thus, the Supreme Court held that the surviving time under the Act read with the TOLA will be available to the revenue to complete the remaining proceedings in furtherance of the deemed notice, including issuance of a reassessment notice under section 148 under the new regime. [Para 10]

■

Therefore, the surviving/balance time limit can be calculated by computing the number of days between the date of issuance of the deemed notice and 30-6-2021. In the instant case, in order to compute the surviving/balance time as per the decision of the Supreme Court, it is relevant to note the various dates. [Para 11]

■

Therefore, computing the surviving/balance time limit, as per the decision of the Supreme Court in Rajeev Bansal (supra), it is found that the revenue had 58 days to issue notice under section 148 of the new regime in the instant case, i.e. till 20-7-2022, after issuance of the show cause notice issued under section 148A(b) on 23-5-2022. However, undisputedly, in the instant case, the notice under section 148 was issued on 27-7-2022, i.e., after the surviving/balance time period as per the decision of the Supreme Court in Rajeev Bansal (supra). Therefore, in the light of the decision of the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1(SC)/ 444 ITR 1 (SC), it is viewed that the notice issued under section 148 on 27-7-2022 is barred by the limitation period specified under section 149. Accordingly, it is viewed that the notice issued under section 148 on 27-7-2022 for the assessment year 2013-14 is void ab initio and bad in law. Therefore, the same is quashed. Consequently, the entire reassessment proceedings and the assessment order passed under section 147 read with section 144 for the assessment year 2013-14 is also quashed. [Para 13]

■

Even in the assessment year 2014-15, the notice under section 148 under the new regime was issued on 27-07-2022, which is beyond the surviving/balance time period as per the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rajeev Bansal (supra). Accordingly, findings/conclusions as rendered in assessee's appeal for the assessment year 2013-14 shall apply mutatis mutandis to the appeal for the assessment year 2014-15. Accordingly, the notice issued under section 148 on 27-07-2022 for the assessment year 2014-15 is void ab initio and bad in law. Therefore, the same is quashed. Consequently, the entire reassessment proceedings and the assessment order passed under section 147 read with section 144 for the assessment year 2014-15 is also quashed. [Para 15]

Accordingly, ground nos. 1 and 2 raised by the revenue are dismissed. Resultantly, grounds raised on the merits of the case are rendered academic and hence not adjudicated upon. [Para 10.2]

■ Now, with respect to the appeal by the revenue and cross objection by the assessee for assessment year 2015-16. Appeal by the revenue is on the merits of the case whereas cross objection by the assessee is on challenging the legal issue of notice under section 148 as bad in law, invalid, void ab initio, to be quashed. Identical chronology of events exists for assessment year 2015-16 as discussed while adjudicating appeal for assessment year 2014-15 in the above paragraphs, except for date of filing of return. Notice under section 148 of the old regime was issued on 30-6-2021. Later, pursuant to the judgment in case of Ashish Agarwal (supra), it was directed among other things that notice issued under section 148 shall be deemed to have been issued under section 148A as substituted by the Finance Act, 2021 and construed or treated to be the show cause notice in terms of section 148A(b). In view of this direction, the said notice under section 148, dated 30-6-2021 was deemed to be a show cause notice under section 148A(b) for which another one was issued on 26-5-2022, complying with the direction given in the case of Ashish Agarwal (supra). [Para 12]

Thereafter, provisions of section 148A(d) were complied with by passing an order, dated 28-7-2022 and issuing a notice under section 148 of the same date (under the new regime). Assessee has contested by raising a ground of cross objection that the notice so issued is bad in law, invalid, void ab initio, to be quashed. The assessee strongly submitted that it is barred by limitation making the impugned reassessment proceedings and resultant reassessment order bad in law. [Para 12.1]

■

At the outset, it is found that this issue has been settled in the case of Rajeev Bansal (supra) wherein reference is made to the submissions made on behalf of the revenue which is relevant. [Para 12.2]

Thus, it can be seen that revenue conceded before the Supreme Court for dropping all the notices issued on or after 1-4-2021 for assessment year 2015-16 as they will not fall for completion during the period prescribed under TOLA. [Para 12.3]

his income, in the prescribed form and verified in prescribed manner. However, the provisions of section 149 prescribe the time-limit for issue of notice under section 148. The Legislature has used two different expressions 'issue' in section 149 and 'serve' in section 148. Section 149 prescribes the time-limit for issue of notice whereas provisions of section 148 require the Assessing Officer to serve the notice before making assessment or reassessment under section 147. [Para 24] From the decisions of the Supreme Court in the case of R.K. Upadhyaya v. Shanabhai P. Patel [1987] 166 ITR 163/33 Taxman 229 and Patna High Court in the case of CIT v.Sheo Kumari Devi [1986] 157 ITR 13/24 Taxman 77(FB), the law is settled that term 'issue' appearing in section 149 cannot mean as 'issue and serve'. The jurisdiction becomes vested in the Assessing Officer to assess/reassess the escaped income, the moment the notice under section 148 is issued. Service under the Act is not a condition precedent to conferment of jurisdiction on the Assessing Officer but a condition precedent only to the making of the order of assessment. Therefore, the contention of the assessee, that without service of notices under section 148 the Assessing Officer was not vested with the power to assess/reassess the escaped income and assessment proceedings were jeopardized, held no water and deserved to be rejected. [Para 26]

It is a settled law that the expression 'issue' means that the notice should leave the custody of the Assessing Officer. The postal department is not agent of the Income-tax department. Once a notice is issued within the period of limitation, jurisdiction becomes vested in the Income-tax Officer to proceed to reassess. The assessment proceedings can be terminated either by passing of the assessment orders within the stipulated time or by dropping of the proceedings initiated under section 147. Thus, the assessment/ reassessment proceedings under section 147 will not terminate by issue of fresh notice under section 148. It is also a settled law that the Assessing Officer can issue as many notices as he may desire as long as other conditions prescribed in law are satisfied. In a case where the Assessing Officer drops the proceedings initiated earlier, again on same material and information, he is debarred to issue fresh notice for the simple reason that issue of notice under such circumstances would amount to change of opinion which is not permitted in view of settled position of law in this regard. [Para 27]

In the assessment years 2001-02 to 2004-05, the Assessing Officer had issued notices under section 148 after recording reasons on 23-9-2005. The said notices were issued through speed post on 23-9-2005. The Assessing Officer again issued notice for assessment year 2001-02 on 25-9-2006 after getting necessary sanction from the Additional Commissioner. After receipt of affidavit on 10-11-2006, the Assessing Officer again issued notices under section 148 on 24-11-2006 for assessment years 2001-02 to 2004-05. This time the approval of the Additional Commissioner was not obtained by the Assessing Officer for the assessment year 2001-02. The sanction issued by the Additional Commissioner on 25-9-2006 could not be used second time. It would require satisfaction on part of Additional Commissioner before he issued such sanction. Moreover, the jurisdiction over the case was transferred to Central Circle-9 from Central Circle -17. On that ground alone, the issue of third notice under section 148 for the assessment year 2001-02 was bad in law and assessment for that assessment year could not be sustained. The fact remained that for the assessment year 2001-02, the Assessing Officer had issued three notices under section 148, i.e., on 23-9-2005, 25-9-2006 and 24-11-2006. For other assessment years, two notices had been issued, i.e., on 23-9-2005 and 24-11-2006. As per the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of R.K. Upadhyay ( supra), the jurisdiction stood vested in the Assessing Officer to assess/reassess the escaped income on 23-9-2005. The assessment powers, thus, vested in the Assessing Officer had not been terminated either by way of assessment or by way of dropping of assessment proceedings initiated under section 147. Therefore, the Assessing Officer had issued notices under section 148 on 25-9-2006 and 24-11-2006 for assessment year 2001-02 and on 24-11-2006 for assessment years 2002-03, 2003-04 and 2004-05 during pendency of assessment proceedings under section 147. [Para 29]

■

The Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC) explaining the ratio laid down in similar judgment of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/444 ITR 1/286 Taxman 183 (SC) wherein the Supreme Court had exercised its discretionary jurisdiction under article 142 of the Constitution of India while explaining the old law and new law under section 148, has created a legal fiction and balancing act on the existing legal framework of procedure of reassessment. Wherever the notice under section 148 were issued under the old regime for which time limit was extended up to 30-6-2021, the Apex Court held that it would be deemed that reassessment notice issued under the old regime shall be treated as show-cause notice issued under section 148A(b) of the new regime. Further the Court directed the revenue to provide all the relevant material/information to the assessee and thereafter, allowed the assessee to respond to the show-cause notice and raised its objection or availing any kind of defenses including available under section 149. Thus, the Supreme Court balanced the equities between the revenue and the assessee by giving effect to the legislative scheme of reassessment as contained under the new regime. The Court thus supplemented the existing legal framework of the procedure of reassessment under the Income-tax Act with the principles grounded in equitable standards. [Para 7]

■

Thus, the Supreme Court had explained the concept of surviving or balance time limit which is to be calculated by computing number of days between dates of issuance of deemed notice and 30-6-2021. Thereafter, the Supreme Court has elaborated the effect of the legal fiction propounded in the case of UOI v. Ashish Agarwal which has been explained. [Para 8]

■

The sequitor of the aforesaid observation and the judgment of the Supreme Court are that-

■

Firstly, exclusion of the period has been explained;

(a)

the date of issuance notice under section 148 under the old regime reckoned to be the date of issuance of the deemed notices under section 148A(b);

(b)

the period from the date of the issuance of the deemed notices till the supply of relevant information and material by the assessing officers to the assessees is to be excluded from the computation of the period of limitation;

(c)

further, period of two weeks granted to the assessee to reply to the show-cause notice is also to be excluded in terms of third proviso to section 149;

■

Secondly, once the response of the assessee to the showcause notice has been received, then "the clock starts ticking for the Revenue", that is, after the receipt of reply, the Assessing Officer has to;

(a)

consider the reply of the assessee under section148A(c);

(b)

take a decision under section148A(d) based on the available material and the reply of the assessee; and

(c)

issue a notice under section148 if it was a fit case for reassessment.

■

Once it is found to be a fit case for re-assessment, the limitation clock starts ticking and it is mandatory for the Assessing Officer to comply with these procedures within the surviving time limit which was available to the Assessing Officer to issue re-assessment notice under section148 of the new regime; and

■

Lastly, the Supreme Court has given an example as how to calculate the surviving time. Calculation of surviving time has been laid down from the period when the first notice u/s.148 was issued under old regime till the last date of limitation for issuance of notice under section148 of the old regime; and that period has been reckoned as the surviving time period left for the Assessing Officer while issuing notice under section148 under the new regime. So whatever surviving time is left the Assessing Officer has to issue notice within that surviving time.[Para 9]

■

If the surviving time like here in this case is only two days, because original notice under section 148 under the old regime was issued on 28-6-2021 and the last date on which notice could have been issued under old regime was up till 30-6-2021; and therefore, the surviving time left was only two days for issuing a notice under the new regime under section 148 after completion of the procedure laid down under section 148A(b) to 148(d).

■

Ergo, the Assessing Officer was required to issue notice under section 148 of the new regime within the time surviving under the Income-tax Act read with TOLA and any notices issued beyond the surviving period was declared to be time barred by the Supreme Court. [Para 10]

■

The confusion on account of limitation has arisen on account of the implementation of the decision of the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal, 2022 SCC Online SC 543. As per the decision of the Supreme Court in aforesaid case, which held that all the Notices for reopen of the assessment for the tax period after 1-4-2021 will have to be dealt under the new regime as in force from 1-4-2021. The period of limitation under the old regime would have been either four years or six years or sixteen years under section 149 as it stood till 31-3-2021. [Para 13]

■

However, in accordance with the new regime, the period for limitation for issuance of Notice under amended section 148 to reopen an assessment, it is three years but not more than 10 years. Correspondingly, the monetary and pecuniary jurisdiction for reopening the assessment were also altered. This has also been captured by the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal, [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70 (SC)/ 2024 SCC OnLine SC 2693. [Para 14]

■

The Supreme Court has also taken note of the relaxation in the period of limitation for various assessment years in the light of the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation & Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 (hereinafter referred to as the 'TOLA') with effect from 20-11-2020 and the Finance Act, 2021 amending the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961 with effect from 1-4-2021. In accordance with TOLA, as far as the assessment year 2017-18 is concerned, the period of limitation for issuance of Notice under section 148 read with section 149 as amended by Finance Act, 2021 with effect from 1-4-2021 would be till 30-6-2021, instead of 30-3-2021 and under the old regime on 31-3-2024. This was also captured in the submissions of the Additional Solicitor General of India on behalf of the Income Tax Department before the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal, (supra). This position has not been disputed. [Para 15]

■

However, the first proviso to section 149 prohibits issuance of a reassessment notice under the new regime if such notices have become time barred under the old regime. Therefore, the last date for issuance of Notice under section 148 would have expired on 30-6-2021, as per the third Proviso to section 149(1)(b) as in force with effect from 1-4-2021. The time during which stay was in operation or the time during which, the assessee took time to file the reply, the Notice issued under section 148(A)(b) stands expelled. In this case, the reply itself was filed by the petitioner only on 31-5-2022, pursuant to which the Impugned Order was passed on 30-6-2022 under section 148(A)(d) and Notice under section 148 was issued. Though the limitation for issuance of a Notice under section 148 under the old regime would have expired on 31-3-2024, a reading of conclusion in the decision of the Supreme Court in UOI v. Rajeev Bansal (supra), however indicates that the Impugned Notice dated 30-6-2022 has to be treated as having been issued beyond the limitation period. [Para 16]

■

Dealing with almost an identical situation pursuant to the decision of the Supreme Court in UOI v. Rajeev Bansal (supra), the Delhi High Court quashed the notice dated 31-3-2021 issued to the assessee under section 148 and the proceedings. Since the law laid down by the Supreme Court in UOI v. Rajeev Bansal (supra) is a settled law, it is binding on this Court. [Para 17]

■

Therefore, this Writ Petition deserves to be allowed and is accordingly allowed. [Para 18]

■

Applying the ratio laid down in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64 /[2022] 286 Taxman 183 /[2022] 444 ITR 1 (SC)/(2023) 1 SCC 617 and Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/469 ITR 46/301 Taxman 238 (SC), particularly, in the light of the limitation for issuance of notice under section 148 prescribed under section 149 read with section 151, it is clear that the notice that was issued after 1-4-2021 under the old regime as it stood till 31-3-2021 has to be treated as a notice under section 148A(b) under the new regime. [Para 8]

■

The time during which the aforesaid notice issued under section 148 under the old regime as it stood till 31-3-2021 were deemed to be stayed from the date of issuance between 1-4-2021 and 30-6-2021 till the supply of relevant information and material by the Assessing Officers to the assessees in terms of the directions issued by this Court in Ashish Agarwal case (supra), and for a further period of two weeks for the assessees to respond to the Show Cause Notices as confirmed by Rajeev Bansal case (supra). [Para 9]

■

A notice under section 148 was required to be issued for reassessment within the time limit surviving under the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) [TOLA] Act, 2020. For the assessment year 2016-17, since the income escaping assessment is less than Rs. 50 lakhs, the notice under section 148 ought to have been issued on 31-3-2020. However, by virtue of TOLA extensions, the said date has been extended up to 30-6-2021. [Para 12]

■

In the light of the ratio in Ashish Agarwal case (supra) and Rajeev Bansal case (supra), the notice issued under section 148 under the old regime on 30-6-2021 is deemed to have been stayed for thirty days for the Income Tax Department to provide to the respective assessees information and material relied upon and two weeks thereafter for the assessees to reply to the Show Cause Notices. [Para 13]

■

In the instant case, notice under section 148 under the old regime itself was issued on the last date of limitation viz., 30-6-2021, after the exclusions i.e., excluding the thirty days and fourteen days time period granted by the Supreme Court there is no further time available for the Assessing Officer to issue Notice under section 148 under the new regime barring the seven days as provided under the fourth proviso to section 149 as amended with effect from 1-4-2021. [Para 14]

■

Therefore, after accounting for all the exclusions, the Assessing Officer in the instant case had no time left for issuance of Notice under section 148 under the new regime. However, applying the fourth proviso to section 149 as amended with effect from 1-4-2021, the Assessing Officer had seven days to issue a Notice under section 148 under the new regime. [Para 15]

■

Thus, the notice under section 148 ought to have been issued within seven days from the date of reply given by the assessee on 3-6-2022. In other words, the notice ought to have been issued on or before 10-6-2022. [Para 16]

■

However, in the instant case, the notice under section 148 under the new regime was issued only on 28-7-2022. [Para 17]

■

Thus, the proceedings initiated on 30-6-2021 which were later substituted by a notice under section 148A(b) dated 20-5-2022 which culminated in the impugned order passed under section 148A(d) dated 28-7-2022 and notice issued under section 148 dated 28-7-2022 are to be held to be beyond time. [Para 18]

■

In view thereof, this writ petition challenging these two proceedings deserve to be allowed and is accordingly allowed. [Para 19]

In R.K. Upadhyaya v. Shanabhai P. Patel [1987] 166 ITR 163, the Supreme Court categorically held that a clear distinction has been made out under the Income-tax Act, 1961 between 'issue of notice' and 'service of notice'. Section 149 prescribes the period of limitation. It prohibits issue of notice under section 148 after the expiry of the prescribed period of limitation. Section 148(1) provides for service of notice as condition precedent to making of the order of assessment. Once a notice is issued within the period of limitation, jurisdiction becomes vested with the ITO to proceed to reassess. The requirement of issue of notice is satisfied when a notice is actually issued Section 148(1) deals with making of the reassessment and mandates that reassessment shall not be made until there has been service. Under the Act, service is not a condition precedent to conferment of jurisdiction on the ITO to deal with the matter but it is a condition precedent to the making of the order of assessment.

In the Instant case, notice under section 148 was issued by the ITO within the period of limitation prescribed under section 149. There was also no controversy about the fact that the order of reassessment was made only after service of notice on the assessee. The ratio of the decision in R.K. Upadhyaya's case (supra ) of the Supreme Court squarely applied to the present case. The ITO having issued the notice under section 148 within limitation, the order of reassessment was valid. Therefore, the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the initiation of reassessment proceedings by the ITO was barred by limitation and in setting aside the orders of the AAC and the ITO.

■

It is an admitted fact that earlier, the notice under section 148 in the case of assessee was issued on 13-4-2021 which was dropped and proceedings under section 148A were initiated in terms of order of Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 and finally the notice under section 148 was issued on 18-7-2022. The Additional Solicitor General of India in the case of Union of India v. Rajiv Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC)has made categorical statement at Bar before the Supreme Court that all the notices issued for assessment year 2015-16 on or after 1-4-2021 will be dropped, however, in the instant case, no such action was taken and re-assessment order was framed in the case of the assessee on the basis of the notice issued under section 148 on 18-7-2022.[Para 10]

Hence, the provision clearly lays down that the aggregation for the purposes of finding out the escaped income could be for the year for which the action was proposed or for that year and the years preceding it. A notice under section 148 has to be issued when an assessment, reassessment or recomputation is made under section 147 to tax income which has escaped assessment. The instant case was not a case of reassessment nor a case of recomputation. It was a case of an assessment without there being an earlier assessment.

Under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, originally there was no time limit for completion of assessment until the amendment made in 1939 and Courts have held that the notice under section 34 was not required to be served if the proceedings were pending on either the assessee filing the return suo moto or by issuance of notice under section 22 (equivalent to section 142 of the Income-tax Act. 1961). After the introduction of the time limit for completing the assessments under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the proceedings could be said to be pending during the period starting from the date of filing of the return by the assessee suo moto or issuance of notice under section 142 by the Assessing Officer up to the lime limit prescribed to complete the assessment under section 153, i.e., two years from the end of the assessment year in which the income was first assessable.

Explanation 2(a) to section 147 includes non-filing of return in the expression ‘escaped assessment’. However, the scope of Explanation 2(a) to section 147 has to be restricted to the failure of the assessee to file a return suo moto or a voluntary return under section 139(1) or section 139(4) within the prescribed time limit and cannot be extended to cases where a notice under section 142(1) requiring the assessee to file return has already been issued. The requirement of ‘where no return of income has been furnished by the assessee’, as appearing in the Explanation, for treating it as a case of ‘income escaping assessment’, has to be seen on the expiry of the period within which the assessee can file the return. Otherwise, even on the first day of the assessment year, i.e., on 1-4-1991 itself, the Assessing Officer can issue notice under section 148 when the process of assessment itself has not yet come into being. It would, thus, be too wide a proposition to be accepted.

As regards the outer limit of issuing notice under section 142(1)(i ), there is apparently no time limit prescribed, but if one reads the other provisions, it can be deduced there from. A reading of section 139(4) gives an impression that the outer limit to furnish return is one year from the end of the assessment year. Otherwise, the assessees failure to submit the return under section 142(1) would not entitle him to file the return thereafter. Therefore, the issuance of notice under section 142(1) has to be before that period, i.e., 31-3-1992 in the instant cases. Once that time limit is over and the assessee has not filed any return, it becomes a case of income escaping assessment and for that issuance of notice under section 148 is a must. The time limit prescribed for completing assessment as per section 153 is 2 years from the end of the assessment year in which it was first assessable. However, this time limit comes into play when the proceedings for assessment have been initiated by filing a return suo moto under section 139(1) or by issuance of a valid notice under section 142(1).

In view of the Supreme Court’s decision in the case of CIT v. Narsee Nagsee & Co. [1960] 40 ITR 307 , the position insofar as income-tax is concerned is that the income escapes assessment the moment the assessment year is over if no proceedings have been initiated during the assessment year itself.

The Assessing Officer cancelled the notice when it was pointed out to him and, therefore, notice under section 148 was issued on 28-3-1996. Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 enacted by the Parliament and received the assent of the President on 28-9-1996. The Act omitted the words ‘not being less than 30 days’ from section 148 with effect from 1-4-1989. When notice dated 1-10-1993 and the fresh notice dated 28-3-1996 were issued, the Finance Act (No. 2) was not in force. The assessing authority had, therefore, rightly applied the then existing law. Section 148 provides for initiation of assessment proceedings which starts with the issue of notice. Initiation of proceedings by the assessing authority on 1-10-1993 was not valid and consequently it was dropped. Fresh notice was, therefore, issued under section 148 in conformity with the time prescribed under section 148. When the Finance Act was passed a legally valid proceeding was in existence. Notice prescribed under section 148 for the purpose of initiating reassessment proceedings is a condition precedent to the validity of an assessment made. The assessing authority was only curing the defect of not following the time-limit when it was pointed out by the assessee and, therefore, notice was issued strictly on the basis of the then existing statutory provision. The mere fact that the time-limit prescribed under section 148(1) was taken away would not make an invalid notice valid so as to render the assessment order dated 26-3-1997 invalid in terms of section 153(2). The assessee could not be allowed to raise such a plea after having persuaded the assessing authority to withdraw notice dated 1-10-1993 pointing out that it was not in conformity with the statutory provision. The assessee could not be allowed to take advantage of the plea of limitation in terms of section 153(2) contending that the notice dated 1-10-1993 was valid due to the omission of time-limit vide the Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 with effect from 1-4-1989. On the strength of notice dated 28-3-1996, the return of income was filed and such return could not be ignored. [Para 7]

The mere fact that the time-limit has been taken away with effect from 1-4-1989 would not vitiate the proceedings validly initiated applying the then existing law. The object and purpose of the amendment is only to take away the time-limit for giving time for the assessee to file a return which the Legislature thought unnecessary. If the Legislature wanted to undo all that was done by the assessing authority applying the then existing law, it should have been specifically provided in the statute. In the absence of specific provision in the Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 invalidating those proceedings initiated by the ITO, it could not be said that the action taken by the ITO applying the then existing law was invalid. Once the notice issued under section 148 on 28-3-1996 was upheld the plea of limitation raised by the assessee under section 153(2) had to be rejected. Section 148 in Chapter XIV was amended by the Finance Act, 2021 with effect from 1-4-2021. After the amendment, Notice was issued under section 148 for income that had allegedly escaped assessment. [Para 19]

However, these Notices were issued under section 148 under the old regime as in force till 31-3-2021 leading to flurry of Writ Petitions in various High Courts. There Section 148 Notices issued on or after 1-4-2021 under the old regime as in force till 31-3-2021 were challenged. Conflicting views were expressed by different High Courts. [Para 20]

■

Therefore, to quell further confusions arising out of different/conflicting views of different High Courts, the Supreme Court stepped in a batch of cases and finally disposed of the cases on 4-5-2024 Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal (supra) [Para 21]

Ashish Agarwal case (supra) was subsequently followed with the Instruction No. 1/2022, dated 11-5-2022 of the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT). The aforementioned Instruction No. 1/2022 specifically stated that reassessment notices would ''travel back in time'' to the original date on which such notices under the old regime have been issued, and that the new section 149 must be applied at that point in time. [Para 24]

The decision of the Supreme Court in Ashish Agarwal case was re-examined by a larger bench of the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC)/2024 SCC Online SC 2693. [Para 25]

Applying the above ratio, particularly, in the light of the limitation for issuance of Notice under section 148 prescribed under section 149 read with section 151, it is clear that the Notice that was issued after 1-4-2021 under the old regime as it stood till 31-3-2021 has to be treated as a Notice under section 148A(b) under the new regime in terms of Ashish Agarwal case and in terms of Rajeev Bansal case. [Para 30]

■

The time during which the aforesaid Show Cause Notices were deemed to be stayed is from the date of issuance of the deemed notice between 1-4-2021 and 30-6-2021 till the supply of relevant information and material by the Assessing Officers to the assessees in terms of the directions issued by the Supreme Court in Ashish Agarwal case, and the period of two weeks allowed to the assessees to respond to the show-cause notices as confirmed by Rajeev Bansal case. [Para 31]

■

Thus, it is clear that the Notice that was issued on 30-6-2021 under section 148 under the old regime as it stood till 31-3-2021 has to be treated as a Notice issued under section 148A(b) in terms of Ashish Agarwal case and Rajeev Bansal case. [Para 32]

Thus, if an assessee replies within the time stipulated in the above illustrations, the Assessing Officer has time up to sixty-one days from the date of reply. The Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC) has clarified that the Assessing Officer was required to complete these procedures within the 'surviving time limit' which can be calculated by computing the number of days between the date of issuance of the deemed notice under section 148A(d) and 30-6-2021 (i.e. the extended time limit provided by TOLA for issuing reassessment notices under section 148, which fell for completion from 20-3-2020 to 31-3-2021). The clock of limitation which has stopped with effect from the date of issuance of section 148 notices under the old regime (which is also the date of issuance of the deemed notices), would start running again when final reply to the notice deemed to have been issued under section 148A(b) is received by the Assessing Officer. In the instant case, notice under section 148 (old regime) was issued on 7-6-2021 and was deemed to be notice issued under section 148A(b) (new regime).
