By explicitly excluding "issued or served," the amendment departs from established legal principles, under which the limitation period for compliance often runs from the date of service (actual receipt) or, at a minimum, the date of issue (dispatch).

The limitation period under the amendment provision should be computed from the date on which notice is signed by the jurisdictional Assessing Officer, which will be considered as the date of the notice, notwithstanding the date on which such notice is issued or served to the assessee. Thus, where a notice is signed on 31-3-2026 but served on the assessee on 3-4-2026, it should allow the assessee to furnish the return on or before the date as specified by the AO in the notice, which cannot be earlier than 30-4-2026 and cannot be beyond 30-6-2026.

16.3B-3b Amendment to ITA, 2025 - The Finance Act, 2026 substituted clause (c) of Section 280(1) with effect from 1-4-2026. The substituted clause provides as follows:

"(c) the period specified in the notice referred to in clause (a) shall not be less than thirty days from the date of such notice but shall not exceed three months from the end of the month in which such notice is issued."

This provision corresponds to Section 148(1) of the ITA, 1961. After this amendment, the limitation period allowed under Section 280(1)(c) of the ITA, 2025 is now on par with Section 148(1) of the ITA, 1961. The impact of this amendment will be the same as discussed in Para 16.3B-3a. Thus, the notice for reassessment under Section 280 (corresponding to Section 148 of the ITA, 1961) issued by the jurisdictional AO should provide at least 30 days from the date of notice, which may extend up to 3 months from the end of the month in which such notice is issued.

16.12 Direction by approving panel to invoke GAAR and finding or direction of the court is included in 'information' to initiate the reassessment [Section 280 of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 148 of the ITA 1961)]

16.12-1 Position under the ITA 1961

To make an assessment, reassessment, or re-computation in section 147 of the ITA 1961, a notice was required to be issued to the assessee under section 148, requiring him to furnish a return of his income or the income of any other person in respect of which he is assessable under this Act. A notice under section 148 could be issued only when the Assessing Officer has information suggesting that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for the relevant assessment year. In the following situations, information shall be deemed to be suggesting that income has escaped assessment:

(a)

any information in the case of the assessee for the relevant assessment year in accordance with the risk management strategy formulated by the Board from time to time;

(b)

any audit objection to the effect that the assessment in the case of the assessee for the relevant assessment year has not been made in accordance with the provisions of this Act;

(c)

any information received under an agreement referred to in section 90 or section 90A of the Act;

(d)

any information made available to the Assessing Officer under the scheme notified under section 135A;

(e)

any information which requires action in consequence of the order of a Tribunal or a Court;

(f)

any information emanating from a survey conducted under section 133A (other than conducted under section 133A(2A) for verifying TDS and TCS) on or after 1-9-2024.

While issuing such a notice, the Assessing Officer is not required to obtain prior approval of the specified authority. However, the procedure prescribed under section 148A must be followed. However, if the Assessing Officer receives information in a faceless manner under the e-Verification Scheme, 2021 (notified under section 135A), the notice can be issued without following the procedure under section 148A. In such cases, prior approval of the specified authority is mandatory before issuing the notice under section 148.

7.4-4 New Reassessment provisions in brief

(1)

There is no change in Section 147. Therefore, AO can assess, by virtue of Explanation to Section 147, any other item of escaped income for which no notice under Section 148A has been issued.

(2)

Before initiating reassessment proceedings, the AO has to issue a notice under Section 148A(1). Such notice has to be issued on the basis of information suggesting that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment.

(3)

The notice should enclose all the information that suggests that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment.

(4)

The information in the case of the assessee shall be in accordance with the Risk Management Strategy formulated by the Board, audit objections, information received under Section 90 or 90A, an order of the Tribunal or Court or material gathered in a survey. However, no notice is required to be issued if information is emerging under the scheme framed under Section 135A.

(5)

Notice under Section 148A can be issued for the relevant assessment year within three or five years from the end of the relevant assessment year. The five-year limitation period will be available if information suggests an escaped income of Rs. 50 lakh or more based on asset, entry or expenditure as per books of account.

(6)

The aforesaid judgments could be relevant in interpreting the amendment to section 147. 7.5-1e Matters involving earlier years - In Singh Enterprises (Exports) (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [1989] 30 ITD 209 (Delhi - Trib.), the assessee-company, a manufacturer and exporter of readymade garments, claimed its status as an industrial company. The ITO while framing assessment under section 143(3) treated the assessee as a non-industrial company, whereupon the assessee moved an application before ITO stating that the Tribunal had in the assessee’s own case in earlier assessment years allowed its claim of being an industrial company. The ITO thereafter passed an order under section 154, accepting the assessee’s claim. The Commissioner by invoking section 263 cancelled ITO’s order holding that the assessee could not be an industrial company inasmuch as a major part of its income was from duty drawbacks and cash incentives. It was held that it was not a case where the Commissioner could have brought into limelight something new. There being no provision under the Act by which an order of assessment passed in conformity with the Tribunal’s decision can come up for review, change or cancellation under section 263, the Commissioner could not have invoked section 263. If the ITO passes an order of assessment in conformity with the Tribunal’s order, though such order is for the earlier assessment years, the Commissioner would not be entitled to exercise his jurisdiction under section 263 and cancel assessment or change the status.

Applying the principle laid down by the aforesaid judgment, it appears that for the purpose of the proviso to section 147, depending on the facts of the issue, the Assessing Officer may be barred from assessing or reassessing income involving matters which are the subject-matter of appeal, etc., in an earlier years.

7.5-2 Date of applicability - The proviso has been inserted with effect from 1-4-2008. So far as matters involving subject-matter of appeal, etc., are concerned, it appears that:

(a) the proviso applies to all reassessment proposed under section 147 on or after 1-4-2008 and a reassessment cannot be initiated on matters involving appeal, etc.

(b) the proviso also applies to reassessments already initiated on or before 1-4-2008 but not completed before that date and hence, a reassessment under section 147 cannot be made on or after 1-4-2008 on matters involving subject-matter of appeal, etc.

So far as other matters in cases where appeals are filed are concerned, the matter is not free from doubt. However, having regard to the fact that the amendment is to reflect the legislative intent which was also supported by a Bombay High Court judgment, it appears that it can no longer be argued that a matter cannot be reassessed even on grounds on which an assessee has not filed an appeal and a better view would be that such matters which are not in appeal can be assessed under section 147 on or after 1-4-2008 even in respect of assessment years prior to assessment year 2008-09.

Sanction for issue of Notice [Section 151]

7.6 Section 151 provides for sanction for issuance of notice.

The reason for an amendment as explained in the Memorandum is as follows:

“Section 151 of the Income-tax Act requires an Assessing Officer to seek the approval of the Joint Commissioner, in a case,—

◆ Where no assessment under section 143(3) or section 147 has been made for the relevant assessment year; and

◆ The notice is to be issued after expiry of four years from the end of the relevant assessment year.

It has been provided that notice in such a situation shall be issued by the Assessing Officer only when the Joint Commissioner is satisfied, on the reasons recorded by the Assessing Officer, that it is a fit case for the issue of such notice. Hon’ble Allahabad High Court in the case of Dr. Shashi Kant Garg v. The legislative intent, in such a situation, has been very clear. The Joint Commissioner is only required to be satisfied on the reasons recorded by the Assessing Officer. ITO [1989] 30 ITD 209 (Delhi - Trib.), the assessee-company, a manufacturer and exporter of readymade garments, claimed its status as an industrial company. The ITO while framing assessment under section 143(3) treated the assessee as a non-industrial company, whereupon the assessee moved an application before ITO stating that the Tribunal had in the assessee’s own case in earlier assessment years allowed its claim of being an industrial company. The ITO thereafter passed an order under section 154, accepting the assessee’s claim. The Commissioner by invoking section 263 cancelled ITO’s order holding that the assessee could not be an industrial company inasmuch as a major part of its income was from duty drawbacks and cash incentives. It was held that it was not a case where the Commissioner could have brought into limelight something new. There being no provision under the Act by which an order of assessment passed in conformity with the Tribunal’s decision can come up for review, change or cancellation under section 263, the Commissioner could not have invoked section 263. If the ITO passes an order of assessment in conformity with the Tribunal’s order, though such order is for the earlier assessment years, the Commissioner would not be entitled to exercise his jurisdiction under section 263 and cancel assessment or change the status.

Applying the principle laid down by the aforesaid judgment, it appears that for the purpose of the proviso to section 147, depending on the facts of the issue, the Assessing Officer may be barred from assessing or reassessing income involving matters which are the subject-matter of appeal, etc., in an earlier years.

7.5-2 Date of applicability - The proviso has been inserted with effect from 1-4-2008. So far as matters involving subject-matter of appeal, etc., are concerned, it appears that:

(a) the proviso applies to all reassessment proposed under section 147 on or after 1-4-2008 and a reassessment cannot be initiated on matters involving appeal, etc.

(b) the proviso also applies to reassessments already initiated on or before 1-4-2008 but not completed before that date and hence, a reassessment under section 147 cannot be made on or after 1-4-2008 on matters involving subject-matter of appeal, etc.

So far as other matters in cases where appeals are filed are concerned, the matter is not free from doubt. However, having regard to the fact that the amendment is to reflect the legislative intent which was also supported by a Bombay High Court judgment, it appears that it can no longer be argued that a matter cannot be reassessed even on grounds on which an assessee has not filed an appeal and a better view would be that such matters which are not in appeal can be assessed under section 147 on or after 1-4-2008 even in respect of assessment years prior to assessment year 2008-09.

1. On 24.04.2023, the Hon'ble Supreme Court delivered a judgment in a batch of Income- tax matters, the lead matter being Principal CIT v. Abhisar Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. [2023] 149 taxmann.com 399/293 Taxman 141 (hereinafter referred to as the Case). The matter of the civil appeal pertained to the scope and ambit of section 153A/153C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (hereinafter referred to as the Act).

2. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 6634 of 2021 in the case of DCIT, Central Circle 20 v. U.K. Paints (Overseas) Ltd. delivered a judgment on 25-4-2023 and dealt with the same issue as was in the case of Abhisar Buildwell case in regard to section 153C of the Act. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the last paragraph of the judgment held that, "However, so far as the prayer made on behalf of the Revenue to permit them to initiate the reassessment proceedings is concerned, it is observed that it will be open for the revenue to initiate the reassessment proceedings in accordance with law and if permissible under the law."

3. Background:

Notices under section 153A were issued for block period (six assessment years prior to year of search) and orders were passed considering incriminating material and other material available with the Assessing Officer (hereinafter referred to as the AO). Further, for a search initiated or requisition made after 1-4-2017, notices for four more years (7th to 10th) could also be issued, if the income represented in the form of asset, which has escaped assessment amounts to or is likely to amount to fifty lakh rupees or more in the relevant assessment year. In some cases, orders were passed considering only other material available in the record in the absence of incriminating material. Hon'ble Delhi High Court delivered a decision on 28-8-2015 in the case of Kabul Chawla [ITA No. 707 of 2014 (Commissioner of Income-tax (Central)-III v. Kabul Chawla)]. It was held that the AO does not have jurisdiction for passing order under Section 153A in the absence of incriminating material found during the search under Section 132 or requisition made under section 132A of the Act.

HEADNOTE: Section  148, read with section  149, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Income escaping assessment -  Issue of notice for (Period of limitation) - Assessment year  2014-15 - Assessee filed instant petition impugning reassessment notice issued under section 148 on 31-8-2022 pursuant to original notice dated 28-06-2021 (issued under old law) which was deemed to be a notice under section 148A(b) in view of Supreme Court ruling in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal l [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC) - It was noted that Assessing Officer had two days to issue notice under section 148 after receipt of assessee's reply - Said time expired on 16-6-2022 - However, impugned notice was issued on 31-8-2022, which was beyond said period - Whether, therefore, notice was beyond period of limitation - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 148 for assessment year 2014-15 on 28-6-2021. The said notice was unsustainable as it was issued in accordance with the statutory regime as existed prior to 31-3-2021. Some High Courts struck down notices that were issued under section 148 after 31-3-2021 but under the unamended provisions relating to the re-assessment of income that had escaped assessment.

■

The revenue appealed the decisions rendered by various High Courts to the Supreme Court of India. In Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC)which was one of such appeals arising from the decision of the Allahabad High Court - the Supreme Court delivered its decision on 4-5-2022, whereby it concurred with the view that the amended provisions which came into force after 31-3-2021 would be applicable to notices issued thereafter.

■

However, the Supreme Court also issued certain directions in exercise of powers under article 142 of the Constitution of India. The Court directed that all notices that were issued under section 148 after 1-4-2021 till the date of the said decision (4-5-2022), including those that had been set aside by the High Courts, would be construed as show cause notices under section 148A(b).

■

The Assessing Officers were directed to provide the information and material relied upon by the revenue for issuance of such notices, to the respective assessees within a period of thirty days from the date of the decision so as to enable the respective assessees to respond to the same.

■

In compliance with the directions issued by the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal (supra), the Assessing Officer provided information and material to the assessee on 30-5-2022. The assessee was granted two weeks' time to respond to the said notice.

■

The assessee responded to the notice dated 30-5-2022 on 11-6-2022. The Assessing Officer passed an order under section 148A(d) on 31-8-2022. According to the assessee, the same was beyond the period as stipulated.

■

On writ:

HELD: ■

In the instant case, the period of six years from the end of the assessment year for issuing a notice under section 148 expired on 31-3-2021. Thus, in terms of section 149, a notice under section 148 could not be issued. However, the said period was extended by the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 [TOLA]. Consequently, the time limit for issuing such a notice was extended to 30-6-2021. The original notice under section 148 was issued on 28-6-2021, which was two (2) days before the expiry of the period of limitation. [Para 6]

■

As per Mauna M. Bhatt, J. [Supplementing View]

It was contended that the decision in the case of UOI v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC) shall apply only to those notices, which were challenged before different High Courts: The Hon'ble Supreme Court in this case has adjudicated on the validity of reassessment notices issued by the Assessing Officers during the period 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021 i.e.; the time extended by TOLA and various notifications issued thereunder. As new law came in to force w.e.f 1-4-2021, it has held that these notices issued under section 148 (between 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021) shall be deemed to be the show cause notices issued under section 148A(b) of the new provision and further directed the Assessing Officer to follow the procedure with respect to such notices. Thus, it has created a fiction by directing to treat the notices issued under section 148 (unamended law), as notices issued under section 148A(b) (substituted provision) with a clear intention to save about 90,000/- proceedings, being conscious of the fact that there were approximately 90,000 such notices, which have been issued on a bonafide belief that old provisions would be applicable. Therefore, to strike a balance between rights of the revenue as well as respective assessees, keeping in mind that the revenue may not suffer as ultimately it is a public exchequer, the Supreme Court in exercise of its power under Article 142 of the Constitution of India, has made the order, which shall be applicable PAN India. Therefore, submissions of petitioners that the decision in the case of Ashish Agarwal (supra) would be applicable to the cases, where such notices have been challenged before different High Courts cannot be agreed upon. [Para 21.1]

It was contended that there cannot be any Notification when the provision itself was repealed. Further, by issuing notification, the executive cannot expand legislative power because it would amount to re-writing the law. By Notification, the subordinate legislation cannot override any statute enacted by Parliament.

On the aforesaid issue it is submitted by all counsel that by virtue of notification Nos. 20 of 2021 and 38 of 2021 dated 31-3-2021 and 27-4-2021 respectively, the time limit for issuing notice under section 148 has been extended up to 30-6-2021. By Notification No. 20 of 2021 dated 31-3-2021, the time limit to issue notice was extended up to 31-4-2021. When the Notification No 20 of 2021, was issued on 31-3-2021, the old law was in existence, and it ceases to exist w.e.f 1-4-2021. When the law itself ceases to exist w.e.f. 1-4-2021, the Notification will die a natural death and therefore there cannot be any Notification in respect of the repealed Act. Moreover, as the Notification No. 38 of 2021, dated 27-4-2021, was in continuation of the earlier Notification dated 31-3-2021 and once earlier notification ceases to apply, the consequential second Notification also ceases to apply. Various High Courts for the precise reason have held the said Notifications to be bad in Law and these findings have been upheld by the Supreme Court. It was further submitted that the two Notifications issued by the CBDT, dated 31-3-2021 and 27-4-2021, respectively amounts to extension of legislation or rewriting of legislation, not permitted under Law.

filed his return of income on 25-9-2015 declaring total income at Rs. 15.93 lakhs. The Assessing Officer on the basis of information that assessee had a suspicious transactions related to long term gain of Rs. 56.69 lakhs through RIL, penny stock company engaged in facilitating bogus LTCG and, therefore, reassessment proceedings under section 147 were initiated and notice under section 148 was issued on 13-4-2021.

■ Thereafter, the notice issued under section 148 dated 13-4-2021 was treated as notice under section 148A(a) and information was supplied under section 148A(b). After considering the submissions of assessee, order under section 148A(d) was passed and, thereafter, notice under section 148 was issued on 18-7-2022.

■

Notices under section 142(1) were issued from time to time which were duly complied by the assessee and finally the reassessment order was passed under section 147 read with section 144 dated 23-5-2023 by making addition of Rs. 56.35 lakhs as unexplained cash credit under section 68 holding the long term capital gain claimed exemption under section 10(38) by the assessee as bogus and further addition of Rs. 1.69 lakhs was made under section 69C on account of unexplained expenditure incurred to obtain such bogus long term capital gain.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the appeal of the assessee.

■

In the instant appeal, the assessee raised cross objection and submitted that the notice under section 148 was issued on 18-7-2022, however, the time limit available as per erstwhile section 149 expired on 31-3-2022 thus was beyond the period of limitation and provisions of TOLA werre not applicable. It was, thus, prayed by the assessee that the notices issued in the instant case for assessment year 2015-16 under section 148 being after 1-4-2021, therefore, the same deserved to be dropped and consequently the reassessment order be quashed.

HELD: ■

It is an admitted fact that earlier, the notice under section 148 in the case of assessee was issued on 13-4-2021 which was dropped and proceedings under section 148A were initiated in terms of order of Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 and finally the notice under section 148 was issued on 18-7-2022. The Additional Solicitor General of India in the case of Union of India v. Rajiv Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC)has made categorical statement at Bar before the Supreme Court that all the notices issued for assessment year 2015-16 on or after 1-4-2021 will be dropped, however, in the instant case, no such action was taken and re-assessment order was framed in the case of the assessee on the basis of the notice issued under section 148 on 18-7-2022.[Para 10]

■

Looking to the facts and considering the assessment year involved is 2015-16, notice issued in the case of originally on 13-4-2021 and later on 18-7-2022 which both the dates have fallen on or after 1-4-2021, therefore, both the notice deserves to be dropped in view of the admission made by the revenue before the Supreme Court. Further, for assessment year 2015-16, no notice under section 148 could be issued after the expiring of six years from the end of the relevant assessment year which limitation expired on 31-3-2022. Further, the Supreme Court in the case of Rajiv Bansal (supra) has observed that TOLA is not applicable for assessment year 2015-16, therefore, even otherwise under the old provisions of section 149, the notice issued under section 148 for assessment year 2015-16 on 18-7-2022 is barred by limitation. [Para 11]

■

In view of the above facts and by respectfully following the judgments of the Supreme Court in the case of Rajiv Bansal (supra) and in the case of Deepak Steel & Power Ltd. v. CBDT [2025] 174 taxmann.com 144/476 ITR 369 (SC) and Asstt.CIT v. Nehal Ashit Shah [SLP (CIVIL) Diary No (s) 57209 of 2024, dated 4-4-2025, the notice issued under section 148 on 18-7-2022 is barred by limitation and, therefore, the same is quashed. The cross objections taken by taken by the assesse are allowed. [Para 14]

ing Officer can take recourse to the extended limitation period if the conditions precedent prescribed in clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 149 are fulfilled. In other words, in a case where three (03) years from the end of the relevant assessment year have elapsed, the Assessing Officer can issue a notice under section 148 provided the conditions prescribed in clause (b) of section 149(1) of the amended 1961 Act are fulfilled. [Para 26] A careful perusal of clause (b) of section 149 would show that one of the conditions for triggering the extended period, which goes up to ten (10) years in cases where three (03) years have elapsed, is that income chargeable to tax which has escaped assessment amounts to, or is likely to amount to Rs. 50 lakhs or more for the assessment year in issue. [Para 27]

Therefore, after the coming into force of FA 2021, in cases where, for the relevant assessment year, the alleged escaped income was less than Rs. 50 lakhs, notice under section 148 could only be issued for commencement of reassessment proceedings within the limitation period provided in clause (a) of section 149(1) of the amended 1961 Act. [Para 28]

Thus, in the ordinary course, the limitation for assessment year 2016-17 would expire on 31-3-2020; likewise, for assessment year 2017-18, the end date for the culmination of the limitation period would be 31-3-2021. [Para 29]

The revenue seeks to take recourse to the provisions of section 3(1) of TOLA and the Notifications issued thereunder, from time-to-time, which, in effect, extended the end date for completion of proceedings and compliances up until 30-6-2021. [Para 30]

In this regard, the last two notifications. Via Notification dated 31-3-2021, the end date was extended till 30-4-2021 may be refund. The Notification immediately following the said Notification, i.e., Notification dated 27-4-2021, extended the end date to 30-6-2021. Thus, the span concerning the extension of end dates was spread between 20-3-2020 and 30-6-2021. [Para 30.1]

It is, therefore, the revenue's case that the impugned actions, which involved passing of orders under section 148A(d) and issuance of notices under section 148 taken between 1-4-2021 (when FA 2021 kicked in) and 30-6-2021 were valid in the eyes of the law. [Para 31]

Briefly, the Supreme Court was called upon to grapple with a piquant situation, which was the creation of the revenue, concerning the viability of notices issued on or after 1-4-2021, when FA 2021 had already kicked in. [Para 32.1]

The Supreme Court noticed that with the enactment and enforcement of FA 2021, sections 147 to 149 and section 151, as they stood on 31-3-2021, had been substituted, bringing about radical and reformative changes in the matters concerning reassessment proceedings. Taking cognizance of this state of affairs, the Supreme Court held that, since the new provisions substituted by FA 2021 were both remedial and benevolent, they would apply to past Assessment years provided section 148 notices had been issued on or after 1-4-2021. This was also the view taken by various High Courts; a view which was sustained by the Supreme Court. [Para 32.2]

The Supreme Court, however, having regard to the fact that the procedure prescribed under the new regime (which was encapsulated in FA 2021) had not been followed, modified the judgments of the High Courts by issuing specific directions to balance the interests of the assessees and the revenue. [Para 32.3]

The Supreme Court was persuaded to modify the judgments, having regard to the fact that if the decisions of various courts, including that of the coordinate bench of this court in Mon Mohan Kohli v. Asstt. CIT [2021] 133 taxmann.com 166/[2022] 441 ITR 207 (Delhi), were to be sustained as is, it would result in the failure of reassessment proceedings, even if the same were "permissible" under FA 2021 and as per the substituted provisions incorporated in the statutes, i.e., sections 147 to 149 and section 151. [Para 32.4]

The directions were issued by the Supreme Court based on a broad consensus arrived at between the learned ASG representing the revenue and counsels representing the assessees. [Para 33]

Notices issued by the Assessing Officer under the unamended section 148 which were the subject matter of writ actions preferred before various High Courts, were deemed to have been issued under section 148A(b). [Para 34]

As would be evident, there was no discussion or deliberation concerning the provisions of TOLA or the Notifications issued thereunder. [Para 35]

The High Court considering order in Daujee Abhushan Bhandar (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2022] 136 taxmann.com 246 (All.) disposed writ petition directing the respondent-authority concerned to decide the objection of the assessee against the notice under section 148, in accordance with law on the point of date of issuance of notice.

Following said direction of the High Court, the respondent No. 4/Assessing Officer rejected objection of the assessee observing that though High Court had quashed such notices issued under section 148 on or after 1-4-2021 but department had filed SLP before the Supreme Court on this issue and therefore till outcome of issue pending before the Supreme Court, it could not be said that notice under section 148 issued to the assessee was not valid.

The High Court having noticed that order passed by the respondent No. 4 in connection with disposal of objection of the assessee was highly contemptuous, whimsical and against all settled principles of propriety directed respondent No. 4 to file a personal affidavit to explain the things.

HELD: From the averments made by the respondent Nos. 2, 3 and 4 in the short counter affidavit, it is evident that the notice under section 148 for the assessment year 2013-14 was issued to the petitioner on 1-4-2021, whereas the limitation of issuing the notice expired on 31-3-2021. Thus notice under section 148 was time barred and consequently it was without jurisdiction. [Para 8]

Since large number of writ petitions are being filed in which the date and time of issuance of notice under section 148 are in issue, and, importantly, those notices are being issued by e-mail, it is directed that the respondent No. 1 shall ensure that the date and time of triggering of e-mail for issuing notices and orders are reflected in the online portal relating to the concerned assessees. FACT: ■

The assessee filed his return of income on 25-9-2015 declaring total income at Rs. 15.93 lakhs. The Assessing Officer on the basis of information that assessee had a suspicious transactions related to long term gain of Rs. 56.69 lakhs through RIL, penny stock company engaged in facilitating bogus LTCG and, therefore, reassessment proceedings under section 147 were initiated and notice under section 148 was issued on 13-4-2021.

■

the period for limitation for issuance of Notice under amended section 148 to reopen an assessment, it is three years but not more than 10 years. Correspondingly, the monetary and pecuniary jurisdiction for reopening the assessment were also altered. This has also been captured by the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal, [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70 (SC)/ 2024 SCC OnLine SC 2693. [Para 14]

■ The Supreme Court has also taken note of the relaxation in the period of limitation for various assessment years in the light of the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation & Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 (hereinafter referred to as the 'TOLA') with effect from 20-11-2020 and the Finance Act, 2021 amending the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961 with effect from 1-4-2021. In accordance with TOLA, as far as the assessment year 2017-18 is concerned, the period of limitation for issuance of Notice under section 148 read with section 149 as amended by Finance Act, 2021 with effect from 1-4-2021 would be till 30-6-2021, instead of 30-3-2021 and under the old regime on 31-3-2024. This was also captured in the submissions of the Additional Solicitor General of India on behalf of the Income Tax Department before the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal, (supra). This position has not been disputed. [Para 15]

■

However, the first proviso to section 149 prohibits issuance of a reassessment notice under the new regime if such notices have become time barred under the old regime. Therefore, the last date for issuance of Notice under section 148 would have expired on 30-6-2021, as per the third Proviso to section 149(1)(b) as in force with effect from 1-4-2021. The time during which stay was in operation or the time during which, the assessee took time to file the reply, the Notice issued under section 148(A)(b) stands expelled. In this case, the reply itself was filed by the petitioner only on 31-5-2022, pursuant to which the Impugned Order was passed on 30-6-2022 under section 148(A)(d) and Notice under section 148 was issued. Though the limitation for issuance of a Notice under section 148 under the old regime would have expired on 31-3-2024, a reading of conclusion in the decision of the Supreme Court in UOI v. Rajeev Bansal (supra), however indicates that the Impugned Notice dated 30-6-2022 has to be treated as having been issued beyond the limitation period. [Para 16]

■

Dealing with almost an identical situation pursuant to the decision of the Supreme Court in UOI v. Rajeev Bansal (supra), the Delhi High Court quashed the notice dated 31-3-2021 issued to the assessee under section 148 and the proceedings. Since the law laid down by the Supreme Court in UOI v. Rajeev Bansal (supra) is a settled law, it is binding on this Court. [Para 17]

■

Therefore, this Writ Petition deserves to be allowed and is accordingly allowed. [Para 18]

HEADNOTE: Section  148A,  read with sections  148  and  149, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  280,  read with sections  279  and  281  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Income escaping assessment – Conducting inquiry, providing opportunity before issue of notice (TOLA) – Assessment year  2015-16  – Based on information that immovable properties had been sold for Rs. 1.88 crores as against stamp duty value of Rs. 16.08 crores, notice under section 148 was issued on 29-6-2021 under unamended provisions – Pursuant to Supreme Court decision in UOI v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC), said notice was treated as one under section 148A; information was supplied, opportunity was granted, order under section 148A(d) was passed and fresh notice under section 148 was issued on 29-7-2022 – CIT(A) quashed reassessment holding that reopening for AY 2015-16 was barred by limitation in view of UOI v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/469 ITR 46/301 Taxman 238 (SC), since TOLA applied only where limitation fell between 20-3-2020 and 31-3-2021 – Whether since revenue failed to point out any infirmity in said finding, said view was to be upheld – Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee filed a return for AY 2015-16 declaring income of about Rs. 66.49 lakhs. Based on information that immovable properties were sold for about Rs. 1.89 crores against stamp duty value of about Rs. 16.08 crores, the case was reopened under section 147 after obtaining prior approval.

■

An original notice under section 148 was issued on 29-6-2021 under the unamended provisions. Pursuant to Supreme Court ruling in UOI v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC), the notice was treated as one under section 148A, an order under section 148A(d) was passed, a fresh notice under section 148 was issued on 29-7-2022, and reassessment was completed on 19-5-2023.

■

On appeal, the CIT(A) quashed the reassessment holding that reopening for assessment year 2015-16 was barred by limitation in view of UOI v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/469 ITR 46/301 Taxman 238 (SC), holding that TOLA applied only where limitation fell between 20-3-2020 and 31-3-2021.

■

On appeal by revenue to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The reassessment in the present case pertains to AY 2015-16. The CIT(A), following the decision of the Supreme Court in Rajeev Bansal (supra), held that the reopening proceedings for AY 2015-16 were barred by limitation, particularly in view of the specific concession recorded on behalf of the revenue. The CIT(A) has given detailed reasons for that conclusion, and the revenue was unable to point out any infirmity in the impugned order. Accordingly, all three grounds raised by the revenue are dismissed. [Para 10]

■

In the result, the appeal of the Assessing Officer is dismissed. [Para 11]

on 28-7-2022 under section 148 of the new regime is barred by limitation and hence bad in law, liable to be quashed, resulting in impugned reassessment proceedings as well as the impugned reassessment order bad in law. Accordingly, ground nos. 1 and 2 raised by the revenue are dismissed. Resultantly, grounds raised on the merits of the case are rendered academic and hence not adjudicated upon. [Para 10.2]

■ Now, with respect to the appeal by the revenue and cross objection by the assessee for assessment year 2015-16. Appeal by the revenue is on the merits of the case whereas cross objection by the assessee is on challenging the legal issue of notice under section 148 as bad in law, invalid, void ab initio, to be quashed. Accordingly, the legal issue raised by the assessee through its cross objection is taken up as it goes to the root of the matter. [Para 11]

■

Identical chronology of events exists for assessment year 2015-16 as discussed while adjudicating appeal for assessment year 2014-15 in the above paragraphs, except for date of filing of return. Notice under section 148 of the old regime was issued on 30-6-2021. Later, pursuant to the judgment in case of Ashish Agarwal (supra), it was directed among other things that notice issued under section 148 shall be deemed to have been issued under section 148A as substituted by the Finance Act, 2021 and construed or treated to be the show cause notice in terms of section 148A(b). In view of this direction, the said notice under section 148, dated 30-6-2021 was deemed to be a show cause notice under section 148A(b) for which another one was issued on 26-5-2022, complying with the direction given in the case of Ashish Agarwal (supra). [Para 12]

■

Thereafter, provisions of section 148A(d) were complied with by passing an order, dated 28-7-2022 and issuing a notice under section 148 of the same date (under the new regime). Assessee has contested by raising a ground of cross objection that the notice so issued is bad in law, invalid, void ab initio, to be quashed. The assessee strongly submitted that it is barred by limitation making the impugned reassessment proceedings and resultant reassessment order bad in law. [Para 12.1]

■

At the outset, it is found that this issue has been settled in the case of Rajeev Bansal (supra) wherein reference is made to the submissions made on behalf of the revenue which is relevant. [Para 12.2]

■

Thus, it can be seen that revenue conceded before the Supreme Court for dropping all the notices issued on or after 1-4-2021 for assessment year 2015-16 as they will not fall for completion during the period prescribed under TOLA. [Para 12.3]

■

In the case of present assessee, since the notice issued under section 148 is dated 28-7-2022, period of six years expired on 31-3-2022 and is thus barred by limitation. Accordingly, notice so issued and re-assessment completed thereafter under section 147 is liable to be quashed, in view of the decision of Supreme Court in the case of Rajeev Bansal (supra). [Para 12.5]

■

HEADNOTE: Section 148 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Reassessment - Notice for - Assessment year 1984-85 - Whether simply preparing notice under section 148 but keeping it on file past limitation period does not tantamount to issuing same, and, thus, such notice is bad in law - Held, yes

FACT: The Assessing Officer completed assessment under section 143(3) for the assessment year 1984-85 on 15-5-1985. Subsequently he wanted to rectify the order. Hence, reasons were recorded by him on 12-10-1988 and the notice under section 148 was prepared on the same day, but it was served on the assessee sometime in November 1989. The reassessment was later completed. The Commissioner (Appeals) cancelled the reassessment as the notice was beyond the time-limit permissible under section 149(1)(a)( i).

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: In the instant case, the reasons were recorded on 12-10-1988. The notice was also made out on the same day. However, there was nothing on record to show that the same was issued by 31-3-1989. All the judicial authorities unequivocally point out that the notice should actually be set in motion for being served on the assessee. Simply preparing the notice but keeping it on file past the limitation period did not tantamount to issuing the same. In the case of CIT v. Sheo Kumari Debi [1986] 157 ITR 13/ 24 Taxman 77 , the Patna High Court quoting from Chamber’s Twentieth Century Dictionary, observed that the relevant meanings of the word ‘issue’ are : act of sending out; to put forth; to put into circulation; to publish; to give out for use. Thus keeping the notice on file after preparing it does not fit into any of these meanings to be described as ‘issued’. After issuing it as described above, it is immaterial when it is served. It may be served even after three years, but the essence is that it should be set into motion for being served. And, the onus to show that it is so issued lies on the department, who in the instant case, had failed to do so.

The revenue’s contention that once the notice was made out, the process of setting it into motion was presumed, was certainly rebuttable.

In the instant case, the glaring facts themselves demolished the presumption laid down in section 114 of the Evidence Act that all official acts are regularly performed. The notice was made out more than five months before the period of limitation was to expire, but was served on the assessee about thirteen months after it was prepared.

The original records of the department did not show that the notice was despatched before 31-3-1989. Under these circumstances, normal presumption would be that the notice must have been set into motion for being served only a few days before 9-11-1989. In the ultimate analysis, just as ‘issue’ and ‘service’ are held not to be synonymous by most of the courts, including the Apex Court, the words ‘preparation’ and ‘issue’ are also not synonymous.

Therefore, the notice under section 148 was bad in law, and the Commissioner (Appeals)’s order called for no interference.

It appeared that the High Court directed the AAC to decide the assessee's appeal in accordance with law and in doing so to also ascertain when the notice under section 148 had been despatched by registered post. There was, thus, no occasion to interfere with the order made by the High Court.

On cross objection :

HELD: ■

The Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC) has clarified that the Assessing Officer was required to complete these procedures within the 'surviving time limit' which can be calculated by computing the number of days between the date of issuance of the deemed notice under section 148A(d) and 30-6-2021 (i.e. the extended time limit provided by TOLA for issuing reassessment notices under section 148, which fell for completion from 20-3-2020 to 31-3-2021). , the issues before the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India were, (a) Whether TOLA and notifications issued under it will also apply to reassessment notices issued after 1 April 2021; and (b) whether the reassessment notices issued under Section 148 of the new regime between July and September, 2022 are valid. Thus, when the revenue in their counter had not relied upon TOLA and since it is not contended that the period is extended or saved by any of the provisions of TOLA the concession that no provision of TOLA is applicable and that the notices have to be dropped cannot be extrapolated to the facts on the instant case as the revenue sought to justify by the interpretations of the Sections 148, 148A and 149 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. On writ petitions before the High Court.

HELD: ■

To determine this question, the ratio laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal (2024) SCC OnLine SC 2693; [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/469 ITR 46/301 Taxman 238 (SC) and Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/444 ITR 1/286 Taxman 183 (SC)/(2023) 1 SCC 617 have to be kept in mind. The legal position as obtained is lucidly explained by the Hon'ble Division Bench in Income-tax Officer v. Mahogany Logistics Services (P.) Ltd. [2025] 176 taxmann.com 478 (Madras). [Para 17]

HEADNOTE: Section  149,  read with sections  147  and  148, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  282,  read with sections  279  and  280  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Income escaping assessment – Time limit for issuance of notice (TOLA) - Assessment year  2015-16  - Pursuant to survey under section 133A in case of Babylon Group, reassessment proceedings were initiated against assessee on allegation of cash receipt of Rs. 1 crore from sale of immovable property - AO issued notice under section 148 on 30-6-2021 and thereafter, pursuant to decision in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64 (SC)/[2022] 286 Taxman 183 (SC)/[2022] 444 ITR 1 (SC) , issued fresh notice under section 148 on 26-7-2023 under new regime - Whether for assessment year 2015-16, notices issued under section 148 on or after 1-4-2021 were liable to be dropped as they would not fall for completion within period prescribed under TOLA - Held, yes - Whether therefore, notice issued under section 148 dated 26-7-2023 and consequential reassessment proceedings were liable to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 13] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, an individual, filed return of income for AY 2015-16 on 30-06-2016 declaring income of about Rs. 7 lakhs. A survey under section 133A was conducted on 30-05-2017 in case of Babylon Group engaged in hotel business, during which a hard disk impounded from premises of Hotel Babylon Continental, Raipur, revealed huge cash transactions relating to investment in hotel project and sale/purchase of immovable properties during FYs 2013-14 to 2016-17. On examination of extracted data, the AO noted that the assessee, being one of sellers of immovable property, had allegedly received cash of Rs. 1 crore during FY 2014-15 which was not reflected in his books of account, though receipts through banking channels were reflected. The AO accordingly recorded reasons and reopened assessment for AY 2015-16.

■

The AO issued notice under section 148 on 30-06-2021 under old regime. Pursuant to decision of Supreme Court in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64 (SC)/[2022] 286 Taxman 183 (SC)/[2022] 444 ITR 1 (SC), the AO issued notice under section 148A(b) on 21-5-2022, passed order under section 148A(d) on 25-7-2023 and thereafter issued fresh notice under section 148 on 26-7-2023 under new regime. The reassessment was completed under section 147 read with section 144B by making addition of Rs. 1 crore under section 69A.

■

On appeal, the CIT(A)/NFAC upheld validity of reassessment proceedings and sustained addition made under section 69A.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

It is an admitted fact that the assessee filed his return of income on 30-6-2016. A survey action under section 133A was carried out on 30-5-2017 in the case of Babylon Group who are engaged in hotel sector. The Assessing Officer, after recording reasons, reopened the assessment and accordingly issued notice under section 148 on 30-6-2021. Subsequently on the basis of decision of Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal (supra), the Assessing Officer issued notice under section 148A(b) on 21-5-2022. After considering the reply of the assessee the Assessing Officer passed an order under section 148A(d) on 25-7-2023 and issued notice under section 148 on 26-7-2023 under the new regime. Thereafter, the Assessing Officer completed the assessment under section 147 read with section 144B wherein he made addition of Rs.1.00 crore under section 69A. The CIT(A)/NFAC upheld the re-assessment proceedings as well addition on merit. Under these circumstances, the issue for determination is whether the notice issued under section 148 for the assessment year 2015-16 on 26-7-2023 is a valid notice or not. [Para 10]

■

HEADNOTE: Section  149, read with section  148, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Income escaping assessment -  Time limit for issuance of notice (Reassessment) - Assessment year  2013-14 - Whether entire process under section 148A(a) to (d) and issuance of notice under section 148 has to be completed within total time available in terms of section 149(1) for issuance of notice - Held, yes - Assessee filed return of income for assessment year 2013-14 - Assessment was completed under section 143(3) - On 29-6-2021, notice under unamended section 148 was issued, which was later treated as a deemed notice under section 148A(b) - Assessing Officer issued final notice under section 148 on 29-7-2022 after supplying reasons and materials and completing process under section 148A - Whether after accounting for permissible exclusions under substituted section 149, time available to complete reassessment process had expired on 23-7-2022 - Held, yes - Whether since notice under section 148 was issued beyond said time, same was barred by limitation and, thus, reassessment proceedings and consequential assessment order were to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 16 to 21] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee filed his return of income for assessment year 2013-14 on 31-3-2014, declaring an income of Rs. 37.18 lakhs. The assessment was completed under section 143(3) on 23-2-2016 at an assessed income of Rs. 60.60 lakhs.

■

On 29-6-2021, a notice under the unamended section 148 was issued to the assessee. Pursuant to the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC), the said notice was treated as a deemed notice under section 148A(b).

■

Subsequently, the Assessing Officer issued reasons for reopening on 20-5-2022. The assessee filed objections and replies dated 3-6-2022 and 28-6-2022, raising jurisdictional and limitation-related grounds, including that the reassessment was time-barred under the amended section 149.

■

Thereafter, the Assessing Officer passed an order under section 148A(d) and issued a notice under section 148 on 29-7-2022.

■

In the instant writ, the assessee challenged the said notice and subsequent assessment proceedings primarily on the ground that the same were time-barred under the substituted provisions of section 149.

HELD: ■

In terms of the decisions in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC) and Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC)the following position emerges in the context of the present case :-

(i)

The period for subject reassessment in terms of section 149 of the old regime is deemed to be extended till 30-6-2021 under the TOLA.

(ii)

The notice dated 29-6-2021 would be deemed to be notice under section 148A(b).

(iii)

The surviving period by excluding the date of re-issuance of notice on 29-6-2021 would be the remainder days in the month of June 2021 (30-6-2021 - 28-6-2021), namely, two days.

(iv)

On 30-6-2021, the extension in terms of the TOLA would come to an end. (v) The period that stands excluded is :

(a)

The period up to 30-6-2021, which is covered by the provisions of the IT Act read with the TOLA.

(b)

The period from 1-7-2021 to 3-5-2022 being the period before the decision of the Supreme Court in Ashish Agarwal (supra).

(c)

The Period from 4-5-2022 till 20-5-2022, which is the date when the material was furnished and the reasons for re-opening were given to the petitioner.

(d)

The issue with regard to issuance of notice for reassessment under section 148 on a dead person is no more res integra in view of the decision of the Gujarat High Court rendered in the case of Bhupendra Bhikhalal Desai v. ITO [2021] 130 taxmann.com 196 (Gujarat), wherein notice issued under section 153C against a dead person is held to be defective and consequently quashed and set aside. [Para 14]

■ The Supreme Court by order dated 3-9-2021 passed in ITO v. Bhupendra Bhikhalal Desai [2021] 131 taxmann.com 40/283 Taxman 189 (SC) dismissed the SLP confirming the order passed by the Gujarat High Court in the case of Bhupendra Bhikhalal Desai (supra). [Para 16]

■

In view of the above conspectus of law, the petition succeeds and is accordingly allowed. Impugned notice issued under section 148 and consequential assessment order passed under section 144 read with section 147 as well as the order passed under section 271F levying penalty are hereby quashed and set aside. [Para 17]

HEADNOTE: Section  149,  read with sections  148  and  148A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  282,  read with sections  280  and  281  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Income escaping assessment – Time limit for issuance of notice (Illustrations) - Assessment year  2015-16  - Assessee, an individual, did not file return under section 139(1) for Assessment year  2015-16  - Information on INSIGHT/NMS portal showed interest income of about Rs. 0.86 lakh and sale of an immovable property for about Rs. 1.22 crores - Proceedings under section 148A were initiated and, after an order under section 148A(d), notice under section 148 was issued on 02.04.2022 - Whether since limitation prescribed under erstwhile provisions of section 149 expired on 31.03.2022, whereas notice under section 148 was issued only on 02.04.2022, impugned notice issued under section 148 on 02.04.2022 for Assessment year  2015-16  was barred by limitation under section 149 (as amended by Finance Act, 2021) and therefore liable to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 10] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, an individual, did not file a return under section 139(1) for AY 2015-16. Information on the INSIGHT/NMS portal showed interest income of about Rs. 0.86 lakh and sale of an immovable property for about Rs. 1.22 crores. Proceedings under section 148A were initiated and, after an order under section 148A(d), notice under section 148 was issued on 02.04.2022. In response, on 26.02.2024, the assessee filed a return declaring total income of about Rs. 9.02 lakhs, including LTCG of about Rs. 7.44 lakhs and claiming deduction under section 54F.

■

During reassessment, the AO sought supporting documents; noting that no sale deed, inheritance proof, cost/improvement evidence, or proof of section 54F investment was furnished and that the original return under section 139(1) was not filed, the AO completed assessment under sections 143(3) r.w.s. 144B and 147 by treating the entire sale consideration of about Rs. 1.22 crores as STCG, denying indexation and section 54F.

■

On appeal, the CIT(A) upheld the validity of the reassessment and sustained the addition, recording that the assessee did not furnish requisite evidences.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The Tribunal has carefully considered the rival submissions and perused the material available on record. Substantial force is found in the legal ground raised by the assessee challenging the validity of the reassessment proceedings. It is an undisputed fact that for Assessment Year 2015-16, the limitation prescribed under the erstwhile provisions of section 149 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 expired on 31.03.2022, whereas the notice under section 148 was issued only on 02.04.2022. In view of the first proviso to section 149 inserted by the Finance Act, 2021, no notice under section 148 could have been issued for AY 2015-16 after 31.03.2022 where such notice had already become time-barred under the erstwhile provisions of the Act. [Para 8]

■

The above legal position now stands conclusively settled by the Supreme Court in ITO v. Sai Kumar Mateti (Civil Appeal No. 6922 of 2026, arising out of SLP (Civil) No. 8682 of 2024, decided on 04-05-2026). The Supreme Court, while considering reassessment notices pertaining to AY 2015-16, categorically held that such notices would be barred by limitation in light of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal ([2024] 167 taxmann.com 70; 469 ITR 46; 301 Taxman 238 (SC); 2024 SCC OnLine SC 2693). The Supreme Court observed that where the reassessment proceedings pertain to AY 2015-16, the notices are liable to be struck down outrightly as being time-barred. [Para 9]

■

that only two days of “surviving time” were available (28.06.2021 to 30.06.2021) and, therefore, the notice dated 28.07.2022 was barred by limitation.

■

The revenue on the other hand argued that since assessee did not reply, the Assessing Officer had 30 days under section 148A to complete the proceedings and notice dated 28.07.2022 was within time.

HELD: ■ The Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC) explaining the ratio laid down in similar judgment of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/444 ITR 1/286 Taxman 183 (SC) wherein the Supreme Court had exercised its discretionary jurisdiction under article 142 of the Constitution of India while explaining the old law and new law under section 148, has created a legal fiction and balancing act on the existing legal framework of procedure of reassessment. Wherever the notice under section 148 were issued under the old regime for which time limit was extended up to 30-6-2021, the Apex Court held that it would be deemed that reassessment notice issued under the old regime shall be treated as show-cause notice issued under section 148A(b) of the new regime. Further the Court directed the revenue to provide all the relevant material/information to the assessee and thereafter, allowed the assessee to respond to the show-cause notice and raised its objection or availing any kind of defenses including available under section 149. Thus, the Supreme Court balanced the equities between the revenue and the assessee by giving effect to the legislative scheme of reassessment as contained under the new regime. The Court thus supplemented the existing legal framework of the procedure of reassessment under the Income-tax Act with the principles grounded in equitable standards. [Para 7]

■

Thus, the Supreme Court had explained the concept of surviving or balance time limit which is to be calculated by computing number of days between dates of issuance of deemed notice and 30-6-2021. Thereafter, the Supreme Court has elaborated the effect of the legal fiction propounded in the case of UOI v. Ashish Agarwal which has been explained. [Para 8]

■

The sequitor of the aforesaid observation and the judgment of the Supreme Court are that-

■

Firstly, exclusion of the period has been explained;

(a)

the date of issuance notice under section 148 under the old regime reckoned to be the date of issuance of the deemed notices under section 148A(b);

(b)

the period from the date of the issuance of the deemed notices till the supply of relevant information and material by the assessing officers to the assessees is to be excluded from the computation of the period of limitation;

(c)

further, period of two weeks granted to the assessee to reply to the show-cause notice is also to be excluded in terms of third proviso to section 149;

■

Secondly, once the response of the assessee to the showcause notice has been received, then "the clock starts ticking for the Revenue", that is, after the receipt of reply, the Assessing Officer has to;

(a)

consider the reply of the assessee under section148A(c);

(b)

take a decision under section148A(d) based on the available material and the reply of the assessee; and

(c)

issue a notice under section148 if it was a fit case for reassessment.

■

Once it is found to be a fit case for re-assessment, the limitation clock starts ticking and it is mandatory for the Assessing Officer to comply with these procedures within the surviving time limit which was available to the Assessing Officer to issue re-assessment notice under section148 of the new regime; and

■

Lastly, the Supreme Court has given an example as how to calculate the surviving time. Calculation of surviving time has been laid down from the period when the first notice u/s.148 was issued under old regime till the last date of limitation for issuance of notice under section148 of the old regime; and that period has been reckoned as the surviving time period left for the Assessing Officer while issuing notice under section148 under the new regime. So whatever surviving time is left the Assessing Officer has to issue notice within that surviving time.[Para 9]

■

If the surviving time like here in this case is only two days, because original notice under section 148 under the old regime was issued on 28-6-2021 and the last date on which notice could have been issued under old regime was up till 30-6-2021; and therefore, the surviving time left was only two days for issuing a notice under the new regime under section 148 after completion of the procedure laid down under section 148A(b) to 148(d).

■

Ergo, the Assessing Officer was required to issue notice under section 148 of the new regime within the time surviving under the Income-tax Act read with TOLA and any notices issued beyond the surviving period was declared to be time barred by the Supreme Court. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: I. Section  69,  read with sections  147,  148  and   148A , of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  103,  read with sections  279  and  280  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained investments (Reassessment) – Assessment year  2015-16  – Whether reassessment proceedings initiated pursuant to notice under section 148 dated 12-4-2022 for AY 2015-16 were barred by limitation and liable to be quashed – Held, yes – Whether further, where Assessing Officer issued notice under section 148 without verifying registered Deed of Apartment and earlier registered Agreement for Sale and proceeded mechanically without application of mind, notice under section 148 and consequent reassessment order were bad in law and void ab initio – Held, yes [Paras 3, 4 and 6.3] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee filed an appeal against the order passed under section 250 dated 23-7-2025 for AY 2015-16 arising from reassessment order dated 26-3-2024 passed under section 147 read with section 144B.

■

The reassessment proceedings were initiated on the basis of information available on the Income Tax Portal that the assessee had purchased an immovable property.

■

The AO issued notice under section 148 dated 12-4-2022 and passed order under section 148A(d) on the same date for AY 2015-16.

■

During reassessment proceedings, the assessee furnished copy of registered Deed of Apartment, which referred to an earlier registered Agreement for Sale dated 12-12-2013 specifying payment schedule relating to property purchase.

■

It was contended that the AO had issued notice under section 148 mechanically without verifying the registered sale documents and relevant facts before reopening assessment.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

In this case the Notice u/s 148 for AY 2015-16 was dated 12-4-2022 and the order u/s 148A(d) was dated 12-4-2022 for AY 2015-16. [Para 2.1]

■

The Supreme Court in the case of Deepak Steel and Power Ltd. v. CBDT [2025] 174 taxmann.com 144/305 Taxman 169/476 ITR 369 (SC)/[2025] 476 ITR 369 (SC) [02-04-2025] held as under: 'The Revenue concedes that for the assessment year 2015-2016, all notices issued on or after 1-4-2021 will have to be dropped as they will not fall for completion during the period prescribed under the Taxation and other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act. As the revenue made a concession in the aforesaid decision that is for the assessment year 2015-16, all notices issued on or after 1-4-2021 will have to be dropped as they would not fall for completion during the period prescribed under the taxation and other laws (Relaxation and Amendment of certain Provisions Act, 2020). Nothing further is required to be adjudicated in this matter as the notices so far as the present litigation is concerned is dated 25-6-2021. In view of the aforesaid, in such circumstances referred to above the original writ petition nos.2446 of 2023, 2543 of 2023 and 2544 of 2023 respectively filed before the High Court of Orissa at cuttack stands allowed. The impugned notice therein stands quashed and set aside.' [Para 3]

■

The above referred decision of the Supreme Court was respectfully followed by the Gujarat High Court in the case of Mayurkumar Babubhai Patel v. Asstt. CIT[2025] 176 taxmann.com 25 (Gujarat). [Para 3.1]

■

HEADNOTE: Section  148,  read with sections  147,  144  and  144B, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Income escaping assessment  -  Issue of notice for  (Limitation) - Assessment year  2015-16  - Whether notice under section 148 issued on 23-4-2022 for assessment year 2015-16, being issued after 1-4-2021, was beyond limitation and therefore without jurisdiction - Held, yes - Whether consequently reassessment order, demand notice, penalty notices/orders and recovery notices were to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 11] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 148 dated 23-4-2022 for assessment year 2015-16 and thereafter passed a reassessment order dated 11-3-2024 under section 147 read with sections 144 and 144B, issued a demand notice under section 156, initiated penalty proceedings, and commenced recovery action, threatening the petitioner with coercive steps.

■

The petitioner filed a writ petition before the High Court seeking to quash the notice issued under section 148 and all consequential proceedings, including the reassessment order, demand notice, and penalty notices/orders, contending that the notice was barred by limitation as it was issued after 1-4-2021 and therefore was without jurisdiction.

■

It was submitted that an appeal against the reassessment order had already been filed before the Commissioner (Appeals) and was pending, and the petitioner undertook to withdraw the appeal if the writ petition was allowed.

HELD: ■

It is not in dispute that the present petition relates to assessment year 2015-16. Further, it is also undisputed that the notice under section 148 has been issued on 23-4-2022. [Para 6]

■

From the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of UOI v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70 /301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC) it is clear, that the department has conceded before the Supreme Court that all the notices issued under section 148 after 1-4-2021 for assessment year 2015-16 have to be dropped. In the present case, the notice under section 148 is dated 23-4-2022 and therefore, has to be dropped. [Para 7]

■

The decision in Rajeev Bansal (supra) has been subsequently followed by the Supreme Court in Deepak Steel and Power Ltd. v. CBDT [2025] 174 taxmann.com 144/305 Taxman 169/476 ITR 369 (SC). [Para 8]

■

Similarly, even in the matter of Asstt. CIT v. Nehal Ashit Shah [SLP (Civil) Diary No.(S) 57209/2024, dated 4-4-2025], the Supreme Court, relying upon paragraphs 19(e) and (f) of the decision in case of Rajeev Bansal (supra), dismissed the SLP filed by the revenue. [Para 9]

■

Lastly, this very Bench on 6-10-2025, in the matter of Verjinia Foods Ltd. v. ITO [2025] 179 taxmann.com 626/307 Taxman 563 (Bombay), has allowed the petition filed by the Petitioner therein by noting that since the notice under section 148 was issued after 1-4-2021, the same was required to be set aside in light of the concession made by the revenue before the Supreme Court in the case of Rajeev Bansal (supra). [Para 10]

■

In light of the above discussion, there is merit in the submissions as canvassed by the assessee. The revenue has categorically made a concession that for assessment year 2015-16 they would drop all notices issued under section 148 after 1-4-2021. Once this is the position, it is appropriate that the notice under section 148 dated 23-4-2022, and the consequential assessment order, notice of demand, penalty notices/orders as well as the recovery notices be quashed and set aside. It is accordingly so ordered. [Para 11]

HEADNOTE: Section 148, read with sections 149 and 151, of the Income tax Act, 1961 - Reassessment - Whether prescribed period of limitation for reassessment is to be reckoned from end of relevant assessment year and not financial year - Held, yes - Whether word ‘issued’ in section 149 is required to carry meaning of expression ‘issued and served’ within prescribed period of limitation - Held, yes - Whether, where notice under section 148 for assessment year 1975-76 was admittedly served on assessee on 30-3-1984, assessment proceedings initiated on basis of such notice were hit by section 149 - Held, no

Section 153 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Reassessment - Time limit for completion of - Assessment year 1975-76 - Two notices under section 148 for assessment year 1975-76 were issued simultaneously - While one notice was served on 30-3-1984 by affixation, other was served on 3-4-1984 by registered post - Assessment was completed on 30-3-1989 - While assessee relied on notice served on 30-3-1984, revenue relied on that served on 3-4-1984 - Case, however, proceeded on basis that notice was served on 30-3-1984 - Whether, on facts of case assessment completed on 30-3-1989 was hit by limitation - Held, yes

Section 159, read with section 148, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Legal representative - Assessment year 1975-76 - Whether, where notices under sections 148 and 142(1) were issued to and served on only one out of three legal heirs even though Assessing Officer was aware of existence of all of them, assessment was vitiated for want of proper representation - Held, yes

FACT: The deceased assessee was a partner of a firm which was later dissolved and the land which the assessee got as his share was compulsorily acquired by the Government. The income arising out of the compensation received was exigible to capital gains tax for the assessment year 1975-76. The assessee, who died in the year 1978, had not filed his return for the year 1975-76. The Assessing Officer issued notices under section 148 to one of the three legal heirs on the ground that due to failure of the assessee to file return under section 139, income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment. The Assessing Officer issued two notices under section 148 simultaneously on 27-3-1984. One of the notices was served on 30-3-1984 by affixation and the other, sent by registered post, was served on 3-4-1984. As no return was filed and notice under section 142(1) was also not responded to, the assessment was completed on 30-3-1989 under section 144. The assessee’s case was (i) that the assessment was not valid as notice was not issued to all the legal heirs, (ii) that as the notice under section 148 was served on him on 30-3-1989, the assessment made on 30-3-1989 was hit by limitation under section 153(2)(a) and (iii) that the notice was bad in law as it had been served on him after the expiry of the period of 8 years as per the provision of section 149(1)(a)( i). The first appellate authority held that the assessment should have been completed by 31-3-1988 in view of the provisions of section 153(2)(a) and, therefore, completion of the assessment on 30-3-1989 was barred by limitation. Accordingly, he cancelled the order of assessment.

On the revenue’s appeal:

HELD: As regards the point of commencement of limitation, a plain reading of the provisions contained in clause (i) of sub-section (1)(a) of section 149 conveys the message that the relative adjective ‘that’ used in that provision has reference to the words ‘assessment year’ used in the opening lines of sub-clause (i). It suggests that the period of eight years is to commence from the end of the relevant assessment year. Nowhere in section 149(1)(a)(i ) has the term ‘financial year’ been used The position has been made clear by the use of the same term ‘assessment year’ in both sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) of section 151. It is, thus, abundantly clear that the prescribed period of eight years or 16 years, as the case may be, is to be reckoned from the end of the relevant assessment year and not the financial year.

Various High Courts for the precise reason have held the said Notifications to be bad in Law and these findings have been upheld by the Supreme Court. It was further submitted that the two Notifications issued by the CBDT, dated 31-3-2021 and 27-4-2021, respectively amounts to extension of legislation or rewriting of legislation, not permitted under Law. It is true that the executives/delegates cannot go beyond the Law enacted by the Parliament. However, one cannot be ignorant about the world wide pandemic situation on account of Covid-19 virus, and enactment of TOLA-2020, which came in to force on 31-3-2020. Under section 3(1) of TOLA -2020, the Legislature has permitted the Government to issue notification extending the time limit for issuance of notice under section 148. Hence, the power of the CBDT to issue the two notifications dated 31-3-2021 and 27-4-2021 pursuant to TOLA-2020 cannot be questioned. However, the said two notifications extending the time limit prescribed under first proviso to section 149(1), cannot be read so as to enlarge the scope of the amended first proviso to section 149(1). Therefore, the submission of the revenue is not agreed upon that as time limit to issue notice under section 148 was extended by TOLA up to 30-6-2021, the proviso to amended section 149(1) would not be applicable. Therefore, though two Notifications dated 31-3-2021 and 27-4-2021 came to be issued by the CBDT, in pursuance to the power vested under section 3 of TOLA 2020, which came into force on 31-3-2020, they cannot be treated to have extended the time limit provided under the amended first proviso to section 149(1). [Para 21.2]

In relation to the CBDT Instruction No. 1 of 2022, which was issued to implement the decision of Supreme Court in case of Ashish Agarwal (surpa), it is submitted that the Board circular issued is binding to the departmental authority and not to the assessee.

The settled legal position is to the effect that Board circular/instructions are binding to the departmental authorities and not to the Court or to the assessee. [Para 21.3]

To consider the submission that in view of express language of proviso to section 149(1), the notices issued between 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021 under section 148, are barred by limitation, following aspects are to be noticed.

The substituted provisions of sections 147 to 151 introduced w.e.f. 1-4-2021, have been elaborately discussed by Supreme Court of the decision in case of Ashish Agarwal (supra), and therefore, do not dilate on the same.

The Supreme Court, for the reasons stated, passed an order construing notices issued under section 148, as those deemed to have been issued under section 148A as substituted by the Finance Act 2021 and treated to be show-cause notices in terms of section 148A(b). The requirement of conducting any inquiry, if any, with the prior approval of specified authority under section 148A(a) has been dispensed with as a one-time measure. The Assessing Officer has been directed thereafter to pass an order under section 148A(d) in respect of each of the concerned assessee and the revenue is also permitted to proceed further with the reassessment proceedings as per the provisions of section 148A, subject to compliance of all the procedural requirements. The defenses, which may be available to the assessee including those available under section 149 of the Act and all rights and contentions available to concerned assessee and Revenue under Finance Act 2021 and law shall continue to be available.
