FACT: ■

The assessee filed a return for AY 2015-16 declaring income of about Rs. 66.49 lakhs. Based on information that immovable properties were sold for about Rs. 1.89 crores against stamp duty value of about Rs. 16.08 crores, the case was reopened under section 147 after obtaining prior approval.

■

An original notice under section 148 was issued on 29-6-2021 under the unamended provisions. Pursuant to Supreme Court ruling in UOI v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC), the notice was treated as one under section 148A, an order under section 148A(d) was passed, a fresh notice under section 148 was issued on 29-7-2022, and reassessment was completed on 19-5-2023.

■

On appeal, the CIT(A) quashed the reassessment holding that reopening for assessment year 2015-16 was barred by limitation in view of UOI v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/469 ITR 46/301 Taxman 238 (SC), holding that TOLA applied only where limitation fell between 20-3-2020 and 31-3-2021.

■

On appeal by revenue to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The reassessment in the present case pertains to AY 2015-16. The CIT(A), following the decision of the Supreme Court in Rajeev Bansal (supra), held that the reopening proceedings for AY 2015-16 were barred by limitation, particularly in view of the specific concession recorded on behalf of the revenue. The CIT(A) has given detailed reasons for that conclusion, and the revenue was unable to point out any infirmity in the impugned order. Accordingly, all three grounds raised by the revenue are dismissed. [Para 10]

■

In the result, the appeal of the Assessing Officer is dismissed. [Para 11]

■

At the outset, it is found that this issue has been settled in the case of Rajeev Bansal (supra) wherein reference is made to the submissions made on behalf of the revenue which is relevant. [Para 12.2]

Section 148(1) provides for service of notice as a condition precedent to making the order of assessment. Service under 1961 Act is not a condition precedent to conferment of jurisdiction on the ITO; it is a condition precedent only to the making of the order of assessment. It was held that the notice was not barred by limitation and the ITO had jurisdiction to complete the assessment. 25. In CIT v. Sheo Kumari Devi [1986] 157 ITR 13/24 Taxman 77 (Pat.)(FB) Hon'ble Patna High Court has occasion to examine the difference between the words "issued" and "served". The words "issued" and "served" are not synonyms. Their plain dictionary meaning runs directly contrary to any such assumption. The gap between the two may be wide both in point of time and place. A statute may require that the issuance of a general order be conveyed by publication in the locality without individual service. The word "issue" is to be construed in the context of section 149, which is an express limitation provision creating a precise bar with regard to reopening of assessments. In sub-section (3) of section 149 the word "employed" is "served" in the first line while in the penultimate line the word "employed" is "issued". Thus in the same short sub-section, the Legislature had used these words as distinct and separate. The hallmark of a limitation provision is that the same must have clear-cut and fixed termini at both ends. Section 149 fixed the terminus a quo from the end of the relevant assessment year i.e., on the 31st March of the said year. On the other hand, the terminus ad quem under clauses (a) and (b) is fixed at 4 years, 8 years and 16 years from the fixed date of 31st March of the relevant assessment year. Clearly enough, if the terminus a quo is fixed as the relevant assessment year, namely, 31st March of the said year the other terminus must equally be fixed with regard to the fixed date of issuance of the notice, which is precise and predictable. The plain scheme of sections 148 and 151 is that the satisfaction and the sanction of the Commissioner or the Board on the reasons recorded by the ITO is necessary before the notice under section 148 is sent out. If the word "issued" used in both these sub-sections is read as "served", it will lead to the strange phenomenon that even after the Income-tax Officer has recorded his reasons and issued the notice, the sanction may, therefore, be recorded before its service on the assessee. A decision is only an authority for what it actually decides, and the quintessence thereof is its ratio and not every observation found therein nor what logically follows from various observations made in it. The Supreme Court in Banarsi Debi v. ITO [1964] 53 ITR 100 further observed that a strange and wide meaning of the word "issue" in order to save the Income-tax (Amendment) Act, 1959, from being rendered nugatory. They did not even remotely considered section 149 of the 1961 Act. Consequently, Hon'ble Patna High Court has held that Banarsi Debi's case (supra) is no warrant for the abstruse proposition that the word "issued" de hors its context must always mean "issued" and "served" in every statute or in section 149 of the Act.

26. Thus from the decisions of Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of R.K. Upadhyaya (supra) and Hon'ble Patna High Court in the case of Sheo Kumari Devi (supra) the law is settled that term "issue" appearing in section 149 of the Act cannot mean as "issue and serve". The jurisdiction becomes vested in the Assessing Officer to assess/reassess the escaped income the moment the notice under section 148 is issued. Service under the Act is not a condition precedent to conferment of jurisdiction on the Assessing Officer but a condition precedent only to the making of the order of assessment. Therefore the contention of Ld. CIT (DR) that without service of notices under section 148 the Assessing Officer is not vested with the power to assess/reassess the escaped income and assessment proceedings were jeopardized holds no water and deserves to be rejected.

It is a settled law that the expression 'issue' means that the notice should leave the custody of the Assessing Officer. The postal department is not agent of the Income-tax department. Once a notice is issued within the period of limitation, jurisdiction becomes vested in the Income-tax Officer to proceed to reassess. The assessment proceedings can be terminated either by passing of the assessment orders within the stipulated time or by dropping of the proceedings initiated under section 147. Thus, the assessment/ reassessment proceedings under section 147 will not terminate by issue of fresh notice under section 148. It is also a settled law that the Assessing Officer can issue as many notices as he may desire as long as other conditions prescribed in law are satisfied. In a case where the Assessing Officer drops the proceedings initiated earlier, again on same material and information, he is debarred to issue fresh notice for the simple reason that issue of notice under such circumstances would amount to change of opinion which is not permitted in view of settled position of law in this regard. "38. It is pertinent to note that a reference to Sections 147 and 148 of the Act in AbhisarBuildwell firstly appears in paragraph 33 of the report and where the Supreme Court observed that in cases where a search does not result in any incriminating material being found, the only remedy that would be available to the Revenue would be to resort to reassessment.

39. However, the Supreme Court caveated that observation by observing that the initiation of reassessment would be ".....subject to fulfilment of the conditions mentioned in Sections 147/148, as in such a situation, the Revenue cannot be left with no remedy". This sentiment came to be reiterated with the Supreme Court observing that the power of the Revenue to initiate reassessment must be saved failing which it would be left with no remedy. It was thereafter observed in paragraph 36.4 of the report that insofar as completed or unabated assessments were concerned, they could be reopened by the AO by invocation of Sections 147/148 of the Act, subject to the fulfillment of the conditions ".as envisaged/mentioned under Sections 147/148 of the Act and those powers are saved".

40. It thus becomes apparent that the liberty which the Supreme Court accorded and the limited right inhering in the Revenue to initiate reassessment was subject to that power being otherwise compliant with the Chapter pertaining to reassessment as contained in the Act. The observations of the Supreme Court cannot possibly be read or construed as a carte blanche enabling the respondents to overcome and override the restrictions that otherwise appear in Section 149 of the Act. The observations of the Supreme Court in AbhisarBuildwell were thus intended to merely convey that the annulment of the search assessments would not deprive or denude the Revenue of its power to reassess and which independently existed. However, the Supreme Court being mindful of the statutory prescriptions, which otherwise imbue the commencement of reassessment, qualified that observation by providing that such an action would have to be in accordance with law. This note of caution appears at more than one place in that judgment and is apparent from the Supreme Court observing that the power to reassess would be subject to the fulfilment of the conditions mentioned in Sections 147 and 148 of the Act.

41. We also bear in mind the order passed on the Miscellaneous Application which was moved by the Revenue before the Supreme Court and more particularly to the prayers that were made therein. The Revenue had specifically alluded to Section 150 of the Act and sought appropriate clarifications enabling it to proceed afresh. It had also sought the liberty to commence proceedings for reassessment within 60 days of the disposal of that application. The said application, however, came to be dismissed with it being left open to the respondents to move a formal application for review, if so chosen and advised. It appears, however, that no such review was ultimately moved.

Regard must also be had to the judgment rendered in the batch of U.K. Paints, and where while according liberty to the respondents to initiate reassessment, the Supreme Court pertinently observed that the same would be subject to the proposed action being in accordance with law and if "permissible in law". Thus, neither AbhisarBuildwell nor U.K. Paints are liable to be read as enabling the respondents to overcome the statutory bar of limitation which may have come into play. Those judgments cannot possibly be construed as freeing the respondents from the obligation of independently establishing that the proposed action for reassessment would otherwise be in accordance with law.

We had in Sumitomo Corporation also taken note of the aspect of limitation and where the respondents had sought to contend that a finding or direction would enable them to overcome the time frames erected by virtue of Section 144C of the Act. An argument, again founded on Section 150, came to be negated with the Court observing that a direction would have to necessarily be in accordance with the scheme of the Act and the statutory prescriptions comprised therein. It was further observed that it would be wholly incorrect for courts to extend a period of limitation that otherwise stands prescribed in the Act.

The ingredients of the proviso could be broken down for analysis as follows:

(i)

no notice under section 148 of the new regime can be issued at any time for an assessment year beginning on or before 1 April 2021;

(ii)

if it is barred at the time when the notice is sought to be issued because of the "time limits specified under the provisions of" 149(1)(b) of the old regime.

Thus, a notice could be issued under section 148 of the new regime for assessment year 2021-2022 and before only if the time limit for issuance of such notice continued to exist under section 149(1)(b) of the old regime.

49.

The first proviso to Section 149(1)(b) requires the determination of whether the time limit prescribed under section 149(1)(b) of the old regime continues to exist for the assessment year 2021-2022 and before. Resultantly, a notice under Section 148 of the new regime cannot be issued if the period of six years from the end of the relevant assessment year has expired at the time of issuance of the notice. This also ensures that the new time limit of ten years prescribed under section 149(1)(b) of the new regime applies prospectively. For example, for the assessment year 2012-2013, the ten year period would have expired on 31 March 2023, while the six year period expired on 31 March 2019. Without the proviso to Section 149(1)(b) of the new regime, the Revenue could have had the power to reopen assessments for the year 2012-2013 if the escaped assessment amounted to Rupees fifty lakhs or more. The proviso limits the retrospective operation of Section 149(1)(b) to protect the interests of the assesses.

7. A combined reading of the above observations of the Hon'ble Supreme Court and the findings of Hon'ble Delhi High Court makes it clear that the test for checking the validity of notices issued under section 148 under new regime for AYs 2021-22 or prior years is whether the period of six years has expired at the time of issue of such notice and in that case the notice under section 148 becomes invalid. These observations also makes it clear that the time limit of ten years as per the amended provisions of section 149(1)(b) can be applied only prospectively. In assessee's case when we apply this test for AY 2015-16, the period of six years has expired on 31.03.2022 and therefore the notice dated 28.07.2022 under section 148 of the Act for AY 2015-16 is invalid since it is barred by limitation. Since we have quashed the order of re-assessment for AY 2015-16 considering the legal contention raised by the assessee in Ground No.2, the rest of the grounds raised on the merits of the issues have become academic.

9. In result, appeal of the assessee is partly allowed.

"The words 'issue' and 'serve' are not synonyms. Their plain dictionary meaning runs directly contrary to any such assumption. The gap between the two may be wide both in point of time and place. A statute may require that the issuance of a general order be conveyed by publication in the locality without individual service. The word 'issue' is to be construed in the context of section 149 which is an express limitation provision creating a precise bar with regard to reopening of assessments. In sub-section (3) of section 149, the word employed is 'served' in the first line while in the penultimate line the word 'employed' is 'issued'. Thus, in the same short sub-section, the Legislature has used these words as distinct and separate. The hallmark of a limitation provision is that the same must have clear cut and fixed termini at both ends. Section 149 fixed the terminus a quo from the end of the relevant assessment year, i.e., on the 31st March, of the said year. On the other hand, the terminus ad quem under clauses ( a) and (b) is fixed at 4 years, 8 years and 16 years, from the fixed date of 31st day of March of the relevant assessment year. Clearly enough, if the terminus a quo is fixed as the relevant assessment year, namely, 31st March of the said year the other terminus must equally be fixed with regard to the fixed date of the issuance of the notice, which is precise and predictable. The plain scheme of sections 148 and 151 is that the satisfaction and the sanction of the Commissioner or the Board on the reason recorded by the Income-tax Officer is necessary before the notice under section 148 is sent out. If the word 'issued' used in both these sub-sections is read as 'served', it will lead to the strange phenomenon that even after the Income-tax Officer has recorded his reason and issued the notice, the sanction therefore may be recorded before its service on the assessee.

A decision is only an authority for what it actually decides, and the quintessence thereof is its ratio and not every observation found therein nor what logically follows from the various observations made in it. In Banarsi Debi v. ITO [1964] 53 ITR 100, the Supreme Court gave strained and wide meaning to the word 'issue' in order to save the Income-tax (Amendment) Act, 1959, from being rendered nugatory. They did not even remotely consider section 149 of the 1961 Act. Consequently, Banarsi Debi's case is no warrant for the abstruse proposition that the word 'issued' de hors its context must always man 'issued' and 'served' in every statute or in section 149 of the Act.

A judgment of a court of law derives its legal sanctity from the direct canvassing of opposite views in the open court and the adjudication made thereon. An ex parte short order by the Supreme Court declining to grant a discretion any leave to appeal under article 136 is not strictu sensu a judgment which is either binding or within the ambit of article 141. , it was naturally considering defences such as limitation when the notice is issued say after 30th June, 2021 and is beyond three years and the escapement is below 50lakh. Otherwise, almost all the 90,000 notices were issued between the extended period of limitation and it cannot be that the Supreme court converted such notices to section 148A(b) notices only for them to travel upto the Supreme Court again and be quashed on the grounds of limitation.

2. A step by step process to understand the above controversy is below:

A.

The old reassessment notices issued within the extended period i.e. on or after 1st April, 2021-30th June, 2021 are converted to show-cause notices under section 148A(b) pursuant to the decision in Ashish Agarwal. Hence, for any fresh notice to be issued under section 148 post passing of the section 148A(d) order, the same cannot be beyond limitation on a plain reading of section 149, otherwise the said judgment in Ashish Agarwal converting the notices will be rendered nugatory or of no effect inasmuch as for obvious reasons the fresh notices to be issued under section 148 will invariably and always without doubt be beyond limitation. For this reason to reconcile the issue, the fresh notice under section 148 must travel back in time to the original date when they were issued i.e. the date of the old notice and limitation should be computed accordingly. The rationale is that the Supreme court judgment cannot be rendered nugatory and must not be defeated by holding that the fresh section 148 notices are beyond limitation.

B.

Hence, when the Supreme Court stated that all defences including limitation will be kept open, it was considering only those cases where the notice is issued after 30th June, 2021 only, for AY 2017-2018 and AY 2016-2017. For example for AY 2017-2018 if the section 148 notice is issued on say 2nd July, 2022, the notice will be beyond limitation if the income escaped assessment is less than Rs. 50 lakh and Ashish Agarwal applies only to these cases, otherwise the Supreme Court would not have sanctioned the reassessment notices by converting them to section 148A(b) notices.

C.

It cannot possibly be said that the defence of limitation can be taken against those notices issued under the extended period under TOLA, 2020 otherwise all the notices would be beyond limitation and there would be no purpose in converting them to show-cause notices. In Ashish Agarwal the period under consideration was precisely that beyond 1st April, 2021. Again, the judgment in Ashish Agarwal would stand defeated and reduced to a mere piece of paper if the notifications extending the limitation are quashed, or it is held that the notices issued during that period are beyond limitation. The notices must travel back in time to the original date failing which the section 148 notices would invariably be beyond limitation and the judgment in Ashish Agarwal will be rendered nugatory.

3.

The next question is of sanction of the 'specified authority'. This is mandated by the Act. However, pursuant to the decision in Ashish Agarwal if the old notices are converted to SCN's as per the judgment, then the defence of sanction becomes a double edged sword in the hands of the assessee. To illustrate, if sanction is incorrectly given for the old notice, it is liable to be quashed and there can be no further proceedings. However, if sanction is given appropriately for the old notice but inappropriately given for the fresh section 148 notice, the fresh notice is invalid and would have to be quashed and reissued if the law permits. The section 148A(d) order must receive sanction from the specified authority being the proper authority and once the appropriate sanction for the section 148A(d) order is obtained, there is no need to obtain fresh sanction for the section 148 notice under proviso 2 to section 1484. As rightly held in the above case, the fresh sanction was provided by the PCIT and not the authorities mentioned under section 151(ii) hence the sanction was bad in law.

Conclusion

The issue of limitation was not dealt with elaborately in the above case but some principles on limitation have been provided to enable a better understanding of the controversy on reassessment which has engulfed both assessee and Department. The issue of sanction was in ,my view, correctly decided by the Hon'ble Court. In my view, the judgment has dealt with the issue of sanction in great detail by analysing all the relevant provisions and has laid down the law correctly. There are other observations made by the learned Judge on change of opinion on the facts of the case. However, to clear all doubts, in my view, sanction can be tested upon the old notice since it is covered by the decision of Ashish Agarwal where all defences are to be kept open, and the issue of fresh sanction under section 148A(d)/section 148 can also be raised before the Courts. Further, it is now well settled that the concept of change of opinion has also been carried forward to the new regime of reassessment

HEADNOTE: Section 148 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Reassessment - Notice for - Assessment year 1984-85 - Whether simply preparing notice under section 148 but keeping it on file past limitation period does not tantamount to issuing same, and, thus, such notice is bad in law - Held, yes

FACT: The Assessing Officer completed assessment under section 143(3) for the assessment year 1984-85 on 15-5-1985. Subsequently he wanted to rectify the order. Hence, reasons were recorded by him on 12-10-1988 and the notice under section 148 was prepared on the same day, but it was served on the assessee sometime in November 1989. The reassessment was later completed. The Commissioner (Appeals) cancelled the reassessment as the notice was beyond the time-limit permissible under section 149(1)(a)( i).

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: In the instant case, the reasons were recorded on 12-10-1988. The notice was also made out on the same day. However, there was nothing on record to show that the same was issued by 31-3-1989. All the judicial authorities unequivocally point out that the notice should actually be set in motion for being served on the assessee. Simply preparing the notice but keeping it on file past the limitation period did not tantamount to issuing the same. In the case of CIT v. Sheo Kumari Debi [1986] 157 ITR 13/ 24 Taxman 77 , the Patna High Court quoting from Chamber’s Twentieth Century Dictionary, observed that the relevant meanings of the word ‘issue’ are : act of sending out; to put forth; to put into circulation; to publish; to give out for use. Thus keeping the notice on file after preparing it does not fit into any of these meanings to be described as ‘issued’. After issuing it as described above, it is immaterial when it is served. It may be served even after three years, but the essence is that it should be set into motion for being served. And, the onus to show that it is so issued lies on the department, who in the instant case, had failed to do so.

The revenue’s contention that once the notice was made out, the process of setting it into motion was presumed, was certainly rebuttable.

In the instant case, the glaring facts themselves demolished the presumption laid down in section 114 of the Evidence Act that all official acts are regularly performed. The notice was made out more than five months before the period of limitation was to expire, but was served on the assessee about thirteen months after it was prepared.

The original records of the department did not show that the notice was despatched before 31-3-1989. Under these circumstances, normal presumption would be that the notice must have been set into motion for being served only a few days before 9-11-1989. In the ultimate analysis, just as ‘issue’ and ‘service’ are held not to be synonymous by most of the courts, including the Apex Court, the words ‘preparation’ and ‘issue’ are also not synonymous.

Therefore, the notice under section 148 was bad in law, and the Commissioner (Appeals)’s order called for no interference.

When proceedings legally and validly started for reassessment were pending, fresh notice under section 148 cannot be issued because it cannot be said that income liable to tax had escaped assessment. 12.6. Hon'ble Supreme Court while dismissing the SLP filed by Revenue in the case of ACIT v. Nehal Ashit Shah [SLP (Civil) Diary No(s). 57209 of 2024, dated 04-04-2025] held that it does not survive for further consideration. While holding so, Hon'ble Court noted in para 5 as under:

"5. In this regard, reference could also be made to paragraph 19(e) and (f) in the case of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal, Civil Appeal No.8629 of 2024 on 03.10.2024 (2024 SCC ONLINE 754) under which the learned Additional Solicitor General for India has made a concession insofar as the assessment year 2015-16 is concerned."

12.7. In view of above stated deliberation, both on facts and law including the applicable jurisprudence, we hold that notice for A.Y. 2015-16 issued on 28.07.2022 u/s 148 of the new regime is barred by limitation and hence bad in law, liable to be quashed, resulting in impugned reassessment proceedings as well as the impugned reassessment order bad in law. Accordingly, grounds of cross objection raised by the assessee are allowed. Resultantly, grounds of appeal raised on the merits of the case by the Revenue are rendered academic and are therefore, dismissed.

13. In the result, for A.Y. 2015-16, appeal by the revenue is dismissed and cross objection by the assessee is allowed. For A.Y. 2014-15, appeal by the revenue is dismissed.

The Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC) explaining the ratio laid down in similar judgment of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/444 ITR 1/286 Taxman 183 (SC) wherein the Supreme Court had exercised its discretionary jurisdiction under article 142 of the Constitution of India while explaining the old law and new law under section 148, has created a legal fiction and balancing act on the existing legal framework of procedure of reassessment. Wherever the notice under section 148 were issued under the old regime for which time limit was extended up to 30-6-2021, the Apex Court held that it would be deemed that reassessment notice issued under the old regime shall be treated as show-cause notice issued under section 148A(b) of the new regime. Further the Court directed the revenue to provide all the relevant material/information to the assessee and thereafter, allowed the assessee to respond to the show-cause notice and raised its objection or availing any kind of defenses including available under section 149. Thus, the Supreme Court balanced the equities between the revenue and the assessee by giving effect to the legislative scheme of reassessment as contained under the new regime. The Court thus supplemented the existing legal framework of the procedure of reassessment under the Income-tax Act with the principles grounded in equitable standards. [Para 7]

■

Thus, the Supreme Court had explained the concept of surviving or balance time limit which is to be calculated by computing number of days between dates of issuance of deemed notice and 30-6-2021. Thereafter, the Supreme Court has elaborated the effect of the legal fiction propounded in the case of UOI v. Ashish Agarwal which has been explained. [Para 8]

■

The sequitor of the aforesaid observation and the judgment of the Supreme Court are that-

■

Firstly, exclusion of the period has been explained;

(a)

the date of issuance notice under section 148 under the old regime reckoned to be the date of issuance of the deemed notices under section 148A(b);

(b)

the period from the date of the issuance of the deemed notices till the supply of relevant information and material by the assessing officers to the assessees is to be excluded from the computation of the period of limitation;

(c)

further, period of two weeks granted to the assessee to reply to the show-cause notice is also to be excluded in terms of third proviso to section 149;

■

Secondly, once the response of the assessee to the showcause notice has been received, then "the clock starts ticking for the Revenue", that is, after the receipt of reply, the Assessing Officer has to;

(a)

consider the reply of the assessee under section148A(c);

(b)

take a decision under section148A(d) based on the available material and the reply of the assessee; and

(c)

issue a notice under section148 if it was a fit case for reassessment.

■

Once it is found to be a fit case for re-assessment, the limitation clock starts ticking and it is mandatory for the Assessing Officer to comply with these procedures within the surviving time limit which was available to the Assessing Officer to issue re-assessment notice under section148 of the new regime; and

■

Lastly, the Supreme Court has given an example as how to calculate the surviving time. Calculation of surviving time has been laid down from the period when the first notice u/s.148 was issued under old regime till the last date of limitation for issuance of notice under section148 of the old regime; and that period has been reckoned as the surviving time period left for the Assessing Officer while issuing notice under section148 under the new regime. So whatever surviving time is left the Assessing Officer has to issue notice within that surviving time.[Para 9]

The confusion on account of limitation has arisen on account of the implementation of the decision of the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal, 2022 SCC Online SC 543. As per the decision of the Supreme Court in aforesaid case, which held that all the Notices for reopen of the assessment for the tax period after 1-4-2021 will have to be dealt under the new regime as in force from 1-4-2021. The period of limitation under the old regime would have been either four years or six years or sixteen years under section 149 as it stood till 31-3-2021. [Para 13]

■

However, in accordance with the new regime, the period for limitation for issuance of Notice under amended section 148 to reopen an assessment, it is three years but not more than 10 years. Correspondingly, the monetary and pecuniary jurisdiction for reopening the assessment were also altered. This has also been captured by the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal, [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70 (SC)/ 2024 SCC OnLine SC 2693. [Para 14]

■

The Supreme Court has also taken note of the relaxation in the period of limitation for various assessment years in the light of the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation & Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 (hereinafter referred to as the 'TOLA') with effect from 20-11-2020 and the Finance Act, 2021 amending the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961 with effect from 1-4-2021. In accordance with TOLA, as far as the assessment year 2017-18 is concerned, the period of limitation for issuance of Notice under section 148 read with section 149 as amended by Finance Act, 2021 with effect from 1-4-2021 would be till 30-6-2021, instead of 30-3-2021 and under the old regime on 31-3-2024. This was also captured in the submissions of the Additional Solicitor General of India on behalf of the Income Tax Department before the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal, (supra). This position has not been disputed. [Para 15]

■

However, the first proviso to section 149 prohibits issuance of a reassessment notice under the new regime if such notices have become time barred under the old regime. Therefore, the last date for issuance of Notice under section 148 would have expired on 30-6-2021, as per the third Proviso to section 149(1)(b) as in force with effect from 1-4-2021. The time during which stay was in operation or the time during which, the assessee took time to file the reply, the Notice issued under section 148(A)(b) stands expelled. In this case, the reply itself was filed by the petitioner only on 31-5-2022, pursuant to which the Impugned Order was passed on 30-6-2022 under section 148(A)(d) and Notice under section 148 was issued. Though the limitation for issuance of a Notice under section 148 under the old regime would have expired on 31-3-2024, a reading of conclusion in the decision of the Supreme Court in UOI v. Rajeev Bansal (supra), however indicates that the Impugned Notice dated 30-6-2022 has to be treated as having been issued beyond the limitation period. [Para 16]

Rajeev Bansal (supra), the Delhi High Court quashed the notice dated 31-3-2021 issued to the assessee under section 148 and the proceedings. Since the law laid down by the Supreme Court in UOI v. Rajeev Bansal (supra) is a settled law, it is binding on this Court. [Para 17]

■

Therefore, this Writ Petition deserves to be allowed and is accordingly allowed. [Para 18]

HELD: ■

To determine this question, the ratio laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal (2024) SCC OnLine SC 2693; [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/469 ITR 46/301 Taxman 238 (SC) and Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/444 ITR 1/286 Taxman 183 (SC)/(2023) 1 SCC 617 have to be kept in mind. The legal position as obtained is lucidly explained by the Hon'ble Division Bench in Income-tax Officer v. Mahogany Logistics Services (P.) Ltd. [2025] 176 taxmann.com 478 (Madras). [Para 17]

■

■

Applying the ratio laid down in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64 /[2022] 286 Taxman 183 /[2022] 444 ITR 1 (SC)/(2023) 1 SCC 617 and Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/469 ITR 46/301 Taxman 238 (SC), particularly, in the light of the limitation for issuance of notice under section 148 prescribed under section 149 read with section 151, it is clear that the notice that was issued after 1-4-2021 under the old regime as it stood till 31-3-2021 has to be treated as a notice under section 148A(b) under the new regime. [Para 8]

■

The time during which the aforesaid notice issued under section 148 under the old regime as it stood till 31-3-2021 were deemed to be stayed from the date of issuance between 1-4-2021 and 30-6-2021 till the supply of relevant information and material by the Assessing Officers to the assessees in terms of the directions issued by this Court in Ashish Agarwal case (supra), and for a further period of two weeks for the assessees to respond to the Show Cause Notices as confirmed by Rajeev Bansal case (supra). [Para 9]

■

A notice under section 148 was required to be issued for reassessment within the time limit surviving under the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) [TOLA] Act, 2020. For the assessment year 2016-17, since the income escaping assessment is less than Rs. 50 lakhs, the notice under section 148 ought to have been issued on 31-3-2020. However, by virtue of TOLA extensions, the said date has been extended up to 30-6-2021. [Para 12]

■

In the light of the ratio in Ashish Agarwal case (supra) and Rajeev Bansal case (supra), the notice issued under section 148 under the old regime on 30-6-2021 is deemed to have been stayed for thirty days for the Income Tax Department to provide to the respective assessees information and material relied upon and two weeks thereafter for the assessees to reply to the Show Cause Notices. [Para 13]

■

In the instant case, notice under section 148 under the old regime itself was issued on the last date of limitation viz., 30-6-2021, after the exclusions i.e., excluding the thirty days and fourteen days time period granted by the Supreme Court there is no further time available for the Assessing Officer to issue Notice under section 148 under the new regime barring the seven days as provided under the fourth proviso to section 149 as amended with effect from 1-4-2021. [Para 14]

■

Therefore, after accounting for all the exclusions, the Assessing Officer in the instant case had no time left for issuance of Notice under section 148 under the new regime. However, applying the fourth proviso to section 149 as amended with effect from 1-4-2021, the Assessing Officer had seven days to issue a Notice under section 148 under the new regime. [Para 15]

■

Thus, the notice under section 148 ought to have been issued within seven days from the date of reply given by the assessee on 3-6-2022. In other words, the notice ought to have been issued on or before 10-6-2022. [Para 16]

■

However, in the instant case, the notice under section 148 under the new regime was issued only on 28-7-2022. [Para 17]

■

Thus, the proceedings initiated on 30-6-2021 which were later substituted by a notice under section 148A(b) dated 20-5-2022 which culminated in the impugned order passed under section 148A(d) dated 28-7-2022 and notice issued under section 148 dated 28-7-2022 are to be held to be beyond time. [Para 18]

■

In view thereof, this writ petition challenging these two proceedings deserve to be allowed and is accordingly allowed. [Para 19]

FACT: ■

The assessee, an individual, filed return of income for AY 2015-16 on 30-06-2016 declaring income of about Rs. 7 lakhs. A survey under section 133A was conducted on 30-05-2017 in case of Babylon Group engaged in hotel business, during which a hard disk impounded from premises of Hotel Babylon Continental, Raipur, revealed huge cash transactions relating to investment in hotel project and sale/purchase of immovable properties during FYs 2013-14 to 2016-17. On examination of extracted data, the AO noted that the assessee, being one of sellers of immovable property, had allegedly received cash of Rs. 1 crore during FY 2014-15 which was not reflected in his books of account, though receipts through banking channels were reflected. The AO accordingly recorded reasons and reopened assessment for AY 2015-16.

■

The AO issued notice under section 148 on 30-06-2021 under old regime. Pursuant to decision of Supreme Court in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64 (SC)/[2022] 286 Taxman 183 (SC)/[2022] 444 ITR 1 (SC), the AO issued notice under section 148A(b) on 21-5-2022, passed order under section 148A(d) on 25-7-2023 and thereafter issued fresh notice under section 148 on 26-7-2023 under new regime. The reassessment was completed under section 147 read with section 144B by making addition of Rs. 1 crore under section 69A.

■

On appeal, the CIT(A)/NFAC upheld validity of reassessment proceedings and sustained addition made under section 69A.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

It is an admitted fact that the assessee filed his return of income on 30-6-2016. A survey action under section 133A was carried out on 30-5-2017 in the case of Babylon Group who are engaged in hotel sector. The Assessing Officer, after recording reasons, reopened the assessment and accordingly issued notice under section 148 on 30-6-2021. Subsequently on the basis of decision of Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal (supra), the Assessing Officer issued notice under section 148A(b) on 21-5-2022. After considering the reply of the assessee the Assessing Officer passed an order under section 148A(d) on 25-7-2023 and issued notice under section 148 on 26-7-2023 under the new regime. Thereafter, the Assessing Officer completed the assessment under section 147 read with section 144B wherein he made addition of Rs.1.00 crore under section 69A. The CIT(A)/NFAC upheld the re-assessment proceedings as well addition on merit. Under these circumstances, the issue for determination is whether the notice issued under section 148 for the assessment year 2015-16 on 26-7-2023 is a valid notice or not. [Para 10]

■

In R.K. Upadhyaya v. Shanabhai P. Patel [1987] 166 ITR 163, the Supreme Court categorically held that a clear distinction has been made out under the Income-tax Act, 1961 between 'issue of notice' and 'service of notice'. Section 149 prescribes the period of limitation. It prohibits issue of notice under section 148 after the expiry of the prescribed period of limitation. Section 148(1) provides for service of notice as condition precedent to making of the order of assessment. Once a notice is issued within the period of limitation, jurisdiction becomes vested with the ITO to proceed to reassess. The requirement of issue of notice is satisfied when a notice is actually issued Section 148(1) deals with making of the reassessment and mandates that reassessment shall not be made until there has been service. Under the Act, service is not a condition precedent to conferment of jurisdiction on the ITO to deal with the matter but it is a condition precedent to the making of the order of assessment.

In the Instant case, notice under section 148 was issued by the ITO within the period of limitation prescribed under section 149. There was also no controversy about the fact that the order of reassessment was made only after service of notice on the assessee. The ratio of the decision in R.K. Upadhyaya's case (supra ) of the Supreme Court squarely applied to the present case. The ITO having issued the notice under section 148 within limitation, the order of reassessment was valid. Therefore, the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the initiation of reassessment proceedings by the ITO was barred by limitation and in setting aside the orders of the AAC and the ITO.

(2)

(3)

Passing of orders in terms of section 148A(d)—The AOs shall thereafter pass an order in terms of s. 148A(d) after following the due procedure as required u/s 148A(b) in respect of each of the concerned assessees.

(4)

All defences available—All the defences which may be available to the assessee u/s 149 and/or which may be available under the Finance Act, 2021 and in law and whatever rights are available to the AO under the Finance Act, 2021 are kept open and/or shall continue to be available.

(5)

Modification of quashed notices u/s 148—The present order shall substitute/modify respective judgments and orders passed by the respective High Courts quashing the similar notices issued under unamended s. 148 Act irrespective of whether they have been assailed before the Apex Court or not.

It has further been held that the above order will strike a balance between the rights of the Revenue as well as the respective assessees as because of a bona fide belief of the Revenue officers in issuing approximately 90,000 such notices under the unamended section 148 between 1-4-2021 and 30-6-2021, the Revenue may not suffer as ultimately it is the public exchequer which would suffer. HEADNOTE: Section  149, read with section  148, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Income escaping assessment -  Time limit for issuance of notice (Reassessment) - Assessment year  2013-14 - Whether entire process under section 148A(a) to (d) and issuance of notice under section 148 has to be completed within total time available in terms of section 149(1) for issuance of notice - Held, yes - Assessee filed return of income for assessment year 2013-14 - Assessment was completed under section 143(3) - On 29-6-2021, notice under unamended section 148 was issued, which was later treated as a deemed notice under section 148A(b) - Assessing Officer issued final notice under section 148 on 29-7-2022 after supplying reasons and materials and completing process under section 148A - Whether after accounting for permissible exclusions under substituted section 149, time available to complete reassessment process had expired on 23-7-2022 - Held, yes - Whether since notice under section 148 was issued beyond said time, same was barred by limitation and, thus, reassessment proceedings and consequential assessment order were to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 16 to 21] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee filed his return of income for assessment year 2013-14 on 31-3-2014, declaring an income of Rs. 37.18 lakhs. The assessment was completed under section 143(3) on 23-2-2016 at an assessed income of Rs. 60.60 lakhs.

■

On 29-6-2021, a notice under the unamended section 148 was issued to the assessee. Pursuant to the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC), the said notice was treated as a deemed notice under section 148A(b).

■

Subsequently, the Assessing Officer issued reasons for reopening on 20-5-2022. The assessee filed objections and replies dated 3-6-2022 and 28-6-2022, raising jurisdictional and limitation-related grounds, including that the reassessment was time-barred under the amended section 149.

■

Thereafter, the Assessing Officer passed an order under section 148A(d) and issued a notice under section 148 on 29-7-2022.

■

In the instant writ, the assessee challenged the said notice and subsequent assessment proceedings primarily on the ground that the same were time-barred under the substituted provisions of section 149.

HELD: ■

In terms of the decisions in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC) and Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC)the following position emerges in the context of the present case :-

(i)

The period for subject reassessment in terms of section 149 of the old regime is deemed to be extended till 30-6-2021 under the TOLA.

(ii)

The notice dated 29-6-2021 would be deemed to be notice under section 148A(b).

(iii)

The surviving period by excluding the date of re-issuance of notice on 29-6-2021 would be the remainder days in the month of June 2021 (30-6-2021 - 28-6-2021), namely, two days.

(iv)

On 30-6-2021, the extension in terms of the TOLA would come to an end. (v) The period that stands excluded is :

(a)

The period up to 30-6-2021, which is covered by the provisions of the IT Act read with the TOLA.

(b)

The period from 1-7-2021 to 3-5-2022 being the period before the decision of the Supreme Court in Ashish Agarwal (supra).

(c)

The Period from 4-5-2022 till 20-5-2022, which is the date when the material was furnished and the reasons for re-opening were given to the petitioner.

(d)

Later, Assessing Officer issued notice under section 148 on basis of information received from NSEL that certain amount was outstanding payable by assessee as on termination of trading activity on NSEL and assessee had received said amount against sale of commodities but failed to deliver commodities or repayment of said amount and, thus there was no actual sale done by assessee and by making such bogus sales assessee had benefitted and accordingly there was an escapement of income - High Court by impugned order held that since Assessing Officer issued impugned notice only on basis of information received from NSEL without considering facts on record to effect that there was no sale or purchase transaction carried by assessee-company on NSEL during relevant assessment year and since there was no question of any income arising in hands of assessee resulting into escapement thereof, assumption of jurisdiction by Assessing Officer to reopen assessment was without any basis and, therefore, notice issued under section 148 was to be set aside - ■

The assessee filed the return of income for the assessment year 2016–17 on 29-07-2016. A notice under section 148 was issued on 30-06-2021 under the old regime, taking benefit of the extended limitation provided by the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 (TOLA). Pursuant to decision of Supreme Court in case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1, the said notice dated 30-06-2021 was treated as a notice under section 148A(b) of the new regime, and accordingly, a fresh notice dated 24-5-2022 under section 148A(b) was issued by the Assessing Officer.

■

Thereafter, the Assessing Officer passed an order under section 148A(d) dated 15-7-2022, alleging that income of Rs.15.60 lakh had escaped assessment. On the same day, a fresh notice under section 148 was also issued.

■

The assessee challenged both the order under section 148A(d) and the notice under section 148 before the High Court, contending that they were issued beyond the permissible time limit.

■

It was submitted that, as held by the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46, the reassessment notice dated 30-06-2021 (issued under the TOLA extension) would only be valid if the subsequent notice under section 148 was issued within the remaining time available under section 149.

■

Since only one day of limitation remained for issuing the section 148 notice, and the assessee was granted 14 days to respond from the date of the Ashish Agarwal judgment (21-05-2022), the last permissible date to issue notice was 12-6-2022.

■

As the impugned notice under section 148 was issued on 15-7-2022, the assessee submitted that it was time-barred, and consequently, the original notice dated 30-06-2021 and all proceedings thereafter were invalid.

■

It is an admitted fact that earlier, the notice under section 148 in the case of assessee was issued on 13-4-2021 which was dropped and proceedings under section 148A were initiated in terms of order of Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 and finally the notice under section 148 was issued on 18-7-2022. The Additional Solicitor General of India in the case of Union of India v. Rajiv Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC)has made categorical statement at Bar before the Supreme Court that all the notices issued for assessment year 2015-16 on or after 1-4-2021 will be dropped, however, in the instant case, no such action was taken and re-assessment order was framed in the case of the assessee on the basis of the notice issued under section 148 on 18-7-2022.[Para 10]

■

Looking to the facts and considering the assessment year involved is 2015-16, notice issued in the case of originally on 13-4-2021 and later on 18-7-2022 which both the dates have fallen on or after 1-4-2021, therefore, both the notice deserves to be dropped in view of the admission made by the revenue before the Supreme Court. Further, for assessment year 2015-16, no notice under section 148 could be issued after the expiring of six years from the end of the relevant assessment year which limitation expired on 31-3-2022. Further, the Supreme Court in the case of Rajiv Bansal (supra) has observed that TOLA is not applicable for assessment year 2015-16, therefore, even otherwise under the old provisions of section 149, the notice issued under section 148 for assessment year 2015-16 on 18-7-2022 is barred by limitation. [Para 11]

■

In view of the above facts and by respectfully following the judgments of the Supreme Court in the case of Rajiv Bansal (supra) and in the case of Deepak Steel & Power Ltd. v. CBDT [2025] 174 taxmann.com 144/476 ITR 369 (SC) and Asstt.CIT v. Nehal Ashit Shah [SLP (CIVIL) Diary No (s) 57209 of 2024, dated 4-4-2025, the notice issued under section 148 on 18-7-2022 is barred by limitation and, therefore, the same is quashed. The cross objections taken by taken by the assesse are allowed. [Para 14]

HEADNOTE: Section  149,  read with sections  148  and  148A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  282,  read with sections  280  and  281  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Income escaping assessment – Time limit for issuance of notice (Illustrations) - Assessment year  2015-16  - Assessee, an individual, did not file return under section 139(1) for Assessment year  2015-16  - Information on INSIGHT/NMS portal showed interest income of about Rs. 0.86 lakh and sale of an immovable property for about Rs. 1.22 crores - Proceedings under section 148A were initiated and, after an order under section 148A(d), notice under section 148 was issued on 02.04.2022 - Whether since limitation prescribed under erstwhile provisions of section 149 expired on 31.03.2022, whereas notice under section 148 was issued only on 02.04.2022, impugned notice issued under section 148 on 02.04.2022 for Assessment year  2015-16  was barred by limitation under section 149 (as amended by Finance Act, 2021) and therefore liable to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 10] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, an individual, did not file a return under section 139(1) for AY 2015-16. Information on the INSIGHT/NMS portal showed interest income of about Rs. 0.86 lakh and sale of an immovable property for about Rs. 1.22 crores. Proceedings under section 148A were initiated and, after an order under section 148A(d), notice under section 148 was issued on 02.04.2022. In response, on 26.02.2024, the assessee filed a return declaring total income of about Rs. 9.02 lakhs, including LTCG of about Rs. 7.44 lakhs and claiming deduction under section 54F.

■

During reassessment, the AO sought supporting documents; noting that no sale deed, inheritance proof, cost/improvement evidence, or proof of section 54F investment was furnished and that the original return under section 139(1) was not filed, the AO completed assessment under sections 143(3) r.w.s. 144B and 147 by treating the entire sale consideration of about Rs. 1.22 crores as STCG, denying indexation and section 54F.

■

On appeal, the CIT(A) upheld the validity of the reassessment and sustained the addition, recording that the assessee did not furnish requisite evidences.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The Tribunal has carefully considered the rival submissions and perused the material available on record. Substantial force is found in the legal ground raised by the assessee challenging the validity of the reassessment proceedings. It is an undisputed fact that for Assessment Year 2015-16, the limitation prescribed under the erstwhile provisions of section 149 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 expired on 31.03.2022, whereas the notice under section 148 was issued only on 02.04.2022. In view of the first proviso to section 149 inserted by the Finance Act, 2021, no notice under section 148 could have been issued for AY 2015-16 after 31.03.2022 where such notice had already become time-barred under the erstwhile provisions of the Act. [Para 8]

■

The above legal position now stands conclusively settled by the Supreme Court in ITO v. Sai Kumar Mateti (Civil Appeal No. 6922 of 2026, arising out of SLP (Civil) No. 8682 of 2024, decided on 04-05-2026). The Supreme Court, while considering reassessment notices pertaining to AY 2015-16, categorically held that such notices would be barred by limitation in light of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal ([2024] 167 taxmann.com 70; 469 ITR 46; 301 Taxman 238 (SC); 2024 SCC OnLine SC 2693). The Supreme Court observed that where the reassessment proceedings pertain to AY 2015-16, the notices are liable to be struck down outrightly as being time-barred. [Para 9]

■

that only two days of “surviving time” were available (28.06.2021 to 30.06.2021) and, therefore, the notice dated 28.07.2022 was barred by limitation.

■

The revenue on the other hand argued that since assessee did not reply, the Assessing Officer had 30 days under section 148A to complete the proceedings and notice dated 28.07.2022 was within time.

HELD: ■ The Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC) explaining the ratio laid down in similar judgment of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/444 ITR 1/286 Taxman 183 (SC) wherein the Supreme Court had exercised its discretionary jurisdiction under article 142 of the Constitution of India while explaining the old law and new law under section 148, has created a legal fiction and balancing act on the existing legal framework of procedure of reassessment. Wherever the notice under section 148 were issued under the old regime for which time limit was extended up to 30-6-2021, the Apex Court held that it would be deemed that reassessment notice issued under the old regime shall be treated as show-cause notice issued under section 148A(b) of the new regime. Further the Court directed the revenue to provide all the relevant material/information to the assessee and thereafter, allowed the assessee to respond to the show-cause notice and raised its objection or availing any kind of defenses including available under section 149. Thus, the Supreme Court balanced the equities between the revenue and the assessee by giving effect to the legislative scheme of reassessment as contained under the new regime. The Court thus supplemented the existing legal framework of the procedure of reassessment under the Income-tax Act with the principles grounded in equitable standards. [Para 7]

■

Thus, the Supreme Court had explained the concept of surviving or balance time limit which is to be calculated by computing number of days between dates of issuance of deemed notice and 30-6-2021. Thereafter, the Supreme Court has elaborated the effect of the legal fiction propounded in the case of UOI v. Ashish Agarwal which has been explained. [Para 8]

■

The sequitor of the aforesaid observation and the judgment of the Supreme Court are that-

■

Firstly, exclusion of the period has been explained;

(a)

the date of issuance notice under section 148 under the old regime reckoned to be the date of issuance of the deemed notices under section 148A(b);

(b)

the period from the date of the issuance of the deemed notices till the supply of relevant information and material by the assessing officers to the assessees is to be excluded from the computation of the period of limitation;

(c)

further, period of two weeks granted to the assessee to reply to the show-cause notice is also to be excluded in terms of third proviso to section 149;

■

Secondly, once the response of the assessee to the showcause notice has been received, then "the clock starts ticking for the Revenue", that is, after the receipt of reply, the Assessing Officer has to;

(a)

consider the reply of the assessee under section148A(c);

(b)

take a decision under section148A(d) based on the available material and the reply of the assessee; and

(c)

issue a notice under section148 if it was a fit case for reassessment.

■

Once it is found to be a fit case for re-assessment, the limitation clock starts ticking and it is mandatory for the Assessing Officer to comply with these procedures within the surviving time limit which was available to the Assessing Officer to issue re-assessment notice under section148 of the new regime; and

■

Lastly, the Supreme Court has given an example as how to calculate the surviving time. Calculation of surviving time has been laid down from the period when the first notice u/s.148 was issued under old regime till the last date of limitation for issuance of notice under section148 of the old regime; and that period has been reckoned as the surviving time period left for the Assessing Officer while issuing notice under section148 under the new regime. So whatever surviving time is left the Assessing Officer has to issue notice within that surviving time.[Para 9]

■

If the surviving time like here in this case is only two days, because original notice under section 148 under the old regime was issued on 28-6-2021 and the last date on which notice could have been issued under old regime was up till 30-6-2021; and therefore, the surviving time left was only two days for issuing a notice under the new regime under section 148 after completion of the procedure laid down under section 148A(b) to 148(d).

■

Ergo, the Assessing Officer was required to issue notice under section 148 of the new regime within the time surviving under the Income-tax Act read with TOLA and any notices issued beyond the surviving period was declared to be time barred by the Supreme Court. [Para 10]

■

In compliance with the directions issued by the Supreme Court in the case of Ashish Agarwal (supra), the Assessing Officer provided information and material to the assessee on 20-5-2022. The assessee was granted two weeks’ time to respond to the said notice i.e. by 2-6-2022. [Para 10]

■

According to section 149, period of six years from the end of relevant assessment year i.e. from 2013-14, got expired on 31-3-2020 and further time period was extended by the Taxation and Other Law Act, 2020 (TOLA) till 30-6-2021. [Para 10.1]

■

The next round of litigation arose before the Supreme Court, and in the landmark judgment of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70 (SC), it was held that notices issued under the erstwhile section 148 for assessment years 2013-14 and 2014-15 shall be deemed to be valid, provided they fall within the permissible time frame (surviving period) as preserved under the directions laid down in the said judgment. The Supreme Court, in the case of Rajeev Bansal, has elaborated upon the concept of the ‘surviving period’ for determining the validity of notices issued under section 148 after the pronouncement of the judgment in Union of India v. Ashish Aggarwal (supra). This interpretation is specifically discussed in the said judgment. The period from the date of the issuance of the erstwhile notice till 4-5-2022, the date on which the Supreme Court had rendered the decision in Ashish Agarwal (supra) is required to be excluded. Additionally, the time provided till the date of providing the material, which should have accompanied a notice under section 148A(b), as well as the time available to the assessee to respond to the said notice was also required to be excluded. The ‘surviving period’ is required to be computed and separately added to determine the validity of the notice issued under section 148. The surviving period is calculated by taking into account the number of days between the original date of issuance of the deemed notice under section 148 and 30-6-2021, as clarified in judicial pronouncements following the judgment in Ashish Agarwal and considering the entire facts of the case and the law laid down by the Apex court in the case of UOI v Rajeev Bansal (supra), it is opined that in the instant case the surviving period was of twenty four days and the revised timeline for issue of notice under section 148 (under the new regime) expired on 26-6-2022 and the notice issued in the instant case on 25-7-2022, is clearly barred by limitation and the impugned reassessment proceedings dated 23-5-2023, passed under section 147 read with section 144 (with 144B), is not legally valid and the same is quashed. [Para 10.2]

■

The arguments of the revenue revolved around the decision of the Apex court in the case of Union of India v. Ashis Agarwal (supra), and he has never concentrated on the next round of litigation in the case of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal (supra) where it was held that notices issued under the erstwhile section 148 for assessment year 2013-14 and 2014-15, shall be deemed to be valid, provided they fall within the permissible time frame (surviving period) as preserved under the directions laid down in the said judgment (specially paragraph 108 of the said decision (already discussed above). The remaining case laws relied upon by the revenue are factually different and does not relate to the issue at hand. [Para 11]

■

Since the appeal of the assessee is allowed on the legal issue, the grounds of appeal on merits do not require any adjudication (more so considering the fact that the assessee has already withdrawn the grounds of appeal on merits in course of hearing). [Para 12]

FACT: The deceased assessee was a partner of a firm which was later dissolved and the land which the assessee got as his share was compulsorily acquired by the Government. The income arising out of the compensation received was exigible to capital gains tax for the assessment year 1975-76. The assessee, who died in the year 1978, had not filed his return for the year 1975-76. The Assessing Officer issued notices under section 148 to one of the three legal heirs on the ground that due to failure of the assessee to file return under section 139, income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment. The Assessing Officer issued two notices under section 148 simultaneously on 27-3-1984. One of the notices was served on 30-3-1984 by affixation and the other, sent by registered post, was served on 3-4-1984. As no return was filed and notice under section 142(1) was also not responded to, the assessment was completed on 30-3-1989 under section 144. The assessee’s case was (i) that the assessment was not valid as notice was not issued to all the legal heirs, (ii) that as the notice under section 148 was served on him on 30-3-1989, the assessment made on 30-3-1989 was hit by limitation under section 153(2)(a) and (iii) that the notice was bad in law as it had been served on him after the expiry of the period of 8 years as per the provision of section 149(1)(a)( i). The first appellate authority held that the assessment should have been completed by 31-3-1988 in view of the provisions of section 153(2)(a) and, therefore, completion of the assessment on 30-3-1989 was barred by limitation. Accordingly, he cancelled the order of assessment.

HELD: As regards the point of commencement of limitation, a plain reading of the provisions contained in clause (i) of sub-section (1)(a) of section 149 conveys the message that the relative adjective ‘that’ used in that provision has reference to the words ‘assessment year’ used in the opening lines of sub-clause (i). It suggests that the period of eight years is to commence from the end of the relevant assessment year. Nowhere in section 149(1)(a)(i ) has the term ‘financial year’ been used The position has been made clear by the use of the same term ‘assessment year’ in both sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) of section 151. It is, thus, abundantly clear that the prescribed period of eight years or 16 years, as the case may be, is to be reckoned from the end of the relevant assessment year and not the financial year.

FACT: For the assessment year 1987-88, the assessee’s return of income was due to be filed on 31-7-1987, but it was not filed even till 25-10-1988, when a notice under section 148 was issued. In response to the said notice, the assessee filed its return on 30-3-1989, and the assessment was completed on 22-8-1990 under section 143(3) read with section 147(a). The assessee appealed against the assessment order contending that the assessment officer was not competent to issue the notice under section 148 until the limitation for filing the return under section 139(4) expired and as such the return filed on 30-3-1989. even after the service of notice under section 148, was to be treated as a return under section 139(4) and the notice under section 148 was non est in law. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that as there was no valid return before the notice was issued, the notice under section 148 was valid and upheld the assessment order.

On second appeal, the assessee reiterating its earlier arguments, contended (i) that the notice under section 148 was invalid; and (ii) that the return filed in response to such notice was to be treated as a return under section 139(4), and hence, the assessment completed on 22-8-1990 was barred by limitation.

HELD: As regards the validity of notice issued under section 148, the first condition laid down in section 148(1) for issuance of notice is that it should be issued before making assessment, re-assessment and re-computation of income. In the instant case, the notice under section 148 was issued on 25-10-1988 and the assessment was completed on 22-8-1990. Thus, the notice issued under section 148 was valid as it was issued before the assessment was made. Then, according to the provisions envisaged and limitation laid down in section 149(1), no notice under section 148 would be issued in cases falling under clause (a) of section 147 for the relevant assessment year if eight years had elapsed from the end of that year. In the instant case, the relevant assessment year was 1987-88 and 8 years from the end of that year would elapse in 1996. But the notice under section 148 was already issued on 25-10-1988 and was, therefore, well within the prescribed time limit of eight years, i.e., before 31-3-1990. The assessee’s contention that the notice under section 148 issued prior to 31-3-1990 could not take the right of the assessee to file the return under section 139(4) was also not tenable as, in the instant case, no return was furnished before the issuance of notice under section 148. Moreover, there was no provision in the Act to invalidate the notice under section 148 by furnishing of return after the issue of such notice.

The very concept of income-tax assessment is that the assessee is taxed by the department based on the returns filed by the assessee. Section 2 of the Act provides 'definitions'. Section 2(8) defines 'assessment includes reassessment'. Thus the very meaning of the assessment provided under the Act includes reassessment also. Thus, the reassessment is not a separate concept and it is included within the meaning of the assessment under section 2(8). Thus, an assessment and reassessment are part and parcel of the procedures and therefore, there cannot be any doubt in respect of the power of reassessment provided under the Act. [Para 77]

The Income Tax Department may not be aware of the income of the individual assessees. They are assessing the tax based on the returns filed by the respective assessees. Thus, the very concept of assessment is that the Officer who is scrutinising the returns did not aware of the income of an individual. For this reason only Act provides adequate power to deal with the cases, where there is evasion or suppression or otherwise by the assessees. The very source of assessment is the returns filed by the assessee concerned. Only after the filing of the returns, the Department of Income Tax came to understand that the income of the person concerned. Thus, the reassessment may arise on several occasions and on several grounds. The Income Tax Department may receive informations from many other sources. The Income Tax Department may get some external materials as well as from various other sources. It is the process of investigation. On receipt of such materials or informations from various other sources, in such circumstances, the authorities must be in a position to reopen the assessment and impose tax. In the absence of any such lucid provision, enabling the Department reopening a case, there is a possibility of escapement of payment of tax by large number of assessees. The very nature of the Act is to ensure that the informations and the materials collected or received from various other sources are also dealt with by the Department of Income Tax appropriately and with reference to the provisions of the Act. [Para 78]

It is now well settled that the ITO cannot issue a notice under section 148 in order to reopen the assessment of an assessee in a case where the right to reopen the assessment was barred under the 1922 Act on the date when the 1961 Act came into force, that is, 1-4-1962. Thus, in the instant case, the assessment could have been reopened only by 31-3-1959. As the notice to reopen the assessment was issued on 26-11-1965, it was bad in law and without jurisdiction.

2. In view of the provisions of section 34(1) of the 1922 Act, the limitation of eight years, however, stands extended if the escaped income exceed Rs. 1 lakh. This may be either for the year for which action is proposed to be taken or for that year and any other year or years after which, or after each of which, eight years have elapsed. Hence, the provision clearly lays down that the aggregation for the purposes of finding out the escaped income could be for the year for which the action was proposed or for that year and the years preceding it. Such aggregation could not be permitted in regard to the years subsequent to the year for which action was sought to be taken. Accordingly, in the instant case, the aggregation could have been allowed for 1948-49 or 1949-50, but not in respect of the years following 1950-51.

3. Having regard to the facts and findings recorded by the Tribunal and in view of the legal proposition that any alleged escaped income for any year subsequent to 1950-51 could not have been taken into consideration, it was only a futile attempt on the part of the department to seek the production of the confidential record at the stage of the Tribunal. Thus, there was no disputed fact involved so as to take out the case from the ambit of section 154.

4. Accordingly, the Tribunal was justified in holding that the reassessment constituted a mistake apparent from record which could be rectified under section 154 and it was, therefore, justified in cancelling the order under section 154 passed by the ITO.

■ Therefore, reliance by the authorities on the order dated 23-9-2021 passed by the Supreme Court is incorrect and misplaced. The said order was passed by the Supreme Court taking suo moto cognizance of the difficulties that might be faced by the litigants in filing petitions/applications/suits/appeals/all other proceedings within the period of limitation prescribed under the general law of limitation or under any special laws and exclusion of time/extension of time was allowed in such cases. Exclusion/extension of time was also allowed where any law prescribed period of limitation for instituting proceedings, outer limits (within which the Court or Tribunal can condone delay) and termination of proceedings by the Court or Tribunal. There is no merit in the contention of the revenue that limitation of two years would apply from the end of the financial year in which the notice under section 148 was issued pursuant section 153(2) as it stood on the date of issue of the notices under section 148 and not the curtailed period of one year consequent to the amendment made by the Finance Act, 2001. The proviso to sub-section (9) of section 153 as it stood at the time when the writ petitions were disposed of by the High Court expressly stipulated completion of reassessment in accordance with the provisions of section 153 as it stood immediately before its substitution by the Finance Act, 2016 in cases where notice under section 148 had been issued prior to 1-6-2016 and the reassessment had not been completed by such date because of stay granted by the Court. Section 153(2) as it stood immediately before its substitution by the Finance Act, 2016 specified one year from the end of the financial year in which the notice under section 148 was served as the time limit for passing the order of the reassessment. Time of two years up to 31-3-2002 was granted only in respect of notices served during the financial year 1999-2000. After the amendment with effect from 1-6-2001, in no other case did the statute grant two years' time from the end of the financial year in which the notice under section 148 was served for completion of reassessment. It is well settled that the law relating to limitation is procedural and applies to pending cases. In the instant case, the amended law of limitation expressly provides how limitation in pending cases is to be determined and no other view can be taken. [Para 14]

HELD: ■

Similar issue pertaining to the challenge of notice issued under section 148 for the assessment year 2015-16, on the ground that the same was beyond the limitation period prescribed under section 149 was decided in favour of the taxpayer in various cases by following the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. According to revenue, reply by the assessee is not within the permissible period of two weeks as provided by the aforesaid judgments and therefore provisions of section 148A(d) which provides for a period of 30 days is to be taken into account for passing the order under section 148A(d) and issuing notice under section 148. [Para 6.1]

■

In the light of these arguments, first specific observations made by the Apex Court in its judgment of Rajeev Bansal (supra) was to be noted wherein it explained the purpose of creating the legal fiction, supplementing the existing legal framework of procedure of reassessment and exercising its discretionary jurisdiction under article 142 of the Constitution of India. It states that purpose is to strike a balance between the rights of the assessees and the revenue, to avoid any further appeals by the revenue on the same issue and to give effect to the legislative scheme of reassessment under the new regime by modifying the procedure of reassessment with a remedy, grounded in equitable standards. [Para 7]

■

The Apex Court while propounding its judgment in Rajeev Bansal (supra) elaborately analysed and discussed about the legal fiction it created, its consequences, incidental or inevitable corollaries, inhibition faced by the Assessing Officers from performing their responsibility under section 148A. The Court also noted that ''…The effect of creating the legal fiction is that this Court has to imagine as real all the consequences and incidents that will inevitably flow from the fiction.'' Thus, to give logical effect to the legal fiction and modified procedure, it brought out the concept of ''exclusion period'' and ''surviving time limit''. [Para 7.1]

■

At this juncture, it is important to note that legal framework of procedure for reassessment under Act created by the Supreme Court through its judgments in Ashish Agarwal and Rajeev Bansal (supra), is a fiction by deeming the notice issued under section 148 of the old regime as a show cause notice under section 148A(b) of the new regime on which modified procedure is to be applied to give it a logical effect. Hence, the modified procedure is to be applied strictly for the purpose to be achieved, as already stated and extracted above. It is a well-established principle of interpretation that the courts must give full effect to a legal fiction by having due regard to the purpose for which the legal fiction is created. A legal fiction is created for a definite purpose and it should be limited to the purpose for which it is enacted or applied. [Para 7.2]

■
