HEADNOTE: Section 148 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Reassessment - Notice for - Assessment year 1984-85 - Whether simply preparing notice under section 148 but keeping it on file past limitation period does not tantamount to issuing same, and, thus, such notice is bad in law - Held, yes

FACT: The Assessing Officer completed assessment under section 143(3) for the assessment year 1984-85 on 15-5-1985. Subsequently he wanted to rectify the order. Hence, reasons were recorded by him on 12-10-1988 and the notice under section 148 was prepared on the same day, but it was served on the assessee sometime in November 1989. The reassessment was later completed. The Commissioner (Appeals) cancelled the reassessment as the notice was beyond the time-limit permissible under section 149(1)(a)( i).

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: In the instant case, the reasons were recorded on 12-10-1988. The notice was also made out on the same day. However, there was nothing on record to show that the same was issued by 31-3-1989. All the judicial authorities unequivocally point out that the notice should actually be set in motion for being served on the assessee. Simply preparing the notice but keeping it on file past the limitation period did not tantamount to issuing the same. In the case of CIT v. Sheo Kumari Debi [1986] 157 ITR 13/ 24 Taxman 77 , the Patna High Court quoting from Chamber’s Twentieth Century Dictionary, observed that the relevant meanings of the word ‘issue’ are : act of sending out; to put forth; to put into circulation; to publish; to give out for use. Thus keeping the notice on file after preparing it does not fit into any of these meanings to be described as ‘issued’. After issuing it as described above, it is immaterial when it is served. It may be served even after three years, but the essence is that it should be set into motion for being served. And, the onus to show that it is so issued lies on the department, who in the instant case, had failed to do so.

The revenue’s contention that once the notice was made out, the process of setting it into motion was presumed, was certainly rebuttable.

In the instant case, the glaring facts themselves demolished the presumption laid down in section 114 of the Evidence Act that all official acts are regularly performed. The notice was made out more than five months before the period of limitation was to expire, but was served on the assessee about thirteen months after it was prepared.

The original records of the department did not show that the notice was despatched before 31-3-1989. Under these circumstances, normal presumption would be that the notice must have been set into motion for being served only a few days before 9-11-1989. In the ultimate analysis, just as ‘issue’ and ‘service’ are held not to be synonymous by most of the courts, including the Apex Court, the words ‘preparation’ and ‘issue’ are also not synonymous.

Therefore, the notice under section 148 was bad in law, and the Commissioner (Appeals)’s order called for no interference.

The Assessing Officer reopened assessment for relevant assessment year by issue of notice under section 148 on 24-2-1993 on ground that assessee had created provision towards unexpired warranty out of sale proceeds; thereby had suppressed sale to that extent; and, thus, income had escaped assessment. However, no action was taken by him. Again he issued notice under section 148 on 13-10-1995 for the same reason and on the basis of said notice, completed assessment under section 143(3)/147 on 31-3-1997. On appeal, the assessee contended that reassessment made was barred by limitation, as the Assessing Officer did not make any assessment with reference to notice issued on 24-2-1993. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that section 153(2) did not bar an assessment on the basis of second notice, as the second initiation was an independent action and, therefore, the Assessing Officer was justified in reopening of assessment by issue of notice dated 13-10-1995.

On second appeal, the assessee submitted that the Assessing Officer had not taken any action on notice issued on 24-2-1993. Therefore, he was satisfied that there was no escapement of income, and issue of second notice was a change of opinion. The assessee further submitted that when notice under section 148 dated 13-10-1995 was issued, no fresh information came into possession of the Assessing Officer and, therefore, the assessment framed was bad in law.

of the President on 28-9-1996. The Act omitted the words ‘not being less than 30 days’ from section 148 with effect from 1-4-1989. When notice dated 1-10-1993 and the fresh notice dated 28-3-1996 were issued, the Finance Act (No. 2) was not in force. The assessing authority had, therefore, rightly applied the then existing law. [Para. 5] Section 148 provides for initiation of assessment proceedings which starts with the issue of notice. Initiation of proceedings by the assessing authority on 1-10-1993 was not valid and consequently it was dropped. Fresh notice was, therefore, issued under section 148 in conformity with the time prescribed under section 148. When the Finance Act was passed a legally valid proceeding was in existence. Notice prescribed under section 148 for the purpose of initiating reassessment proceedings is a condition precedent to the validity of an assessment made. The assessing authority was only curing the defect of not following the time-limit when it was pointed out by the assessee and, therefore, notice was issued strictly on the basis of the then existing statutory provision. The mere fact that the time-limit prescribed under section 148(1) was taken away would not make an invalid notice valid so as to render the assessment order dated 26-3-1997 invalid in terms of section 153(2). The assessee could not be allowed to raise such a plea after having persuaded the assessing authority to withdraw notice dated 1-10-1993 pointing out that it was not in conformity with the statutory provision. The assessee could not be allowed to take advantage of the plea of limitation in terms of section 153(2) contending that the notice dated 1-10-1993 was valid due to the omission of time-limit vide the Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 with effect from 1-4-1989. [Para 6]

On the strength of notice dated 28-3-1996, the return of income was filed and such return could not be ignored. [Para 7]

The mere fact that the time-limit has been taken away with effect from 1-4-1989 would not vitiate the proceedings validly initiated applying the then existing law. The object and purpose of the amendment is only to take away the time-limit for giving time for the assessee to file a return which the Legislature thought unnecessary. If the Legislature wanted to undo all that was done by the assessing authority applying the then existing law, it should have been specifically provided in the statute. In the absence of specific provision in the Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 invalidating those proceedings initiated by the ITO, it could not be said that the action taken by the ITO applying the then existing law was invalid. FACT: For the assessment year 1987-88, the assessee’s return of income was due to be filed on 31-7-1987, but it was not filed even till 25-10-1988, when a notice under section 148 was issued. In response to the said notice, the assessee filed its return on 30-3-1989, and the assessment was completed on 22-8-1990 under section 143(3) read with section 147(a). The assessee appealed against the assessment order contending that the assessment officer was not competent to issue the notice under section 148 until the limitation for filing the return under section 139(4) expired and as such the return filed on 30-3-1989. even after the service of notice under section 148, was to be treated as a return under section 139(4) and the notice under section 148 was non est in law. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that as there was no valid return before the notice was issued, the notice under section 148 was valid and upheld the assessment order.

On second appeal, the assessee reiterating its earlier arguments, contended (i) that the notice under section 148 was invalid; and (ii) that the return filed in response to such notice was to be treated as a return under section 139(4), and hence, the assessment completed on 22-8-1990 was barred by limitation.

HELD: As regards the validity of notice issued under section 148, the first condition laid down in section 148(1) for issuance of notice is that it should be issued before making assessment, re-assessment and re-computation of income. In the instant case, the notice under section 148 was issued on 25-10-1988 and the assessment was completed on 22-8-1990. Thus, the notice issued under section 148 was valid as it was issued before the assessment was made. Then, according to the provisions envisaged and limitation laid down in section 149(1), no notice under section 148 would be issued in cases falling under clause (a) of section 147 for the relevant assessment year if eight years had elapsed from the end of that year. In the instant case, the relevant assessment year was 1987-88 and 8 years from the end of that year would elapse in 1996. But the notice under section 148 was already issued on 25-10-1988 and was, therefore, well within the prescribed time limit of eight years, i.e., before 31-3-1990. The assessee’s contention that the notice under section 148 issued prior to 31-3-1990 could not take the right of the assessee to file the return under section 139(4) was also not tenable as, in the instant case, no return was furnished before the issuance of notice under section 148. Moreover, there was no provision in the Act to invalidate the notice under section 148 by furnishing of return after the issue of such notice.

The notice under section 148 for all the relevant assessment years was served upon the assessee on 7-12-1964. After having repeatedly sought time for filing the returns of income for those three years in compliance with the said notice, the assessee filed the returns on 15-3-1965. However, period to that, the assessee had filed the writ petition challenging the validity of the said notice and the High Court had stayed all further proceedings for all the assessment years on 12-3-1965. The said stay order was vacated on 25-7-1975, when the writ petition was dismissed. Thereafter, the assessee was allowed eight weeks time in two instalments to enable it to file an appeal from the said order of the High Court dismissing the writ petition. The assessment proceedings were thus stayed during the period from 12-3-1965 to 18-9-1975. The High Court again stayed the proceedings on 29-9-1975, in the appeal filed against the order dismissing the writ petition and disposed of the appeal with the direction that the respondents would, however, be at liberty to proceed with the reassessment but the final orders, if any, and notice of demand would not be served on the petitioner pending disposal of this application. The said order of the High Court stood vacated on 12-7-1979, when the appeal was dismissed and, thereafter, the assessee filed a special leave petition before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held that all further proceedings in respect of the three purported draft orders of assessment should go on but final orders should not be passed. That order of the Supreme Court stood vacated on 4-8-1980, when the special leave petition was dismissed. During the assessment proceedings, the draft assessment order was forwarded by the ITO to the IAC on 17-9-1979, the copy of which was received by the assessee on 19-9-1979, and the directions of the IAC after hearing the objections of the assessee were communicated to the ITO on 14-10-1980. The ITO completed the assessments for all the three years on 15-10-1980. The assessee contended that all the assessment orders were bad since they were barred by limitation. However, this contention was rejected.

INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed against order of High Court that where Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 148 on basis of information that assessee had entered into transaction of Rs. 62.77 crores in form of inward and outward remittances, since assessee had produced all details of foreign remittance during course of regular assessment, impugned notice issued on change of opinion and only on borrowed satisfaction without there being any fresh tangible material was quashed and set aside

The case as put forth by the revenue was that the Commissioner (Appeals) had erred in quashing the order by holding that the re-assessment order passed under section 147 read with section 148 dated 30-12-2008 was invalid. The contention of the revenue was that the Tribunal's decision dated 11-7-2008 for block period from 1-4-1990 to 3-11-2000 had not become final and the High Court vide its order had granted liberty to the revenue to issue fresh notice if they wanted to do so and hence, the issue regarding validity of notice under section 148 pending with the subordinate judicial authorities was merged with the order of the High Court and as such fresh notice under section 148 dated 8-1-2008 issued by the Assessing Officer was in accordance with law. On the other hand, the assessee had submitted that the Commissioner (Appeals) had correctly quashed the notice in question as the notice was clearly time barred as per the provisions of the Act. [Para 4]

After cogitating the material available on record, it was held that the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) were correct and no interference was called for. The reasons were manifold. It was an undisputed and admitted fact that the directions given by the Commissioner (Appeals) under section 150 had been quashed by the Tribunal and they no longer survived. Under section 150, a notice under section 148 may be issued at any time for the purpose of making an assessment or re-assessment or recomputation in consequence of or to give effect to any finding or direction contained in an order-passed by any authority in any proceedings under this Act by way of appeal, reference or revision (or by a Court in any proceeding under any other law). Sub-section (2) of section 150 qualifies the first clause which permits re-assessment in pursuance of an order on appeal etc. [Para 5]

From the provisions of section 150, it was clear that the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 150 would not apply, in any case where any such assessment etc., in respect of which an assessment, re-assessment or re-computation would not have been made at the time the order which was the subject matter of the appeal, reference or refund, as the case may be, was made by reason of any other provision limiting the time within which any action for assessment, re-assessment or recomputation may be taken. That clearly showed that the period of limitation as provided under section 149 would always be available and even the direction given under section 150 could not enlarge the scope of limitation. [Para 6]

From the perusal of section 149, it was clear that time limit for issuance of notice under section 148 has been provided in the given circumstances of a case. It was an open secret that the direction given by the Commissioner (Appeals) to reopen the assessment order already completed, as per law had been quashed by the Tribunal and hence, it no longer survived. The order passed by the High Court, whereby permission to issue fresh notice under section 148 had been given, was definitely subjected to section 149. The High Court had not enlarged and could not enlarge the scope of limitation. The limitation is not a contractual obligation but is a statutory necessity which prohibits filing of appeals or the revision after a certain period with the aim to attain finality in regard to disputed and contested issues raised by way of appeals, etc. The High Court had given liberty to issue notice as per law which meant that if the notice fulfilled the other conditions laid down in the Act, the Assessing Officer could issue notice, afresh. Otherwise also, the very section 147 empowers the Assessing Officer to initiate re-assessment action in respect of escaped income within the prescribed lime, and no authority can stop him for doing so. But the question in instant case was different. In instant case, after striking down the directions of the Commissioner (Appeals) by the Tribunal the liberty was granted by the High Court only for issuance of notice under section 148 which the Assessing Officer otherwise possesses. The reasons recorded were the same and identical on the basis of which action under section 147/148 was initially initiated. So, on the basis of same reasons which had already been quashed by the Tribunal, notice issued under section 148 would not survive. When the particular direction/liberty had been quashed by the Tribunal such a direction no longer survived. There was no question of merger of authority as had been stated and contended by the revenue. There is no provision in law to take action under section 147 under the direction of any authority or Court. For the foregoing reasons, the appeal of the revenue could not be allowed and hence, dismissed. The action of the Commissioner (Appeals) stood approved. [Para 7]

Resultantly, the appeal of the revenue stood dismissed [Para 8]

We now come to the various decisions relied on by the learned Counsel for the assessee and at the out set we would refer to the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Mahendra’s case (supra) where the relevant facts were that on 5th January, 1962, the Income-tax Officer issued a notice to the assessee under section 34(1)(a) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 to reopen his assessment for the assessment year 1946-47. The Hon’ble High Court quashed the notice vide its order dated 6th March,

1963 on the ground that the notice was barred by limitation. In the meantime the Income-tax Act, 1961 came into force on 1st April, 1962 and thereafter the Income-tax Officer once again issued a notice on 26th March, 1963 under section 148 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. On the matter travelling to the Hon’ble Supreme Court at the instance of the assessee, their Lordships held that though the proceedings on the basis of the notice dated 5th January, 1962 under the 1922 Act were quashed for the reason that the notice was issued beyond time, it could not be said that no proceedings under section 34 of the 1922 Act were either factually or legally pending at the time when the 1961 Act came into force. That since the proceedings initiated under section 34 of the 1922 Act were pending at the time when the 1961 Act came into force, the Income-tax Officer was not competent to issue any fresh notice under section 148 of the 1961 Act. FACT: The deceased assessee was a partner of a firm which was later dissolved and the land which the assessee got as his share was compulsorily acquired by the Government. The income arising out of the compensation received was exigible to capital gains tax for the assessment year 1975-76. The assessee, who died in the year 1978, had not filed his return for the year 1975-76. The Assessing Officer issued notices under section 148 to one of the three legal heirs on the ground that due to failure of the assessee to file return under section 139, income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment. The Assessing Officer issued two notices under section 148 simultaneously on 27-3-1984. One of the notices was served on 30-3-1984 by affixation and the other, sent by registered post, was served on 3-4-1984. As no return was filed and notice under section 142(1) was also not responded to, the assessment was completed on 30-3-1989 under section 144. The assessee’s case was (i) that the assessment was not valid as notice was not issued to all the legal heirs, (ii) that as the notice under section 148 was served on him on 30-3-1989, the assessment made on 30-3-1989 was hit by limitation under section 153(2)(a) and (iii) that the notice was bad in law as it had been served on him after the expiry of the period of 8 years as per the provision of section 149(1)(a)( i). The first appellate authority held that the assessment should have been completed by 31-3-1988 in view of the provisions of section 153(2)(a) and, therefore, completion of the assessment on 30-3-1989 was barred by limitation. Accordingly, he cancelled the order of assessment.

On the revenue’s appeal:

HELD: As regards the point of commencement of limitation, a plain reading of the provisions contained in clause (i) of sub-section (1)(a) of section 149 conveys the message that the relative adjective ‘that’ used in that provision has reference to the words ‘assessment year’ used in the opening lines of sub-clause (i). It suggests that the period of eight years is to commence from the end of the relevant assessment year. Nowhere in section 149(1)(a)(i ) has the term ‘financial year’ been used The position has been made clear by the use of the same term ‘assessment year’ in both sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) of section 151. It is, thus, abundantly clear that the prescribed period of eight years or 16 years, as the case may be, is to be reckoned from the end of the relevant assessment year and not the financial year.

FACT: ■

The Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 148 for assessment year 2014-15 on 28-6-2021. The said notice was unsustainable as it was issued in accordance with the statutory regime as existed prior to 31-3-2021. Some High Courts struck down notices that were issued under section 148 after 31-3-2021 but under the unamended provisions relating to the re-assessment of income that had escaped assessment.

■

The revenue appealed the decisions rendered by various High Courts to the Supreme Court of India. In Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC)which was one of such appeals arising from the decision of the Allahabad High Court - the Supreme Court delivered its decision on 4-5-2022, whereby it concurred with the view that the amended provisions which came into force after 31-3-2021 would be applicable to notices issued thereafter.

■

However, the Supreme Court also issued certain directions in exercise of powers under article 142 of the Constitution of India. The Court directed that all notices that were issued under section 148 after 1-4-2021 till the date of the said decision (4-5-2022), including those that had been set aside by the High Courts, would be construed as show cause notices under section 148A(b).

■

The Assessing Officers were directed to provide the information and material relied upon by the revenue for issuance of such notices, to the respective assessees within a period of thirty days from the date of the decision so as to enable the respective assessees to respond to the same.

■

In compliance with the directions issued by the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal (supra), the Assessing Officer provided information and material to the assessee on 30-5-2022. The assessee was granted two weeks' time to respond to the said notice.

■

The assessee responded to the notice dated 30-5-2022 on 11-6-2022. The Assessing Officer passed an order under section 148A(d) on 31-8-2022. According to the assessee, the same was beyond the period as stipulated.

■

On writ:

HELD: ■

In the instant case, the period of six years from the end of the assessment year for issuing a notice under section 148 expired on 31-3-2021. Consequently, the time limit for issuing such a notice was extended to 30-6-2021. The original assessment for the relevant assessment year was made in 1952. In 1966, the ITO issued notice under section 148 to reopen the assessment for the relevant assessment year that was originally completed in 1952. The assessee filed a return and revised return under protest claiming that no income had escaped assessment and that the notice under section 148 was illegal and barred by time. On writ, the Single Judge held that according to the affidavit filed by the department, the escaped income in the case was more than Rs. 1 lakh and since in respect of the escaped income of over a lakh of rupees the Act of 1922 did not prescribe any period of limitation, the reopening was not barred under the old Act. The Single Judge, however, held that since the department had not disclosed material on the basis of which the ITO could form the belief that there had been omission or failure on part of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts, it could not be said that the belief was held by the ITO in good faith.

INCOME TAX: Where High Court upheld Tribunal's order setting aside reassessment proceedings on ground that addition made in said proceedings was beyond scope of section 147, read with section 148, SLP filed against said order was to be dismissed

■

The assessee filed a writ petition under Article 226 challenging the reassessment notice dated 30.06.2022 issued under section 148 for AY 2017-18 as invalid and time barred. The respondents were the AO and the Income Tax Department.

■

The AO had earlier issued a notice under section 148 on 11.06.2021 for AY 2017-18 during the extended period under TOLA. Pursuant to the Supreme Court directions in Ashish Agarwal, the said notice was to be treated as a notice under section 148A(b). The AO supplied information on 17.05.2022, allowing 15 days to respond, making the reply due on 01.06.2022. The petitioner submitted its reply on 30.05.2022. The AO thereafter passed an order under section 148A(d) and issued a fresh notice under section 148 on 30.06.2022.

■

Considering the limitation under the Act read with TOLA and the Supreme Court directions, the last permissible date to issue the notice under section 148 was 18.06.2022.

■

On writ petition before the High Court.

A notice under section 148 has to be issued when an assessment, reassessment or recomputation is made under section 147 to tax income which has escaped assessment. The instant case was not a case of reassessment nor a case of recomputation. It was a case of an assessment without there being an earlier assessment.

Under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, originally there was no time limit for completion of assessment until the amendment made in 1939 and Courts have held that the notice under section 34 was not required to be served if the proceedings were pending on either the assessee filing the return suo moto or by issuance of notice under section 22 (equivalent to section 142 of the Income-tax Act. 1961). After the introduction of the time limit for completing the assessments under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the proceedings could be said to be pending during the period starting from the date of filing of the return by the assessee suo moto or issuance of notice under section 142 by the Assessing Officer up to the lime limit prescribed to complete the assessment under section 153, i.e., two years from the end of the assessment year in which the income was first assessable.

Explanation 2(a) to section 147 includes non-filing of return in the expression ‘escaped assessment’. However, the scope of Explanation 2(a) to section 147 has to be restricted to the failure of the assessee to file a return suo moto or a voluntary return under section 139(1) or section 139(4) within the prescribed time limit and cannot be extended to cases where a notice under section 142(1) requiring the assessee to file return has already been issued. The requirement of ‘where no return of income has been furnished by the assessee’, as appearing in the Explanation, for treating it as a case of ‘income escaping assessment’, has to be seen on the expiry of the period within which the assessee can file the return. Otherwise, even on the first day of the assessment year, i.e., on 1-4-1991 itself, the Assessing Officer can issue notice under section 148 when the process of assessment itself has not yet come into being. It would, thus, be too wide a proposition to be accepted.

As regards the outer limit of issuing notice under section 142(1)(i ), there is apparently no time limit prescribed, but if one reads the other provisions, it can be deduced there from. A reading of section 139(4) gives an impression that the outer limit to furnish return is one year from the end of the assessment year. Otherwise, the assessees failure to submit the return under section 142(1) would not entitle him to file the return thereafter. Therefore, the issuance of notice under section 142(1) has to be before that period, i.e., 31-3-1992 in the instant cases. Once that time limit is over and the assessee has not filed any return, it becomes a case of income escaping assessment and for that issuance of notice under section 148 is a must. The time limit prescribed for completing assessment as per section 153 is 2 years from the end of the assessment year in which it was first assessable. However, this time limit comes into play when the proceedings for assessment have been initiated by filing a return suo moto under section 139(1) or by issuance of a valid notice under section 142(1).

In view of the Supreme Court’s decision in the case of CIT v. Narsee Nagsee & Co. [1960] 40 ITR 307 , the position insofar as income-tax is concerned is that the income escapes assessment the moment the assessment year is over if no proceedings have been initiated during the assessment year itself.

In the light of these arguments, first specific observations made by the Apex Court in its judgment of Rajeev Bansal (supra) was to be noted wherein it explained the purpose of creating the legal fiction, supplementing the existing legal framework of procedure of reassessment and exercising its discretionary jurisdiction under article 142 of the Constitution of India. It states that purpose is to strike a balance between the rights of the assessees and the revenue, to avoid any further appeals by the revenue on the same issue and to give effect to the legislative scheme of reassessment under the new regime by modifying the procedure of reassessment with a remedy, grounded in equitable standards. [Para 7]

■

The Apex Court while propounding its judgment in Rajeev Bansal (supra) elaborately analysed and discussed about the legal fiction it created, its consequences, incidental or inevitable corollaries, inhibition faced by the Assessing Officers from performing their responsibility under section 148A. The Court also noted that ''…The effect of creating the legal fiction is that this Court has to imagine as real all the consequences and incidents that will inevitably flow from the fiction.'' Thus, to give logical effect to the legal fiction and modified procedure, it brought out the concept of ''exclusion period'' and ''surviving time limit''. [Para 7.1]

■

At this juncture, it is important to note that legal framework of procedure for reassessment under Act created by the Supreme Court through its judgments in Ashish Agarwal and Rajeev Bansal (supra), is a fiction by deeming the notice issued under section 148 of the old regime as a show cause notice under section 148A(b) of the new regime on which modified procedure is to be applied to give it a logical effect. Hence, the modified procedure is to be applied strictly for the purpose to be achieved, as already stated and extracted above. It is a well-established principle of interpretation that the courts must give full effect to a legal fiction by having due regard to the purpose for which the legal fiction is created. A legal fiction is created for a definite purpose and it should be limited to the purpose for which it is enacted or applied. [Para 7.2]

■

On the contention of revenue that since assessee did not furnish its response within the stipulated time of two weeks to the show cause notice issued by the Assessing Officer on 26-5-2022, it is out of the purview of the judgments of Rajeev Bansal (supra), one cannot ascribe to the same since Apex Court very categorically laid down the law on pan India applicability from its judgment in Ashish Agarwal and Rajeev Bansal (supra) to include ninety thousand reassessment notices issued under the old regime during the period from 1-4-2021 to 30-6-2021. Instant case of the assessee unhesitatingly falls well within the purview of both the judgments. [Para 8]

1. It is now well settled that the ITO cannot issue a notice under section 148 in order to reopen the assessment of an assessee in a case where the right to reopen the assessment was barred under the 1922 Act on the date when the 1961 Act came into force, that is, 1-4-1962. Thus, in the instant case, the assessment could have been reopened only by 31-3-1959. As the notice to reopen the assessment was issued on 26-11-1965, it was bad in law and without jurisdiction.

2. In view of the provisions of section 34(1) of the 1922 Act, the limitation of eight years, however, stands extended if the escaped income exceed Rs. 1 lakh. This may be either for the year for which action is proposed to be taken or for that year and any other year or years after which, or after each of which, eight years have elapsed. Hence, the provision clearly lays down that the aggregation for the purposes of finding out the escaped income could be for the year for which the action was proposed or for that year and the years preceding it. Such aggregation could not be permitted in regard to the years subsequent to the year for which action was sought to be taken. Accordingly, in the instant case, the aggregation could have been allowed for 1948-49 or 1949-50, but not in respect of the years following 1950-51.

3. Having regard to the facts and findings recorded by the Tribunal and in view of the legal proposition that any alleged escaped income for any year subsequent to 1950-51 could not have been taken into consideration, it was only a futile attempt on the part of the department to seek the production of the confidential record at the stage of the Tribunal. Thus, there was no disputed fact involved so as to take out the case from the ambit of section 154.

4. Accordingly, the Tribunal was justified in holding that the reassessment constituted a mistake apparent from record which could be rectified under section 154 and it was, therefore, justified in cancelling the order under section 154 passed by the ITO.

It is trite law that the issue of a notice under section 148 is a condition precedent to the validity of any assessment under section 147, and, therefore, if no such notice is issued or if the notice issued is invalid or vague or is not served in accordance with law, the assessment would be bad. Assessing authority had not followed the time-limit prescribed while notice under section 148 was issued on 1-10-1993. The assessee filed his return of income on 27-3-1995. The assessee had also pointed out to the ITO that in the notice dated 1-10-1993 which was issued under section 148, the assessee was not given the statutory minimum period of time for filing the return of income. The law that was in force at the relevant point of time cast a statutory duty on the assessing authority to give minimum 30 days’ time. The Assessing Officer cancelled the notice when it was pointed out to him and, therefore, notice under section 148 was issued on 28-3-1996. Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 enacted by the Parliament and received the assent of the President on 28-9-1996. The Act omitted the words ‘not being less than 30 days’ from section 148 with effect from 1-4-1989. When notice dated 1-10-1993 and the fresh notice dated 28-3-1996 were issued, the Finance Act (No. 2) was not in force. The assessing authority had, therefore, rightly applied the then existing law. [Para. 5]

Section 148 provides for initiation of assessment proceedings which starts with the issue of notice. Initiation of proceedings by the assessing authority on 1-10-1993 was not valid and consequently it was dropped. Fresh notice was, therefore, issued under section 148 in conformity with the time prescribed under section 148. When the Finance Act was passed a legally valid proceeding was in existence. Notice prescribed under section 148 for the purpose of initiating reassessment proceedings is a condition precedent to the validity of an assessment made. The assessing authority was only curing the defect of not following the time-limit when it was pointed out by the assessee and, therefore, notice was issued strictly on the basis of the then existing statutory provision. The mere fact that the time-limit prescribed under section 148(1) was taken away would not make an invalid notice valid so as to render the assessment order dated 26-3-1997 invalid in terms of section 153(2). The assessee could not be allowed to raise such a plea after having persuaded the assessing authority to withdraw notice dated 1-10-1993 pointing out that it was not in conformity with the statutory provision. The assessee could not be allowed to take advantage of the plea of limitation in terms of section 153(2) contending that the notice dated 1-10-1993 was valid due to the omission of time-limit vide the Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 with effect from 1-4-1989. [Para 6]

On the strength of notice dated 28-3-1996, the return of income was filed and such return could not be ignored. [Para 7]

The mere fact that the time-limit has been taken away with effect from 1-4-1989 would not vitiate the proceedings validly initiated applying the then existing law. The object and purpose of the amendment is only to take away the time-limit for giving time for the assessee to file a return which the Legislature thought unnecessary. If the Legislature wanted to undo all that was done by the assessing authority applying the then existing law, it should have been specifically provided in the statute. In the absence of specific provision in the Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 invalidating those proceedings initiated by the ITO, it could not be said that the action taken by the ITO applying the then existing law was invalid. Once the notice issued under section 148 on 28-3-1996 was upheld the plea of limitation raised by the assessee under section 153(2) had to be rejected. The Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 as amended would not validate an invalid notice which was issued under section 148(1). [Para 9]

We have heard the learned departmental representative and the counsel for the assessee. The departmental position so far as the assessment years 1957-58 to 1959-60 on the one hand, and 1960-61 on the other hand, is clearly contradictory. Admittedly, the first notice under section 148 was never served on the assessee or her power of attornery holder. [1977] 110 ITR 36 that the limitation under section 148 is only to the issuance of a notice and there is no limitation as to the service of the notice. Therefore, the ITO could have proceeded to serve the notice afresh under section 148
for the four years on the assessee's agent and to have made the reassess-ments. That the ITO failed to do so. Reassessment made for the assessment year 1960-61 without service of notice on the assessee or on her agent is, therefore, totally invalid and unsustainable in law. The order of the AAC annulling that order of the assessment is, therefore, upheld.

9. So far as the assessment years 1957-58 to 1959-60 are concerned, the position is more or less similar. The proceedings were pending before the ITO after he reopened the ex parte assessments under section 146 and it was incumbent on the ITO to have served the notice on the assessee to make the reassessment. The ITO failed to do so. While those proceedings were pending he submitted a proposal to the Beard to reopen the assess-ments. Strangely enough, even in the Board the proposal does not seem to have been scrutinised and the approval to reopen the assessment was mechanically given because if the proposal had been scrutinised properly, it would have been noticed that the proceedings on the basis of an earlier notice under section 148 were still pending. When proceedings legally and validly started for reassessment were pending, fresh notice under section 148 cannot be issued because it cannot be said that income liable to tax had escaped assessment. Therefore, on this basis alone the reopen- ing of the assessment under section 148 under the authority of the approval granted by the CBDT had to be annulled because proceedings on the basis of an earlier notice under section 148 issued by the ITO were then pending. We, accordingly, uphold the orders of the AAC in all the three years. In view of this finding it is not necessary to go into the merits and to consider whether or not there was a material for reopening the assessments and whether or not the income escaped assessments exceeded Rs. 50,000 in each of these years to justify the Board to exercise its power. The order of the AAC for all the four years are, accordingly, upheld.

FACT: ■

The assessee, engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of steel products, filed its return of income for relevant assessment year 2014-15 on 31-7-2014.

■

The Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 148 on 29-7-2022, followed by assessment order dated 30-5-2023 along with consequential demand and penalty proceedings.

■

In instant writ petition, the assessee contended that re-opening of assessment was barred by limitation under section 149 as amended by Finance Act, 2021 and, even after applying relaxations under TOLA.

HELD: ■

The Finance Act, 2021 substituted the entire scheme of reassessment under sections 147 to 151 with effect from 1-4-2021. [Para 7]

■

Prior to the coming into force of Finance Act, 2021 initiation of reassessment proceedings was governed by the provisions of sections 147 to 151. [Para 8]

■

Despite the substituted sections 147 to 151, by the Finance Act, 2021 which came into force on 1-4-2021 many reassessment notices under section 148 were issued to the assessees after coming into force of Finance Act, 2021 i.e. after 1-4-2021, which were assailed before different High Courts on different grounds. Different High Courts quashed the reassessment notices under section 148. Union of India challenged the judgments passed by different High Courts setting aside reassessment notices under section 148, which were issued after 1-4-2021 i.e. after coming into force of Finance Act, 2021 before the Supreme Court in Union of India and Others v. Ashish Aggarwal [2022] 140 taxmann.com 1 (SC). The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeals filed by the Union of India. [Para 9]

■

Therefore, in above referred to judgment of the Supreme Court in case of Union of India and Others v. Ashish Aggarwal (supra), the Supreme Court held that the impugned notices under section 148 issued to the respective assessees which were issued under unamended section 148 and were subject matter of writ petitions before the various respective High Courts shall be deemed to have been issued under section 148A as substituted by the Finance Act, 2021 and be construed or treated to be show cause notices in terms of section 148A(b). It was further held that the Assessing Officer shall, within 30 days from the date of passing of the judgment i.e. 4-5-2022, provide to the respective assessees information and material relied upon by the revenue, so that the assessees can reply to the show cause notices within 2 weeks thereafter. It was further held by the Supreme Court that the requirement of conducting any enquiry, if required, with the prior approval of specified authority under section 148A(a) is dispensed with as one time measure viz-a-viz those notices which were issued under section 148 of the unamended act from 1-4-2021 (Finance Act, 2021) till date i.e. 4-5-2022 (Decision in Ashish Aggarwal). Further that the Assessing Officer shall thereafter pass orders in terms of section 148A(d) in respect of each of the concerned assessees and thereafter, after following the procedure as required under section 148A may issue notice(s) under section 148 (as substituted). [Para 10]

In R.K. Upadhyaya v. Shanabhai P. Patel [1987] 166 ITR 163, the Supreme Court categorically held that a clear distinction has been made out under the Income-tax Act, 1961 between 'issue of notice' and 'service of notice'. Section 149 prescribes the period of limitation. It prohibits issue of notice under section 148 after the expiry of the prescribed period of limitation. Section 148(1) provides for service of notice as condition precedent to making of the order of assessment. Once a notice is issued within the period of limitation, jurisdiction becomes vested with the ITO to proceed to reassess. The requirement of issue of notice is satisfied when a notice is actually issued Section 148(1) deals with making of the reassessment and mandates that reassessment shall not be made until there has been service. Under the Act, service is not a condition precedent to conferment of jurisdiction on the ITO to deal with the matter but it is a condition precedent to the making of the order of assessment.

In the Instant case, notice under section 148 was issued by the ITO within the period of limitation prescribed under section 149. There was also no controversy about the fact that the order of reassessment was made only after service of notice on the assessee. The ratio of the decision in R.K. Upadhyaya's case (supra ) of the Supreme Court squarely applied to the present case. The ITO having issued the notice under section 148 within limitation, the order of reassessment was valid. Therefore, the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the initiation of reassessment proceedings by the ITO was barred by limitation and in setting aside the orders of the AAC and the ITO.

During the course of proceedings before us, the learned AR reiterated the arguments as taken before the learned CIT(A). 6. It was submitted that as per section 153(2) of the Income-tax Act, no order of re-assessment shall be made after the expiry of one year from the end of financial year, in which, the notice under section 148 was served. If the services of notice is regarded as being the same as on date of issue that is 25-3-2003, then the time for completing the assessment would have been expired on 31-3-2004. However, the assessment order has been passed on 30-3-2005. The learned AR submitted that under section 27 of General Clauses Act, the word 'serve', give, send all are used. As per the decision of the Apex Court in the case of Banarsi Debi ( supra) all these words are interchangeable words. It means that they convey the same idea. In a limited sense, the word 'issue' may also means sent. The intention of section 147 would be effectuated, if a wider meaning is given to the word 'issued'. In the context of 1922 Act, the Supreme Court in Banarsi Debi's case (supra) held that the word 'issued' shall have to be held as served. In that case, notice was served beyond the period of limitation, since, it was issued prior to that date, the Apex Court held that issuance should be regarded as equivalent to serve. On the basis of this judgment, the learned AR argued that services of notice under section 148 should be taken as the date, on which, the notice was issued, i.e., 25-3-2003. The time limit for completion of assessment should be linked from such date. The law draws a time-frame within which an action by AO has to be completed. It cannot be said that the assumption of jurisdiction should happen by one who yardstick and the time for completion should be judged by another yardstick. It was argued that the time-limit should be linked from the date of assumption of jurisdiction. The learned AR further drew our attention to the decision of the Apex Court in the case of R.K. Upadhyaya v. Shanabhai P. Patel [1987] 166 ITR 163, in which, it was held that services is not a condition precedent to conferment of jurisdiction, on the ITO. It is condition precedent only to the making of the order of the assessment. The learned AR pointed out that the decision of the Apex Court is a very short one and the assessee was not represented in that case. In that case ratio of the Supreme Court decision in the case of Banarsi Debi ( supra) was not followed. It was, therefore, submitted that decision of Supreme Court in the case of R.K. Upadhyaya ( supra) is, therefore, regarded as per incuriam. The learned AR submitted the decision of R.K. Upadhyay's case (supra) is by two-member Bench while the decision in the case of Banarsi Debi (supra) is by three member Bench.

7. On the other hand, the learned DR submitted that the word 'issued' under section 153(2) cannot be equated to be 'served'. The Legislature has used the words 'issue' and 'serve' and it was clear to the Legislature that these two words have different meanings. The learned DR, therefore, argued that the time-limit for completion of assessment should be considered from the date of services of notice under section 148. In the instant case, notice under section 148 was served on 4-4-2004 and, therefore, the assessment have been completed within the time limit prescribed under section 153(2) of the Income-tax Act.

"Section 153(2).—No order of assessment, reassessment or re-computation shall be made under section 147 after the expiry of one year from the end of the financial year in which the notice under section 148 was served :—

Provided that where the notice under section 148 was served on or after the 1-4-1999 but before the 1st day of April, 2000, such assessment, reassessment or re-computation may be made at any time up to 31st day of March, 2002."

The petitioner [Assessee] has filed the present petition, inter alia, impugning a notice dated 31.08.2022 [the impugned notice] issued under Section 148 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 [the Act] in respect of the Assessment Year [AY] 2014-15. It is the Assessee's case that the impugned notice has been issued beyond the prescribed period of limitation.

2. The initial notice under Section 148 of the Act for AY 2014-15 was issued on 28.06.2021. The said notice was unsustainable as it was issued in accordance with the statutory regime as existed prior to 31.03.2021. This court in the case of Mon Mohan Kohli v. Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax [2021] 133 taxmann.com 166/[2022] 441 ITR 207 (Delhi)/Neutral Citation No.: 2021:DHC:4181-DB had set aside such notices that were issued after 31.03.2021 without following the procedure as prescribed under Section 148A of the Act. Some of the other High Courts also took a similar view and struck down notices that were issued under Section 148 of the Act after 31.03.2021 but under the unamended provisions relating to the re-assessment of income that had escaped assessment

3. The Revenue appealed the decisions rendered by various High Courts to the Supreme Court of India. In Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC)/2022 SCC OnLine SC 543 - which was one of such appeals arising from the decision of the Allahabad High Court - the Supreme Court delivered its decision on 04.05.2022, whereby it concurred with the view that the amended provisions which came into force after 31.03.2021 would be applicable to notices issued thereafter. However, the Supreme Court also issued certain directions in exercise of powers under Article 142 of the Constitution of India. The Court directed that all notices that were issued under Section 148 of the Act after 01.04.2021 till the date of the said decision (04.05.2022), including those that had been set aside by the High Courts, would be construed as show cause notices under Section 148A(b) of the Act. The Assessing Officers were directed to provide the information and material relied upon by the Revenue for issuance of such notices, to the respective assessees within a period of thirty days from the date of the decision so as to enable the respective assessees to respond to the same.

4. In compliance with the directions issued by the Supreme Court in the case of Ashish Agarwal (supra), the Assessing Officer [AO] provided information and material to the Assessee on 30.05.2022. The Assessee was granted two weeks' time to respond to the said notice. The Assessee responded to the notice dated 30.05.2022 on 11.06.2022.

5. The AO passed an order under Section 148A(d) of the Act on 31.08.2022. According to the Assessee, the same was beyond the period as stipulated.

6. In the present case, the period of six years from the end of the assessment year for issuing a notice under Section 148 of the Act expired on 31.03.2021. Thus, in terms of Section 149 of the Act, a notice under Section 148 of the Act could not be issued. However, the said period was extended by the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 [TOLA]. Consequently, the time limit for issuing such a notice was extended to 30.06.2021. The original notice under Section 148 of the Act was issued on 28.06.2021, which was two (2) days before the expiry of the period of limitation.

The only issue which arises for consideration (and that too concerning assessment year 2016-17 and 2017-18) is whether the impugned order passed under section 148A(d) and the consequent notice issued under section 148 of the amended 1961 Act [as obtaining with the enactment of FA 2021], falls foul of the limitation prescribed in clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 149? [Para 25]

Section 149(1) of the amended 1961 Act mandates that no notice under section 148 would be issued for the relevant assessment year if three (03) years have elapsed from the end of the said assessment year. The Assessing Officer can take recourse to the extended limitation period if the conditions precedent prescribed in clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 149 are fulfilled. In other words, in a case where three (03) years from the end of the relevant assessment year have elapsed, the Assessing Officer can issue a notice under section 148 provided the conditions prescribed in clause (b) of section 149(1) of the amended 1961 Act are fulfilled. [Para 26]

A careful perusal of clause (b) of section 149 would show that one of the conditions for triggering the extended period, which goes up to ten (10) years in cases where three (03) years have elapsed, is that income chargeable to tax which has escaped assessment amounts to, or is likely to amount to Rs. 50 lakhs or more for the assessment year in issue. [Para 27]

Therefore, after the coming into force of FA 2021, in cases where, for the relevant assessment year, the alleged escaped income was less than Rs. 50 lakhs, notice under section 148 could only be issued for commencement of reassessment proceedings within the limitation period provided in clause (a) of section 149(1) of the amended 1961 Act. [Para 28]

Thus, in the ordinary course, the limitation for assessment year 2016-17 would expire on 31-3-2020; likewise, for assessment year 2017-18, the end date for the culmination of the limitation period would be 31-3-2021. [Para 29]

The Notification immediately following the said Notification, i.e., Notification dated 27-4-2021, extended the end date to 30-6-2021. Thus, the span concerning the extension of end dates was spread between 20-3-2020 and 30-6-2021. [Para 30.1]

It is, therefore, the revenue's case that the impugned actions, which involved passing of orders under section 148A(d) and issuance of notices under section 148 taken between 1-4-2021 (when FA 2021 kicked in) and 30-6-2021 were valid in the eyes of the law. [Para 31]

Briefly, the Supreme Court was called upon to grapple with a piquant situation, which was the creation of the revenue, concerning the viability of notices issued on or after 1-4-2021, when FA 2021 had already kicked in. [Para 32.1]

The Supreme Court noticed that with the enactment and enforcement of FA 2021, sections 147 to 149 and section 151, as they stood on 31-3-2021, had been substituted, bringing about radical and reformative changes in the matters concerning reassessment proceedings. Taking cognizance of this state of affairs, the Supreme Court held that, since the new provisions substituted by FA 2021 were both remedial and benevolent, they would apply to past Assessment years provided section 148 notices had been issued on or after 1-4-2021. This was also the view taken by various High Courts; a view which was sustained by the Supreme Court. [Para 32.2]

The Supreme Court, however, having regard to the fact that the procedure prescribed under the new regime (which was encapsulated in FA 2021) had not been followed, modified the judgments of the High Courts by issuing specific directions to balance the interests of the assessees and the revenue. [Para 32.3]

Applying the ratio laid down in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64 /[2022] 286 Taxman 183 /[2022] 444 ITR 1 (SC)/(2023) 1 SCC 617 and Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/469 ITR 46/301 Taxman 238 (SC), particularly, in the light of the limitation for issuance of notice under section 148 prescribed under section 149 read with section 151, it is clear that the notice that was issued after 1-4-2021 under the old regime as it stood till 31-3-2021 has to be treated as a notice under section 148A(b) under the new regime. [Para 8]

■

The time during which the aforesaid notice issued under section 148 under the old regime as it stood till 31-3-2021 were deemed to be stayed from the date of issuance between 1-4-2021 and 30-6-2021 till the supply of relevant information and material by the Assessing Officers to the assessees in terms of the directions issued by this Court in Ashish Agarwal case (supra), and for a further period of two weeks for the assessees to respond to the Show Cause Notices as confirmed by Rajeev Bansal case (supra). [Para 9]

■

A notice under section 148 was required to be issued for reassessment within the time limit surviving under the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) [TOLA] Act, 2020. For the assessment year 2016-17, since the income escaping assessment is less than Rs. 50 lakhs, the notice under section 148 ought to have been issued on 31-3-2020. However, by virtue of TOLA extensions, the said date has been extended up to 30-6-2021. [Para 12]

■

In the light of the ratio in Ashish Agarwal case (supra) and Rajeev Bansal case (supra), the notice issued under section 148 under the old regime on 30-6-2021 is deemed to have been stayed for thirty days for the Income Tax Department to provide to the respective assessees information and material relied upon and two weeks thereafter for the assessees to reply to the Show Cause Notices. [Para 13]

■

In the instant case, notice under section 148 under the old regime itself was issued on the last date of limitation viz., 30-6-2021, after the exclusions i.e., excluding the thirty days and fourteen days time period granted by the Supreme Court there is no further time available for the Assessing Officer to issue Notice under section 148 under the new regime barring the seven days as provided under the fourth proviso to section 149 as amended with effect from 1-4-2021. [Para 14]

■

Therefore, after accounting for all the exclusions, the Assessing Officer in the instant case had no time left for issuance of Notice under section 148 under the new regime. However, applying the fourth proviso to section 149 as amended with effect from 1-4-2021, the Assessing Officer had seven days to issue a Notice under section 148 under the new regime. [Para 15]

■

Thus, the notice under section 148 ought to have been issued within seven days from the date of reply given by the assessee on 3-6-2022. In other words, the notice ought to have been issued on or before 10-6-2022. [Para 16]

■

However, in the instant case, the notice under section 148 under the new regime was issued only on 28-7-2022. [Para 17]

■

Thus, the proceedings initiated on 30-6-2021 which were later substituted by a notice under section 148A(b) dated 20-5-2022 which culminated in the impugned order passed under section 148A(d) dated 28-7-2022 and notice issued under section 148 dated 28-7-2022 are to be held to be beyond time. [Para 18]

■

In view thereof, this writ petition challenging these two proceedings deserve to be allowed and is accordingly allowed. [Para 19]

within the period of limitation, jurisdiction becomes vested in the Income-tax Officer to proceed to reassess. Section 148(1) provides for service of notice as a condition precedent to making the order of assessment. Service under 1961 Act is not a condition precedent to conferment of jurisdiction on the ITO; it is a condition precedent only to the making of the order of assessment. It was held that the notice was not barred by limitation and the ITO had jurisdiction to complete the assessment. 25. In CIT v. Sheo Kumari Devi [1986] 157 ITR 13/24 Taxman 77 (Pat.)(FB) Hon'ble Patna High Court has occasion to examine the difference between the words "issued" and "served". The words "issued" and "served" are not synonyms. Their plain dictionary meaning runs directly contrary to any such assumption. The gap between the two may be wide both in point of time and place. A statute may require that the issuance of a general order be conveyed by publication in the locality without individual service. The word "issue" is to be construed in the context of section 149, which is an express limitation provision creating a precise bar with regard to reopening of assessments. In sub-section (3) of section 149 the word "employed" is "served" in the first line while in the penultimate line the word "employed" is "issued". Thus in the same short sub-section, the Legislature had used these words as distinct and separate. The hallmark of a limitation provision is that the same must have clear-cut and fixed termini at both ends. Section 149 fixed the terminus a quo from the end of the relevant assessment year i.e., on the 31st March of the said year. On the other hand, the terminus ad quem under clauses (a) and (b) is fixed at 4 years, 8 years and 16 years from the fixed date of 31st March of the relevant assessment year. Clearly enough, if the terminus a quo is fixed as the relevant assessment year, namely, 31st March of the said year the other terminus must equally be fixed with regard to the fixed date of issuance of the notice, which is precise and predictable. The plain scheme of sections 148 and 151 is that the satisfaction and the sanction of the Commissioner or the Board on the reasons recorded by the ITO is necessary before the notice under section 148 is sent out. If the word "issued" used in both these sub-sections is read as "served", it will lead to the strange phenomenon that even after the Income-tax Officer has recorded his reasons and issued the notice, the sanction may, therefore, be recorded before its service on the assessee. A decision is only an authority for what it actually decides, and the quintessence thereof is its ratio and not every observation found therein nor what logically follows from various observations made in it. The Supreme Court in Banarsi Debi v. ITO [1964] 53 ITR 100 further observed that a strange and wide meaning of the word "issue" in order to save the Income-tax (Amendment) Act, 1959, from being rendered nugatory. They did not even remotely considered section 149 of the 1961 Act. Consequently, Hon'ble Patna High Court has held that Banarsi Debi's case (supra) is no warrant for the abstruse proposition that the word "issued" de hors its context must always mean "issued" and "served" in every statute or in section 149 of the Act.

26. Thus from the decisions of Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of R.K. Upadhyaya (supra) and Hon'ble Patna High Court in the case of Sheo Kumari Devi (supra) the law is settled that term "issue" appearing in section 149 of the Act cannot mean as "issue and serve". The jurisdiction becomes vested in the Assessing Officer to assess/reassess the escaped income the moment the notice under section 148 is issued. Service under the Act is not a condition precedent to conferment of jurisdiction on the Assessing Officer but a condition precedent only to the making of the order of assessment. Therefore the contention of Ld. CIT (DR) that without service of notices under section 148 the Assessing Officer is not vested with the power to assess/reassess the escaped income and assessment proceedings were jeopardized holds no water and deserves to be rejected.

" is unsustainable in law for the following reasons:

(a)

The law does not support the travel back in time theory propounded by the revenue. Such theory is neither borne out from the decision rendered by the Supreme Court in Ashish Agarwal's case nor does it have any roots in the provisions of the 1961 Act as amended by FA 2021. As a matter of fact, TOLA also does not support this theory.

(b)

Contrary to the revenue's submission, TOLA has created no such legal fiction which would allow the notices issued under section 148, which were issued in and about May-June 2022, to be treated as having been issued on or before 31-3-2021, to calculate the period of limitation prescribed in Section 149(1)(a) of the 1961 Act. [See Keenara Industries (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2023] 147 taxmann.com 585/453 ITR 51 (Guj.)/2023 (3) TMI 104 (Gujarat High Court); Rajeev Bansal v. Union of India [2023] 147 taxmann.com 549/453 ITR 153 (All.)/2023 (2) TMI 1081 (Allahabad Court) and Mon Mohan Kohli (Delhi High Court) paras 86 to 89]

(c)

The Instruction dated 11-5-2022 issued by the CBDT, which states in paragraph 6.1 that the extended reassessment notices would travel back in time to their original date when such notices were issued, provides no clarity as to what that "original date" would be.

(d)

The fallacy in the revenue's stand is that while it wishes to travel back in time by applying the period of limitation available prior to FA 2021 coming into force, it simultaneously seeks to apply the amended provisions. Therefore, if the unamended provisions are applied, the end date for expiration of limitation for AYs 2016-17 and 2017-18 would be 31-3-2023 and 31-3-2024, respectively. In such a situation, TOLA would have no application, contrary to what is contended by revenue, as it applied to compliances and proceedings whose limitation expired between 20-3-2020 and 31-3-2021.

(e)

The decision of the Supreme Court rendered in Ashish Agarwal's case clearly mandated that post 31-3-2021, the new regime, as encapsulated in FA 2021, would apply. There was no reference in the said judgment to the travel back theory propounded on behalf of the revenue. All that the Supreme Court indicated in the said judgment that Section 148 notices issued between 1-4-2021 and 30-6-2021 would be treated as notices under section 148A(b), i.e., the new regime. No suggestion was made in the Supreme Court's decision that the impugned notices issued under section 148 would be deemed as having been issued before 31-3-2021, as per the unamended provisions. As is evident upon perusal of the judgment of the Supreme Court, its direction to treat Section 148 notices as notices issued under the new regime was to quell the possibility of reassessment proceedings failing, even where they were viable under FA 2021. [See paragraph 8 of the judgment]

(iv)

The directions contained in the judgment of the Supreme Court in Ashish Agarwal's case, while exercising its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution, were issued keeping the aforesaid object in mind while specifically holding that all defences would be available to the assessees. Thus, notices issued on or before 31-3-2021 will be governed by the old regime, while those issued on or after 1-4-2021 must be aligned with the new regime. Accordingly, all those notices issued between 1-4-2021 and 30-6-2021 stood converted to notices issued under section 148A(b) of the new regime and were, thus, subject to the amended Section 149 of the 1961 Act.

The Supreme Court also held that applying this principle to test whether a notice under Section 148 is issued within the period of limitation one would have to give effect to the terms of the first proviso to Section 149(1)(b). The first proviso to Section 149(1)(b) enacts that a notice issued after 1 April 2021 has to be issued within such time as was permissible under the unamended Section 149(1)(b). Thus, for Assessment Year 2014-15, the notice under Section 148 under the unamended section provisions could have been issued in terms of Section 149(1)(b) by 31 March 2021. On this basis, Counsel urged that as the impugned notice is dated 27 July 2022, the same is beyond the period of limitation. It was further submitted that the Supreme Court thereafter held that in order to construe whether the notice was issued within the period of limitation one would have to give effect to the provisions of TOLA as well as the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ashish Agarwal and the requirements of the provisos to Section 149. The Court held that during the period from the date of issuance of the deemed notice under Section 148A(b) and the date of the judgment in Ashish Agarwal (supra), [i.e. from 29th June 2021 to 4th May 2022] the Assessing Officers were deemed to have been prohibited from passing a reassessment order, and thus, the show cause notices were deemed to have been stayed by an order of the Supreme Court from the date of the issuance till 4 May 2022. The Court further extended this limitation and stated that the show cause notices were deemed to have been stayed not only upto 4 May 2022 but till the date when the Assessing Officer provided the relevant information and material to the Assessee in terms of the directions issued in its judgment in Ashish Agarwal (supra). The Court further noted that the provisos to Section 149 allows the exclusion of time allowed to an Assessee to respond to the show cause notice under Section 148A(b) to compute the period of limitation. The Hon'ble Supreme Court therefore summarized that the total time that is excluded for computation of the period of limitation within which the notice is to be issued as encompassing the time during which the show cause notices were effectively stayed, that is, from the date of the original notice under Section 148 till the supply of the relevant information or material by the Assessing Officers to the Assessee in terms of the directions in Ashish Agarwal and a further period of two weeks to allow to the Assessee to respond to the show cause notice. The effect of this conclusion of the Supreme Court was that the time surviving under the Act read with TOLA that will be available to the revenue to issue the reassessment notice under Section 148 of the new regime will have to be calculated by computing the number of days between the date of the issuance of the deemed notice, till 30 June 2021, and accordingly, the reassessment notices to be issued must be within the time limit surviving. Thus, in the present case it would be within two days of the furnishing of the reply by the Petitioner.

In absence of any saving clause, to save the pre-existing (and now substituted) provisions, the revenue authorities could only initiate reassessment proceeding on or after 1-4-2021, in accordance with the substituted law and not the pre-existing laws.

(iii) A reassessment proceeding is not just another proceeding emanating from a simple show cause notice. Both, under the pre-existing law as also under the law enforced from 1-4-2021, that proceeding must arise only upon jurisdiction being validly assumed by the assessing authority. Till such time jurisdiction is validly assumed by assessing authority - evidenced by issuance of the jurisdictional notice under section 148, no re-assessment proceeding may ever be said to be pending before the assessing authority. The admission of the revenue authorities that all re-assessment notices involved in this batch of writ petitions had been issued after the enforcement date 1-4-2021, is tell-tale and critical. As a fact, no jurisdiction had been assumed by the assessing authority against any of the petitioners, under the unamended law. Hence, no time extension could ever be made under section 3(1) of the Enabling Act, read with the Notifications issued thereunder.

(iv)

The submission of the learned Additional Solicitor General of India that the provision of Section 3(1) of the Enabling Act gave an overriding effect to that Act and therefore saved the provisions as existed under the unamended law, cannot be accepted. That saving could arise only if jurisdiction had been validly assumed before the date 1-4-2021. In the first place Section 3(1) of the Enabling Act does not speak of saving any provision of law. It only speaks of saving or protecting certain proceedings from being hit by the rule of limitation. That provision also does not speak of saving any proceeding from any law that may be enacted by the Parliament, in future. For both reasons, the submission advanced by learned Additional Solicitor General of India is unacceptable.

(v)

It may also be clarified, Section 3(1) of the Enabling Act does not itself speak of reassessment proceeding or of Section 147 or Section 148 of the Act as it existed prior to 1-4-2021. It only provides a general relaxation of limitation granted on account of general hardship existing upon the spread of pandemic COVID -19. After enforcement of the Finance Act, 2021, it applies to the substituted provisions and not the pre-existing provisions. In absence of any specific delegation made, to allow the delegate of the Parliament, to indefinitely extend such limitation, would be to allow the validity of an enacted law i.e. the Finance Act, 2021 to be defeated by a purely colourable exercise of power, by the delegate of the Parliament.

(vi)

Unless specifically enabled under any law and unless that burden had been discharged by the respondents, we are unable to accept the further submission advanced by the learned Additional Solicitor General of India that practicality dictates that the reassessment proceedings be protected. Practicality, if any, may lead to legislation. Once the matter reaches Court, it is the legislation and its language, and the interpretation offered to that language as may primarily be decisive to govern the outcome of the proceeding. To read practicality into enacted law is dangerous. Also, it would involve legislation by the Court, an idea and exercise we carefully tread away from.

49.

The first proviso to Section 149(1)(b) requires the determination of whether the time limit prescribed under section 149(1)(b) of the old regime continues to exist for the assessment year 2021-2022 and before. Resultantly, a notice under Section 148 of the new regime cannot be issued if the period of six years from the end of the relevant assessment year has expired at the time of issuance of the notice. This also ensures that the new time limit of ten years prescribed under section 149(1)(b) of the new regime applies prospectively. For example, for the assessment year 2012-2013, the ten year period would have expired on 31 March 2023, while the six year period expired on 31 March 2019. Without the proviso to Section 149(1)(b) of the new regime, the Revenue could have had the power to reopen assessments for the year 2012-2013 if the escaped assessment amounted to Rupees fifty lakhs or more. The proviso limits the retrospective operation of Section 149(1)(b) to protect the interests of the assesses.

7. A combined reading of the above observations of the Hon'ble Supreme Court and the findings of Hon'ble Delhi High Court makes it clear that the test for checking the validity of notices issued under section 148 under new regime for AYs 2021-22 or prior years is whether the period of six years has expired at the time of issue of such notice and in that case the notice under section 148 becomes invalid. These observations also makes it clear that the time limit of ten years as per the amended provisions of section 149(1)(b) can be applied only prospectively. In assessee's case when we apply this test for AY 2015-16, the period of six years has expired on 31.03.2022 and therefore the notice dated 28.07.2022 under section 148 of the Act for AY 2015-16 is invalid since it is barred by limitation.
