3. In a landmark decision by the Delhi High Court in L.R. Gupta v. UOI [1992] 194 ITR 32/[1991] 59 Taxman 305, the Court quashed the authorization for search. The brief facts of the case are that agricultural lands in Delhi of one Mr. L.R. Gupta and his family were acquired. The District Judge awarded him a sum of Rs. 28.77 crores as compensation and interest thereupon. The Gaon Sabha, the owners and the Union of India moved the Delhi High Court challenging the said award of the District Judge. The High Court allowed the assessees to withdraw the said amount on furnishing bank guarantee. The said assessees did not offer this amount as their income for the year of receipt as the matter was sub-judice and there was no ‘debt’ due nor did they have any absolute and enforceable right over the said money. They claimed that they were mere custodians of the money, which they were holding ‘in trust’ and were not liable for tax in view of the Apex Court’s decision in CIT v. Hindustan Housing & Land Development Trust Ltd. [1986] 161 ITR 524/27 Taxman 450A. The Delhi High Court on the facts and circumstances of the case held thus :

". . . It may be that the opinion of the assessee that the receipt of such amount is not taxable may be incorrect and, in law, the same may be taxable but where the department is aware of the existence of such an asset or the receipt of such an amount by the assessee, then the department may be fully justified in issuing a notice under section 148 of the act, but no action can be taken under section 132(1)(c). . . ." (p. 35)

The Court went on to say further thus :

". . . Non-filing of the return may give a right or jurisdiction to the respondents to invoke the provisions of sections 147 and 148 of the Income-tax Act in an effort to tax the same. This is not a case where money was received surreptitiously or the department did not have knowledge of the receipt of the money by the petitioners. The respondents have taken recourse to proceedings under sections 147 and 148 and the provisions of section 132(1) are not, in our opinion, a substitute for action under sections 147 and 148 of the Act. . . ." (p. 50)

Thus, where an assessee is denying its exigibility to service tax, search and seizure operations should not be resorted to but notices under sections 73 and 73B of the Finance Act, 1994 should be issued and proceedings initiated. Resort can also be made to section 74C of the Act, whereby provisional attachment can be made to protect revenue in certain cases. Interest and penalty under sections 75, 76, 77 and 78 can be levied on defaulting service providers. By resorting to search and seizure operations in such cases, the very purpose for which these provisions have been enacted shall stand frustrated. Difference in opinion as to the taxability, legally cannot give rise to search and seizure operations.

It must be an express direction necessary for the disposal of the case and one that the authority or Court is empowered to give. A mere observation or leaving it to the option and discretion of the AO to take action would not qualify as a 'direction' for the purpose of Section 150(1). The following are the relevant rulings in this regard: The Allahabad High Court in CIT v. Smt. Maya Rastogi [2010] 8 taxmann.com 253 (Allahabad), addressed the scenario where an assessment proceeding was initiated in pursuance of an award regarding compensation by the Supreme Court under the Land Acquisition Act. The Court held that such an award constituted a 'finding' recorded by a Court under 'other law' within the meaning of section 150(1), thereby confirming that there was no limitation for the issue of a notice seeking to initiate assessment proceedings.

The Mumbai ITAT in Asstt. CIT v. Dilip S. Dahanukar [2004] 90 ITD 525 (Mumbai), emphasised that it must be established beyond doubt that there is a 'finding' or 'direction' in the relevant order, and the assessment or reassessment is framed in consequence of or to give effect to such finding or direction. The ITAT held that a High Court's order merely dismissing a writ petition challenging the validity of reassessment proceedings did not contain any 'finding' or 'direction' that necessitated reassessment. This clarifies that a mere removal of a hurdle or an observation, without a specific finding or direction, does not invoke the unlimited period under section 150(1).

The Supreme Court in CIT v. Tarajan Tea Co. (P.) Ltd. [1999] 102 Taxman 697 (SC), held that an order passed by the AAC in another assessee's case was not 'information' within the meaning of section 147(b) (prior to its amendment). This indicates that while judicial pronouncements can be 'information', they must generally relate to the assessee whose income is sought to be reassessed, or at least establish a direct nexus to the escapement of income for that assessee.

In conclusion, the 'finding' or 'direction' must be a necessary and explicit part of the external court's order, directly impacting the assessee's income tax liability, and not merely an incidental observation or a general dismissal of a writ petition.

In a recent decision, the Supreme Court, in the case of Correspondence, RBANMS Educational Institution v. B. Gunashekar [2025] 173 taxmann.com 586 (SC), issued the following directions to all courts:

(a)

Whenever a suit is filed with a claim that Rs. 2 lakhs and above is paid by cash towards any transaction, the courts must intimate the same to the jurisdictional Income Tax Department to verify the transaction and the violation of section 269ST of the Income Tax Act, if any.

(b)

Whenever any such information is received either from the court or otherwise, the Jurisdictional Income Tax authority shall take appropriate steps by following the due process in law.

(c)

Whenever a sum of Rs. 2 lakhs and above is claimed to be paid by cash towards consideration for conveyance of any immovable property in a document presented for registration, the jurisdictional Sub-Registrar shall intimate the same to the jurisdictional Income Tax Authority, who shall follow the due process in law before taking any action.

(d)

Whenever, it comes to the knowledge of any Income Tax Authority that a sum of Rs. 2 lakhs or above has been paid by way of consideration in any transaction relating to any immovable property from any other source or during the course of search or assessment proceedings, the failure of the registering authority shall be brought to the knowledge of the Chief Secretary of the State/UT for initiating appropriate disciplinary action against such officer who failed to intimate the transactions.

The taxpayer is required to file the return considering the provisions of the section 153A/153C relating to assessment year falling within the period of six assessment years or for the relevant assessment year or years as referred in section 153A/153C. However, where the taxpayer's assessment is pending, due the notice already issued under section 143(2) or under section 148 of the Act and assessment is not completed up to date of search, in these circumstances the assessments pending on the date of search shall gets abate in view of the second proviso to section 153A of the said Act. Therefore, once assessment gets abated, than the assessment for such years will be made u/s 153A/153C. It is open for the AO to complete the assessment by verifying the contents of the original return as well as the income un-earthed out of the incriminating documents. Consequently, it is open for both the parties, i.e. the assessee as well as revenue to make claims for allowance or to make disallowance, as the case may be, etc. Taxpayer can lodge a new claim for deduction etc. which remained to be claimed in his earlier/regular return of income. In such a case, the return of income filed under section 153A(1) of the said Act, would be construed to be one filed under section 139(1) of the Act and the provisions of the said Act shall apply to the same accordingly and all legitimate claims would be open to the assessee to raise in the return of income filed under section 153A(1).

Subsequent proceedings following the conclusion of the CIRP will take place in the name of the Successful Resolution Applicant, who assumes control of the company. After the CIRP, the company is considered to have a 'clean slate,' meaning any prior claims, including legal proceedings or liabilities, are extinguished. As a result, the new entity is not burdened with the past Tax cases or demands of the erstwhile entity, ensuring a fresh start. Now the Question arises that after the conclusion of CIRP process some undisclosed income pertaining to the period prior to the approval of resolution plan by NCLT comes to the notice of the department then whether the department can issue reassessment notice under section 147/148. the Delhi High Court in Ireo Fiveriver (P.) Ltd. v. ITD [2024] 161.taxmann.com 772 has held that any liability other than those specified in the Resolution Plan which is pertaining to the period prior to Resolution Plan is bad in law and to be set aside. In the above case involving Section 148A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and Section 31 of the IBC, 2016 the issue arose regarding the reassessment of income for the assessment year 2017-18. The assessee, a corporate debtor, had undergone a resolution process under the IBC, and the resolution plan was approved by the NCLT on 6th August 2021. However, a reassessment notice was issued under Section 148A(d) of the Income-tax Act, which pertained to a period prior to the approval of the resolution plan. The notice for reassessment was issued without considering the legal implications of the successful resolution process. In view of decision in case of Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Ltd. v. Satish Kumar Gupta[2019] 111 taxmann.com 234 (SC) that successful resolution, the applicant could not be foisted with any liabilities other than those which were specified and factored in resolution plan and which might pertain to a period prior to resolution plan itself having been approved, impugned order dated 30-7-2022 issued under section 148A(d) was to be set aside.

Overriding effect:

Now after analysing the synergy between the IBC and the Income tax law, the question arises is which of the two has an overriding effect over the other that is whether the provisions of IBC will have an overriding effect in case there arises any conflict between the two laws.

In this regards, it is pertinent to note that Section 238 of IBC gives overriding effect over any other contrary provisions in any other laws. Section 238 establishes that if there is a conflict between the provisions of the IBC and any other law, the provisions of the IBC will prevail. This means that the IBC has overriding effect in cases of insolvency and bankruptcy, even if they are in conflict with other laws, whether they are special or general laws.

Conclusion

The treatment of tax dues under the IBC underlines the Code's core objective of reviving financially distressed companies while balancing the interests of the stakeholders. Although the classification of tax dues as operational debts has streamlined the resolution process, it also throws open the need for tax authorities to adapt to the IBC framework. Stronger cooperation between tax agencies and insolvency professionals can ensure smoother insolvency proceedings and better outcomes for all parties.

LETTER [F.NO.292/62/2012-IT (INV.III)/26]., DATED 23-4-2018

The undersigned is directed to say that the reward scheme for informants, named 'Guidelines for grant of rewards to Informants, 2007', as was issued in 2007 vide Board's letter referred above, has been revised and "Income Tax Informants Rewards Scheme, 2018" has been issued in supersession of it with effect from date of issue. Further, guidelines containing procedure to be followed by Departmental officers for implementation of the Reward Scheme is issued separately. While the "Income Tax Informants Rewards Scheme, 2018" is for public circulation, the "Guidelines for Departmental officers" is for departmental use. Copy of the revised reward scheme is enclosed herewith.

Introduction

1. In supersession of the 'Guidelines for grant of rewards to Informants, 2007' and other existing guidelines on the subject, the following new reward scheme is hereby introduced for regulating grant and payment of reward to a person who is an informant under this scheme. A person can get reward up to Rs. Five crore by giving specific information about evasion of Income tax on income and assets in India and abroad. Identity of the informant shall be kept confidential.

Short Title

1.1. This scheme shall be called "Income Tax Informants Reward Scheme 2018".

Commencement

1.2. This scheme comes into effect on the date of issue.

Scope

1.3.This scheme shall regulate the grant and payment of reward to informants in cases where information is received by a JDIT (Inv) from the informant on or after the date of issue of this Scheme that leads to detection of substantial tax evasion under the provisions of Income Tax Act, 1961 and/or the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income & Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015. This scheme shall not be applicable to information regarding recovery of irrecoverable taxes as the Central Board of Direct Taxes has issued separate Guidelines for the same vide F. No. 385/21/2015-IT (B) dated 26-8-2015.

1.3.1. However, the 'Guidelines for grant of rewards to Informants, 2007' shall continue to be applicable in cases where information was received before the date of issue of this Scheme.
